Trinimac's remains became the Changed Ones, the Orcs. The exodus founded Velothi civilization and set the religious and cultural foundations of Morrowind.
topic_desc_basic: The Velothi exodus was the migration of Aldmeri dissidents led by the prophet Veloth from Summerset to Resdayn. Boethiah revealed the Tri-Angled Truth to them and, with Mephala, taught the foundations of their new culture. This journey established Velothi civilization in Morrowind.

title: Dunmer funerary rites
topic_desc: Dunmer funerary rites center on venerating ancestors whose spirits protect and advise the living. Each household maintains a shrine, the Waiting Door, where families offer prayers and receive blessings. The paramount duty is interring remains at a City of the Dead like Necrom, where spirits find comfort. Alternatively, honored ancestors may will their bones for ghost fences, bound by solemn magic to guard clan precincts. Since the Armistice, however, most remains have been dedicated to the Great Ghost Fence at Dagoth Ur, causing private tombs and clan fences to fall into disfavor; the Temple now encourages venerating ancestor relics kept at local temples. Foreigners often mistake these practices for necromancy, an abomination to the Dunmer when performed upon elven remains.
topic_desc_basic: Dunmer funerary rites involve venerating ancestors at household Waiting Door shrines, offering prayers for guidance and protection. Traditionally, remains are interred at Cities of the Dead like Necrom, or used in clan ghost fences. Recently, most remains have gone to the Great Ghost Fence, and the Temple now encourages venerating ancestor relics at local temples. Foreigners often confuse these sacred customs with necromancy.

title: Tribunal Temple canon
topic_desc: Tribunal Temple canon comprises the orthodox doctrines and priestly writings—known as the Heirographa—governing the faith of the Dunmer. It holds that Almalexia, Vivec, and Sotha Sil achieved divine substance through superhuman virtue and supernatural insight, thereafter serving as loving ancestors and stern guardians of Morrowind. The faithful are bound to fourfold duties: Faith, Family, Masters, and all that is good, alongside charity, pilgrimage, and veneration of the saints and ancestors. However, the hidden Apographa and Dissident Priests challenge this orthodoxy, questioning the Tribunal's apotheosis by suggesting it derived from profane Dwemer tools, disputing official accounts of the Battle of Red Mountain, and condemning the Ordinators' use of terror and the hierarchy's corruption. These conflicting accounts reveal deep fractures within Temple doctrine.
topic_desc_basic: Tribunal Temple canon is the orthodox religious doctrine of the Dunmer, teaching that Almalexia, Vivec, and Sotha Sil achieved divinity through virtue and wisdom. The faithful honor these living gods, venerate ancestors and saints, and follow duties of faith, family, and charity. Dissident Priests challenge these orthodox teachings, questioning the Tribunal's apotheosis and criticizing the hierarchy's corruption.

title: Dwemer law
topic_desc: Dwemer law denotes the legal customs and codes of the Deep Elves, which scholarly analysis traces to Altmeri roots. The legal framework addressed liability and compensation, particularly regarding slaves and constructs. In the laws of Karndar Watch, if a slave killed a freeman, the owner surrendered the slave's body and paid three instruments. If an Animunculi killed a worker, the victim's associates could disassemble the construct and claim its parts within thirty days. This principle of liability for one's property or creations mirrors broader Aldmeri legal traditions, where owners bore responsibility for the actions of their dependents and beasts.
topic_desc_basic: Dwemer law encompasses the legal codes of the Deep Elves, which scholars trace to Altmeri origins. These laws addressed liability and compensation, holding masters accountable for their slaves and even their Animunculi constructs. If a construct killed a worker, the victim's associates could disassemble it for parts.

title: Dwemer freeholds
topic_desc: The Dwemer freeholds were the independent colonial city-states of the Deep Elves, each governed by its own council. Chronicles of Nchuleft, recorded in Aldmeris, details the political dynamics of these freeholds, revealing that they maintained broader assemblies such as the Council Meet at Bamz-Amschend. Rivalries between freehold leaders could turn deadly; the death of Lord Ihlendam of Nchuleft followed a bitter quarrel with Councilor Bluthanch, who was widely suspected of conjuring the creatures that ambushed him at Chinzinch Pass. These records demonstrate that the freeholds were fractious polities prone to internal intrigue and factional violence, even while sharing cultural and political institutions.
topic_desc_basic: The Dwemer freeholds were the independent city-states of the Deep Elves. Each freehold colony was governed by its own council, though they occasionally gathered for broader assemblies. Ancient chronicles reveal that these freeholds were fractious and prone to fierce rivalries, political intrigue, and factional violence among their leaders.

title: Tonal Architecture
topic_desc: Tonal Architecture is the Dwemer discipline of shaping reality through sound, vibration, and precisely ordered resonance. Its greatest known practitioner was Lord Kagrenac, High Priest and Tonal Architect of Vvardenfell. After the discovery of the Heart of Lorkhan, Kagrenac devised Wraithguard, Sunder, and Keening to study and manipulate the Heart's divine power. Dwemer accounts and later scholarship associate this work with an attempt to create a new god for the Dwemer. The entire race vanished during the Battle of Red Mountain when Kagrenac used his tools, but surviving accounts disagree over whether his experiment caused their disappearance or merely coincided with it.
topic_desc_basic: Tonal Architecture is a Dwemer discipline that uses sound and resonance to alter reality. Lord Kagrenac applied it through Wraithguard, Sunder, and Keening to manipulate the Heart of Lorkhan. The Dwemer vanished when the tools were used at Red Mountain, though the exact cause remains disputed.

title: conflicting accounts of Red Mountain
topic_desc: The Battle of Red Mountain and its aftermath remain the most fiercely contested subject in Dunmeri history. Temple doctrine, recorded in the Hierographa, holds that Nerevar died of his wounds after the Dwemer vanished, that Dagoth Ur was corrupted by the tools, and that the Tribunal later ascended to divinity through righteous devotion. The Ashlander tradition, preserved in the Apographa, claims the Tribunal murdered Nerevar using poisoned candles, robes, and invocations, then broke their oath to Azura by claiming Kagrenac's tools for their apotheosis. Even Vivec's own account to a Dissident Priest contains contradictions, acknowledging the oath was broken while denying murder. The Dunmeri transformation and Azura's promised return of Nerevar further complicate any definitive record.
topic_desc_basic: The Battle of Red Mountain ended the First Council and caused the Dwemer's disappearance. Temple doctrine states Nerevar died of wounds and the Tribunal rightfully ascended. Ashlander tradition insists the Tribunal murdered Nerevar and broke their oath to Azura. The true events remain deeply disputed.

title: Alessian Empire
topic_desc: The Alessian Empire, also called the First Empire of Cyrodiil, was established in 1E 243 after the Alessian Slave Rebellion overthrew the Ayleid Empire. Founded by Saint Alessia upon receiving the Amulet of Kings and lighting the Dragonfires, it endured for over two millennia. The zealously monotheistic Alessian Order profoundly shaped the Empire, formally enforcing its doctrines from 1E 361 and eventually wielding power rivaling the emperors. The Order's Marukhati Selective even caused the Dragon Break known as the Middle Dawn. Imperial territory fluctuated: Empress Hestra expanded reaches into High Rock and Black Marsh, while Colovian kingdoms resisted the Order's dogma. The Empire declined when internal strife within the Order prompted Colovian secession, sparking the War of Righteousness in 1E 2321. This decade-long conflict devastated the Iliac Bay and dissolved the Order, ending the Empire by 1E 2331. Cyrodiil remained divided until Reman I founded the Second Empire.
topic_desc_basic: The Alessian Empire, or First Empire of Cyrodiil, was founded by Saint Alessia in 1E 243 after overthrowing the Ayleids. Enduring over two thousand years, it was heavily defined by the monotheistic Alessian Order, which enforced strict doctrines and wielded immense power. The empire collapsed in 1E 2331 following the destructive War of Righteousness, leaving Cyrodiil divided until the rise of the Second Empire.

title: Alessian Order
topic_desc: The Alessian Order was a hugely influential, austere religious sect of the First Era that preached strict monotheism centered on the One. Founded by the prophet Marukh after reported visions of Saint Alessia, the Order's Seventy-Seven Inflexible Doctrines enforced a severe theocracy notorious for anti-elven cruelty, the destruction of Ayleid settlements and writings, and the erasure of entertainment. Rising from Colovia's lower classes, the Order became the dominant power of the Alessian Empire by 1E 361. Its extremist Marukhati Selective sect allegedly caused the millennium-long Dragon Break known as the Middle Dawn by attempting to purge elven elements from Akatosh. Internal schisms, western Cyrodiil's secession forming the Colovian Estates, and military defeats like the Battle of Glenumbra Moors culminated in the Order's collapse during the War of Righteousness in 1E 2321.
topic_desc_basic: The Alessian Order was a severe monotheistic religious sect that ruled the Alessian Empire during the First Era. Founded by the prophet Marukh, the Order enforced the strict Seventy-Seven Inflexible Doctrines, which were fiercely anti-elven and notorious for their cruelty. The Order eventually collapsed in 1E 2321 during the War of Righteousness, but its doctrines profoundly shaped later Tamrielic religion and law.

title: Marukh
topic_desc: A First Era Imga prophet whose visions of Saint Alessia inspired a radical monotheistic movement. He authored the Alessian Doctrines, which merged spiritual and political authority, declaring that resisting the Emperor meant resisting the Gods. His credo that all are guilty until proven innocent remains foundational to Tamrielic law. While his pantheon codification gave Cyrodiil a lasting identity, his increasingly abstract vision of a Single God fueled the zealotry of the Marukhati Selective and provoked severe hostility with the Camoran Dynasty, ultimately shaping the tumultuous Alessian Empire.
topic_desc_basic: A First Era Imga prophet whose teachings founded the Alessian Order and transformed Cyrodiil. He wrote the Alessian Doctrines, established the legal principle that all are guilty until proven innocent, and preached an uncompromising monotheism that merged religious and imperial authority.

title: Reman Empire
topic_desc: The Reman Empire, formally the Second Empire of Cyrodiil, was the first regime to unite the provinces of Tamriel under a single Cyrodiilic sovereign. Founded by Reman Cyrodiil after the defeat of the Akaviri invaders at the Battle of Pale Pass in the First Era, it established the imperial bureaucracy and integrated Akaviri martial and administrative traditions. The Reman Dynasty's Dragonborn emperors ruled until the assassination of Reman III, after which the Akaviri Potentate governed until the Empire's dissolution in the Second Era. Its political and cultural foundations profoundly shaped the later Septim Dynasty.
topic_desc_basic: The Reman Empire, also called the Second Empire of Cyrodiil, was the first to unite Tamriel under Cyrodiilic rule. Founded by Reman Cyrodiil in the First Era after repelling the Akaviri, it established many imperial traditions later continued by the Septim Dynasty. It ended in the Second Era following the assassination of its last Akaviri Potentate.

title: Akaviri Potentate
topic_desc: The Akaviri Potentate denotes the ruling period of the Second Empire following the assassination of Reman III and the extinction of the Reman Dynasty. Originally, the potentate served as chief adviser to the Reman Emperors. The Akaviri official Versidue-Shaie subsequently assumed sovereign authority and governed Tamriel for centuries during the late Second Era. The Potentate preserved Imperial administration after the Reman line ended, but its own violent collapse opened the long Interregnum that preceded Tiber Septim's rise.
topic_desc_basic: The Akaviri Potentate was the governing regime of the Second Empire after the Reman Dynasty ended. Originally the chief advisor to the Reman Emperors, the Akaviri Potentate assumed sovereign rule and administered Tamriel for centuries during the late Second Era before its collapse.

title: Septim Dynasty
topic_desc: The Septim Dynasty is the ruling bloodline of the Third Empire of Tamriel, founded by Tiber Septim in 2E 896 when his conquests ended the Interregnum and inaugurated the Third Era. The line's pure blood is debated; some scholars mark its decline with the murder of Kintyra II, while others point to Empress Katariah I, a Dark Elf who nonetheless continued Tiber's lineage through her son. The dynasty has weathered severe crises, including the War of the Red Diamond, the Camoran Usurper's rampage, and Jagar Tharn's decade-long Imperial Simulacrum. Now ruled by Uriel Septim VII, the Empire strives to restore the unity and justice of Tiber's legendary reign.
topic_desc_basic: The Septim Dynasty is the imperial bloodline of Tamriel, founded by Tiber Septim in 2E 896. His conquests ended the chaotic Interregnum and began the Third Era. The dynasty has survived succession wars, Usurpers, and the Imperial Simulacrum. Uriel Septim VII currently rules, striving to restore the Empire's unity.

title: wars of Tiber Septim
topic_desc: The wars of Tiber Septim were the military campaigns that ended the Interregnum and unified Tamriel under the Third Empire. Beginning with the consolidation of Cyrodiil, the conflicts expanded through the human kingdoms and into Morrowind, Valenwood, Elsweyr, Black Marsh, and Summerset Isle. The conquest concluded in 2E 896 after Numidium forced the Altmer's submission. Orthodox Imperial histories portray these wars as the restoration of order. The Arcturian Heresy instead claims that Wulfharth secretly powered Septim's early victories, that Septim later betrayed and trapped him in the Mantella, and that Zurin Arctus was falsely blamed for the resulting deaths.
topic_desc_basic: The military campaigns waged by Tiber Septim that ended the long Interregnum and unified Tamriel under Imperial rule. Concluding in 2E 896 with the subjugation of Summerset Isle, these wars forcibly brought peace and order to a previously chaotic and divided continent, initiating the Third Era.

title: Imperial Simulacrum
topic_desc: The Imperial Simulacrum denotes the decade from 3E 389 to 3E 399 when Imperial Battlemage Jagar Tharn imprisoned Emperor Uriel Septim VII within an extra-dimensional prison and assumed his aspect through illusion magic. During this usurpation, Tharn abused imperial privilege while abandoning Uriel VII's schedule of reconquest, causing the Empire's gradual disintegration. Though Tharn's precise ambitions remain uncertain, his magical deception successfully concealed the coup from the Elder Council and the provincial subjects. The Simulacrum ended in 3E 399 when an enigmatic Champion defeated Tharn in the Imperial Palace dungeons and freed the true Emperor, though the stagnation inflicted upon imperial cohesion persists.
topic_desc_basic: The Imperial Simulacrum was a decade-long period from 3E 389 to 3E 399 when Imperial Battlemage Jagar Tharn imprisoned Emperor Uriel Septim VII and used illusion magic to rule in his guise. Tharn abandoned the Emperor's reconquest efforts, causing significant imperial decline before being defeated and the true Emperor freed.

title: War of the Red Diamond
topic_desc: The War of the Red Diamond was a devastating Septim succession conflict fought primarily between 3E 121 and 3E 127, named for the dynasty's iconic badge. Queen Potema of Solitude challenged Empress Kintyra II's legitimacy, alleging bastardy, and secured support from Skyrim and northern High Rock. Uriel captured Kintyra and seized the Imperial City, ruling as Uriel III until his defeat and mob execution at the Battle of Ichidag. His uncles, Cephorus and Magnus, then claimed the throne, though Potema continued waging war from Solitude with necromantic and Daedric forces until her death in 3E 137.
topic_desc_basic: A devastating succession war within the Septim Dynasty from 3E 121 to 3E 137, named for the family's red diamond badge. Queen Potema of Solitude challenged Empress Kintyra II's right to rule, supporting her son Uriel III's claim. The conflict tore Tamriel apart until Uriel's capture and death, after which his uncles Cephorus and Magnus eventually defeated Potema.

title: Potema
topic_desc: Potema Septim, the infamous Wolf Queen of Solitude, was born in 3E 67 to Emperor Pelagius II. Married at fourteen to the elderly Nordic King Mantiarco, she swiftly became the true power in Solitude. After bearing a son, Uriel, she orchestrated a vast conspiracy to place him on the Imperial throne. Following Emperor Antiochus's death in 3E 112, Potema challenged Empress Kintyra II's succession, igniting the devastating War of the Red Diamond. After Uriel III's capture and murder in 3E 127, the aging queen descended into madness, employing daedra and necromancy to wage relentless war against Emperor Cephorus I. Surrounded by undead servants in a kingdom of death, Potema ultimately died in 3E 137 following a month-long siege of her castle. Theologians debate whether her formidable spirit transformed into a daedra, and legends attribute the subsequent madness of her nephew, Pelagius III, to her lingering influence.
topic_desc_basic: Potema Septim, the Wolf Queen of Solitude, was a ruthless Imperial princess who sparked the War of the Red Diamond to secure the throne for her son, Uriel III. After his death, she turned to necromancy and daedra summoning, terrorizing Skyrim until her death in 3E 137 following a siege on her castle.

title: Cephorus Septim
topic_desc: Cephorus Septim was an Emperor of the Septim Dynasty, son of Pelagius II and brother to Antiochus, Potema, and Magnus. Raised in the Imperial City during the early Third Era, he became a principal claimant during the War of the Red Diamond. After defeating his nephew Uriel III at the Battle of Ichidag in Hammerfell in 3E 127, Cephorus was proclaimed Emperor Cephorus I. His reign was consumed by continued civil war against his sister Potema, who commanded Daedric and undead forces from Solitude. He outlasted her rebellion and maintained Imperial authority until her death in 3E 137.
topic_desc_basic: Cephorus Septim is a Septim Emperor, son of Pelagius II and brother of Antiochus, Potema, and Magnus. He claimed the imperial throne after defeating his nephew Uriel III at the Battle of Ichidag in 3E 127, ending Uriel's brief reign. As Emperor Cephorus I, he waged protracted civil war against his sister Potema and her undead hordes until her death in 3E 137.

title: Pelagius III
topic_desc: Pelagius Septim III, called Pelagius the Mad, reigned as the twelfth Emperor of the Septim Dynasty from 3E 145 to 3E 153. Son of Magnus I and Utheilla of the Direnni line, he was installed as King of Solitude after the siege that ended Potema's rebellion. His eccentricities—alarming weight fluctuations, public undressing, and erratic conduct toward dignitaries—intensified upon his accession to the Ruby Throne. His Dunmer wife Katariah Ra'athim and the Elder Council governed in his stead; Katariah was named regent after Pelagius began attacking palace visitors. He spent his final six years in asylums, dying at thirty-four in the Temple of Kynareth on the Isle of Betony. The 2nd of Suns Dawn is celebrated as Mad Pelagius, a festival of sanctioned foolishness honoring his perversely enduring fame.
topic_desc_basic: Pelagius Septim III, known as Pelagius the Mad, ruled as Emperor of Tamriel from 3E 145 to 3E 153. Infamous for erratic and bizarre behavior, he never truly governed; his wife Katariah and the Elder Council held power. He died at thirty-four in an asylum on the Isle of Betony. The festival of Mad Pelagius commemorates his notorious reign.

title: Symmachus
topic_desc: General Symmachus was a Dunmer officer who served Tiber Septim during the conquest of Morrowind. Recognizing the young Barenziah among the ruins of Mournhold, he persuaded the Emperor to spare and foster her as a future Imperial vassal. He later recovered the runaway princess in Rifton, escorted her to the Imperial City, and subsequently guided her assumption of Mournhold's throne. The two eventually married and ruled together for centuries, producing heirs Helseth and Morgiah. Symmachus remained a steadfast pillar of Imperial authority in Mournhold until the Simulacrum, when civil unrest—fomented by Jagar Tharn's machinations—erupted into open rebellion. He fell in battle against the revolting populace, a casualty of the impostor Emperor's destabilization of the province. A grand state memorial honored his long service to the Septim Dynasty, and his glass ceremonial dagger remains a treasured relic of Mournhold.
topic_desc_basic: General Symmachus was a Dunmer officer of Tiber Septim who saved the young Princess Barenziah during the fall of Mournhold and later became her husband and co-ruler. He served the Empire for centuries until he was slain during a civil rebellion in Mournhold orchestrated by the impostor Jagar Tharn. He was the father of Helseth and Morgiah.

title: Zurin Arctus
topic_desc: Zurin Arctus served as Tiber Septim's Imperial Battlemage during the late Second Era and played a pivotal role in the activation of Numidium. Researching the Dwemer construct, Arctus believed Lorkhan's Heart was required to power it. Instead, a soulgem was used to trap the life force of the Underking—whom the Arcturian Heresy identifies as Ysmir Kingmaker—creating the Mantella. The process blasted a hole through Arctus's chest, killing him. Tiber Septim subsequently claimed Arctus had attempted a coup. After Numidium's deployment against Summerset Isle, a rotting undead wizard destroyed the construct. Mainstream tradition identifies this being as Arctus returned as the Underking, though the Heresy disputes his claim to that title entirely.
topic_desc_basic: Zurin Arctus served as Tiber Septim's Imperial Battlemage and was instrumental in activating the Dwemer construct Numidium. He reportedly channeled his life force into the Mantella to power the device, an act that killed him. Arctus later returned as the Underking to destroy Numidium, though conflicting accounts dispute whether he truly held that title.

title: Wulfharth
topic_desc: Atmora-born High King of Skyrim elected circa 1E 500 after Hoag Merkiller fell at Glenumbria Moors. His legendary thu'um forced scribes to record his oaths. He purged the Alessian heresy and restored the traditional Nordic pantheon. After dying from age—having shaken too many years onto himself to save his people from Alduin Time-Eater—Shor remade him from scattered ashes as the Ash-King to lead the Nordic host at Red Mountain. There Vehk destroyed him again, though Kyne bore his ashes skyward. According to the Arcturian Heresy, Wulfharth endured as the undead Underking, Ysmir the Grey Wind, consumed by vengeance against the Tribunal. He aided Hjalti Early-Beard—Tiber Septim—in his conquests, but abandoned the Empire when the Armistice validated Tribunal worship. Lured back by Septim's promises, he was ambushed; Zurin Arctus trapped his heart in a soulgem, creating the Mantella that powered Numidium.
topic_desc_basic: High King of Skyrim elected after Hoag Merkiller's death at Glenumbria Moors circa 1E 500. An Atmora-born warrior of immense thu'um, he reinstated the traditional Nordic pantheon and destroyed Alessian temples. Known as Ysmir, Dragon of the North, Shor's Tongue, and the Ash-King, he died and was reborn to fight at Red Mountain.

title: the Underking
topic_desc: The Underking is a disputed figure bound to Tiber Septim, Numidium, and the Mantella. Orthodox Imperial accounts identify him with Zurin Arctus, the Grand Battlemage whose life force was torn from him when Numidium was activated. The Arcturian Heresy instead names Ysmir Wulfharth, the ash-formed Nord king secretly used and betrayed by Septim. For centuries an undead power associated with the Underking sought the Mantella, described as his missing heart. During the Warp in the West of 3E 417, the Underking is said to have recovered it and finally died. Whether Arctus, Wulfharth, or some union of both stood behind the name remains unresolved.
topic_desc_basic: The Underking is a mysterious figure associated with Tiber Septim, Numidium, and the Mantella. Some accounts identify him as the betrayed battlemage Zurin Arctus; others name the ancient Nord king Wulfharth. He is said to have recovered the Mantella during the Warp in the West and finally died, though his true identity remains disputed.

title: the Mantella
topic_desc: The Mantella was a vast green soul gem, called a Crux of Transcendence, created to power the Dwemer construct Numidium. Accounts disagree whether it held the life force of Zurin Arctus, Ysmir Wulfharth, or the being remembered as the Underking. Tiber Septim used its power to activate Numidium during his conquest of Tamriel. After the construct's destruction, the gem was hidden in the Mantellan Crux, a plane of Aetherius. During the Warp in the West of 3E 417, the Underking is said to have reclaimed the Mantella and finally died, ending the artifact's long separation from its bound spirit.
topic_desc_basic: The Mantella was a vast green soul gem used to power Numidium. It contained the life force associated with the Underking, though accounts dispute whether that spirit was Zurin Arctus or Wulfharth. The Underking is said to have recovered it during the Warp in the West of 3E 417 and finally died.

title: Warp in the West
topic_desc: The Warp in the West, also called the Miracle of Peace or the Second Numidian Effect, was a Dragon Break that reshaped the Iliac Bay on the 9th through 11th of Frostfall, 3E 417. The activation of Numidium via the Totem of Tiber Septim caused temporal fracture, allowing multiple factions to simultaneously wield the brass tower. The paradoxical outcome consolidated forty-four squabbling city-states into four Imperial-aligned powers: Daggerfall, Wayrest, Sentinel, and Orsinium. The Underking reclaimed his heart from the construct, finally achieving death and generating a vast anti-magic zone. Mannimarco leveraged the event to ascend as the God of Worms. The Imperial Chapel attributes the sudden peace and catastrophic spatial-temporal anomalies to divine intervention, but Blades archivists conclude the event defies plausible historical reconstruction.
topic_desc_basic: The Warp in the West, or Miracle of Peace, was a Dragon Break that struck the Iliac Bay on the 9th of Frostfall, 3E 417. Activation of the ancient Numidium caused time to fracture, allowing multiple factions to wield it simultaneously. The paradox overnight consolidated forty-four city-states into four stable kingdoms: Daggerfall, Wayrest, Sentinel, and Orsinium.

title: the Arcturian Heresy
topic_desc: The Arcturian Heresy is an anonymously presented and controversial account of Tiber Septim's rise and the Underking's nature. Its opening names 'The Underking, Ysmir Kingmaker,' but does not securely identify an author. The text claims the Nord hero Wulfharth survived Red Mountain as the ash-formed Underking, aided Hjalti Early-Beard at Old Hrol'dan, and secretly drove the conquest of Cyrodiil. It further alleges that Septim murdered Cuhlecain and later ambushed the Underking to capture the Mantella, framing Grand Battlemage Zurin Arctus as a traitor. These claims fundamentally contradict orthodox Imperial history.
topic_desc_basic: A disputed historical text challenging orthodox accounts of Tiber Septim's rise. It claims the Underking was the Nord hero Wulfharth, who secretly aided Septim's conquests before being betrayed and ambushed to fuel the Numidium with his captured essence.

title: founding of the Mages Guild
topic_desc: The founding of the Mages Guild occurred in the early Second Era when Vanus Galerion, a Psijic of Artaeum, began gathering magic-users in Firsthold. His proposal to pool resources for research and public charity, and to sell magical items and spells to the general populace, broke radically with the era's solitary and aristocratic magical traditions. Summoned before Iachesis and King Rilis XII, Galerion secured a charter for his new fraternity. The Order of the Lamp was established the following year to provide the Guild with loyal security. Despite periodic local prohibitions, the institution expanded across Summerset and mainland Tamriel, governed by a hierarchy of Archmagisters and Masters, though Galerion ultimately lamented its descent into political infighting.
topic_desc_basic: In the early Second Era, the Psijic Vanus Galerion founded the Mages Guild in Firsthold, breaking from solitary magical traditions. He proposed pooling resources for research and making spells and items available to the public. After securing a charter, the Guild expanded across Tamriel, protected by the Order of the Lamp.

title: Vanus Galerion
topic_desc: Vanus Galerion, born the serf Trechtus on Summerset Isle in the early Second Era, rose from illiteracy and oppression to become one of Tamriel's most renowned mages. After his father was executed for violating his lord's ban on literate serfs, the fugitive youth was taken to the Isle of Artaeum, where the Psijic Magister Iachesis accepted him as a pupil. Galerion's experiences with injustice shaped his revolutionary philosophy: that magical knowledge should not be hoarded by aristocrats and hermits but shared publicly. Leaving the secretive Psijic Order, he founded the Mages Guild in Firsthold, making spells, potions, and enchanted items available to the common populace. He established the Order of the Lamp for the Guild's protection and structured its governance under a council of Archmagisters. Ultimately, Galerion grew disillusioned, famously denouncing the institution as an intricate morass of political infighting before departing Tamriel.
topic_desc_basic: Vanus Galerion, born the serf Trechtus in the early Second Era, founded the Mages Guild after training with the Psijic Order on Artaeum. His revolutionary philosophy held that magical knowledge and services should be available to the general public, not restricted to the aristocracy. He later grew disillusioned with the Guild's political infighting and departed Tamriel.

title: Psijic Order
topic_desc: The Psijic Order is the oldest monastic group in Tamriel, devoted to the study and practice of Mysticism, known as the Old Ways. Based on the Isle of Artaeum, the Order believes the Daedra and gods are merely powerful ancestor spirits. Historically serving as counsellors to Summurset's rulers, they select members through complex, secretive rituals and employ life extension to accommodate centuries of study. Their philosophy emphasizes diluting harmful change and encouraging enlightenment. When Vanus Galerion departed to found the Mages Guild, making magic publicly accessible, the Order remained insular. Artaeum itself can become insubstantial to repel unwanted visitors, shielding the Order's mysteries from the unenlightened.
topic_desc_basic: The Psijic Order is the oldest monastic group in Tamriel, devoted to the practice of Mysticism, known as the Old Ways. Based on the elusive Isle of Artaeum, they historically served as counsellors to Summurset's rulers. The Order selects members through secretive rituals and remains highly insular. Former Psijic Vanus Galerion departed to found the Mages Guild, making magic accessible to the public.

title: Artaeum
topic_desc: The third largest island in the Summurset archipelago, Artaeum is home to the Psijic Order, Tamriel's oldest monastic group. The Order practices the Elder Way, a philosophy binding natural forces to individual will. Artaeum is geographically unstable; it vanished from Nirn at the Second Era's dawn, returning five centuries later with no explanation for its absence or the fate of Ritemaster Iachesis. Now led by Loremaster Celarus, the Council's political influence waxes and wanes. The island features idyllic landscapes and the pre-Altmeri Ceporah Tower. Its inhabitants can render Artaeum insubstantial to repel invaders, and the last four emperors have refused its ambassadors.
topic_desc_basic: The third largest island in the Summurset archipelago, Artaeum is home to the Psijic Order, Tamriel's oldest monastic group. The island is notoriously difficult to chart, as it can vanish or shift location at the Council's decree. It features idyllic landscapes and the ancient Ceporah Tower.

title: the Old Ways
topic_desc: The esoteric philosophical and magical tradition of the Psijic Order, centered on Artaeum. The Old Ways hold that the spirits of the dead—ancestors—guide Mundus from an invisible afterworld, and that gods and Daedra are merely powerful ancestral spirits. Practitioners perform the sacred duty of seliffrnsae, providing grave and faithful counsel to rulers to prevent oegnithr, or bad change, which feeds malevolent entities like Boethiah and Vaernima. Rather than revolution or assassination, Psijics counter tyrants through patience, humiliation, or imprisonment. The tradition reveres change as the most sacred of the Eleven Forces, to be encouraged where it brings enlightenment and diluted where it breeds cruelty. Observances include the Rites of Moawita and the Vigyld to empower salutary spirits. A Psijic bound to a lord who orders acts contrary to the Old Ways faces dire choices: unwilling obedience risking corruption, exile and permanent banishment from Artaeum, or suicide.
topic_desc_basic: The ancestral magical and philosophical tradition of the Psijic Order of Artaeum. It teaches that the unseen spirits of the dead influence Mundus, and that gods and Daedra are merely the ghosts of exceptionally powerful mortals. Adherents seek to guide rulers and dilute harmful change while encouraging enlightenment, observing sacred rites to empower benevolent spirits.

title: Green Pact
topic_desc: The Green Pact, also known as the Treaty of Frond and Leaf, is the sacred covenant between the Bosmer and the god Y'ffre, governing their existence in Valenwood. Its core tenets forbid harming the forest, consuming plant life, killing wastefully, and shapeshifting into beasts. In return, Y'ffre grants the Bosmer patronage and the limited ability to ask the Green to shape itself for shelter. The notorious Meat Mandate obliges Bosmer to consume fallen enemies within three days, a practice that has diminished outside remote villages. Violators face the Ooze or ritual sacrifice to placate the Green. The Spinners of Y'ffre enforce the Pact, which permits using imported wood and animal products. In dire need, the Wild Hunt transforms participants into savage beasts to defend Valenwood.
topic_desc_basic: The Green Pact is the sacred covenant between the Bosmer and the god Y'ffre. It forbids harming Valenwood's forests, eating plants, killing wastefully, and shapeshifting. In return, the Green provides shelter and food. The pact's Meat Mandate requires consuming fallen enemies, a practice shocking to outsiders but increasingly rare. Violators face severe spiritual and physical consequences.

title: Wild Hunt
topic_desc: The Wild Hunt is a collective ritual innate to the Bosmer, invoking ancient knowledge of the Ehlnofey to defy the Earthbones established by Y'ffre. By unraveling the Names that grant them stable form, participants revert to the primordial chaos of the Ooze, transforming into an ever-shifting horde of feral, unrecognizable beasts. This metamorphosis is irreversible; the resulting monstrosities are undying, violently devouring all in their path before eventually turning upon themselves. Though every monster in the world is claimed to descend from a previous Hunt, the Bosmer consider the rite an act of sheer desperation and deeply shun its use.
topic_desc_basic: The Wild Hunt is a desperate ritual available to the Bosmer. By collectively unraveling the stable forms granted by Y'ffre, participants revert to the primordial chaos of the Ooze, transforming into an ever-shifting horde of feral, unrecognizable beasts. This irreversible metamorphosis creates undying monstrosities that devour everything in their path before consuming themselves. The Bosmer deeply shun this practice, invoking it only in utter desperation.

title: Orsinium
topic_desc: Orsinium, meaning Orc-Town in Aldmeris, is the city of the Orsimer. It has been sacked and rebuilt repeatedly across eras due to persistent conflict with Breton and Redguard neighbors. The original settlement in High Rock grew powerful in the First Era. In 3E 399, the Orc Gortwog gro-Nagorm won a legally sanctioned duel against the Breton Lord Bowyn to claim a tract of land between Menevia and Wayrest, establishing Nova Orsinium. This Third Era relocation grants the Orsimer a provincial seat in the Wrothgarian region under Imperial legal recognition. The Orsimer themselves are the transformed followers of Trinimac, who became Malacath after Boethiah's corruption, and their city remains a symbol of their enduring struggle for sovereignty.
topic_desc_basic: Orsinium is the city of the Orsimer, repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt over the centuries. In 3E 399, Gortwog gro-Nagorm won a legal duel to claim land between Wayrest and Menevia, establishing Nova Orsinium. The name means Orc-Town in Aldmeris.

title: Snow Elves
topic_desc: The Snow Elves were a Merish people who inhabited Skyrim and Solstheim before the Nordic conquests. Nordic tradition remembers them as the Elven foe driven from Skyrim by Ysgramor's people. Their final great stand on Solstheim came at the Battle of the Moesring, where the Snow Prince rallied their broken ranks and nearly reversed the battle before the young squire Finna killed him. The Nords honored the fallen champion with a noble barrow, but his death shattered the remaining Elven resistance. By 3E 427, the ultimate fate of any survivors is unknown.
topic_desc_basic: The Snow Elves were an elven people driven from Skyrim by the Nords. Their last great stand on Solstheim ended when the Snow Prince fell at the Battle of the Moesring. His death shattered their resistance, and the fate of any surviving Snow Elves is unknown in 3E 427.

title: Battle of Moesring
topic_desc: The Battle of the Moesring was the decisive final conflict between the Nord invaders and the native Snow Elves on Solstheim. Led by Ysgramor's forces, who had already driven the Elves from Skyrim, the Nords initially dominated the fighting. The Elven ranks rallied, however, with the sudden arrival of the Snow Prince, a warrior who commanded ice and snow, slaying several renowned Nord champions. The battle's outcome shifted unexpectedly when Finna, a twelve-year-old squire, avenged her mother Jofrior by hurling a sword that struck and killed the Snow Prince. Demoralized by their champion's fall, the remaining Elves were routed. The victorious Nords honored their formidable foe with a proper barrow burial. This Nord victory secured their dominance over Solstheim.
topic_desc_basic: The Battle of the Moesring was the final clash between Nords and Snow Elves on Solstheim. The Nords held the advantage until the Snow Prince entered the fray, killing several champions. He was slain by Finna, a young squire avenging her mother. The Elves were routed, securing Nord dominance over the island.

title: the Snow Prince
topic_desc: The Snow Prince was a Snow Elf warrior of extraordinary prowess who rallied his doomed kin at the Battle of the Moesring on Solstheim. Wielding a gleaming spear and commanding ice and snow, he slew several renowned Nord champions and nearly turned the tide against Ysgramor's forces. His death came unexpectedly when Finna, a twelve-year-old Nord girl avenging her mother Jofrior, threw a sword that struck him down. So great was the awe he inspired that the victorious Nords forsook their custom of burning enemy dead; instead, they interred him with royal honors in a barrow, though they withheld Stalhrim preservation. His fall shattered Elven resistance on Solstheim.
topic_desc_basic: The Snow Prince was a mighty Snow Elf warrior who fought at the Battle of the Moesring on Solstheim. He wielded powerful ice magic and nearly turned the tide against the Nords before being slain by Finna, a young Nord girl avenging her mother. The Nords honored his valor by burying him in a barrow rather than burning his body.

title: Atmora
topic_desc: Atmora, called Altmora in Aldmeris, translates to the Elder Wood. This northern continent is the ancestral homeland of the Nedic peoples, including the forebears of the Nords. Once a green land with forests and marshes, it suffered a catastrophic climate shift known as the Frostfall, rendering it a frozen wasteland of permanent winter. Expeditions in the Third Era found no sign of human habitation. The last recorded migration occurred in the First Era, though legends claim Tiber Septim later emigrated from its shores.
topic_desc_basic: Atmora, meaning Elder Wood, is a frozen continent north of Tamriel and the ancestral homeland of the Nords. Once a green land, it suffered the Frostfall and became an uninhabitable wasteland of permanent winter. Third Era expeditions found no surviving civilization there.

title: the Mane
topic_desc: The Mane serves as the spiritual leader and temporal ruler of the Khajiit people, dwelling in the palaces of Torval. Khajiit tradition holds that only one Mane exists at any time, being reborn in different bodies; whether this reflects metaphysical truth or the ruling Mane's elimination of rivals remains uncertain. A new Mane is born only under a rare alignment of Masser and Secunda, when legend claims a third moon appears. Historically, all Khajiit shaved their manes in deference, braiding the hair into the Mane's headdress until it grew so heavy that travel required a palanquin. As population grew, this practice became impractical, and the headdress now incorporates hair only from the Mane's tribe and Warrior Guard. Those born under the eclipse but not chosen as the Mane are known as Forgotten Manes.
topic_desc_basic: The Mane is the spiritual and temporal ruler of the Khajiit, traditionally believed to be a single soul reborn in different bodies. A new Mane is born only under a rare alignment of the moons Masser and Secunda. The Mane's ceremonial headdress, woven from the braided manes of Khajiit subjects, grows so heavy that travel by palanquin is often necessary.

title: Lunar Lattice
topic_desc: The Lunar Lattice, or ja-Kha'jay, is the cosmic barrier and stabilizing force created by the primal spirit Fadomai. Bestowed upon the Moons, its eternal motions shield creation from the anger of Ahnurr. In Khajiiti belief, the Lattice is inextricably bound to their nature; Azurah tied the Khajiit to its phases, making them its secret defenders. Should Masser and Secunda fail, the Khajiit are charged with climbing to restore their courses. The Lattice also governs the diverse forms of the Khajiit, who are shaped by the moons' alignments. While Aldmeri faith recognizes Jode and Jone as separate deities, Khajiiti tradition holds them as mere aspects of the greater Lattice, a structure that defines and protects their people.
topic_desc_basic: The Lunar Lattice, or ja-Kha'jay, is the cosmic order governing the moons Masser and Secunda. In Khajiiti faith, it is a protective barrier and the force that shapes the Khajiit into their many forms, binding them to the moons' phases.

title: Lorkhaj
topic_desc: Lorkhaj is the Khajiiti interpretation of the Missing God, known as the Moon Beast or Moon Prince. Born last in the Great Darkness, his heart was filled with the Great Darkness, which knew its name as Namiira. He created a place for Nirni to bear her children, but his dark heart drove him to trick his siblings into the new realm. For this, Fadomai's children tore out his heart and hid it deep within Nirni, cursing him to walk the world. As a Sky Spirit, Lorkhaj is honored for making his own path and uniting spirits to create Nirni. As a Dark Spirit, Namiira's corruption made him the first dro-m'Athra. Azurah ultimately redeemed him, freeing his true spirit as the Hidden Moon to protect the Lunar Lattice. The third moon, the Dark Moon, is believed to be his darkness-free corpse.
topic_desc_basic: Lorkhaj, the Moon Beast, is the Khajiiti form of the Missing God Lorkhan. He made a place for Nirni's children but tricked his siblings into the mortal realm. For this, his heart was torn out and hidden within Nirni, and he was cursed to walk the world. Khajiiti tradition holds that the Dark Moon visible in the sky is his corpse.

title: Azurah
topic_desc: Azurah is the Khajiiti name and cultural understanding of the Daedric Prince Azura, revered as the spirit of dusk and dawn and the favored daughter of Fadomai. Khajiiti myth says Fadomai entrusted her greatest secrets to Azurah. Using them, Azurah shaped the forest people into the Khajiit, bound their many forms to the Lunar Lattice, and charged them with protecting the moons. These traditions emphasize roles and relationships distinct from Dunmeri teachings about Azura, while recognizing the same divine being through a Khajiiti cosmological lens.
topic_desc_basic: Azurah is the Khajiiti name and understanding of Azura, the spirit of dusk and dawn. Khajiiti tradition says she received Fadomai's secrets, shaped the forest people into the Khajiit, and bound their many forms to the Lunar Lattice.

title: Khajiit furstocks
topic_desc: Khajiit furstocks are the diverse morphological forms of the Khajiit, determined by the phases of Masser and Secunda at birth. According to the Words of Clan Mother Ahnissi, Azurah shaped the Khajiit from torn forest people, binding them to the Lunar Lattice and making them of many shapes, one for every purpose. This lunar determinism produces forms ranging from elf-like quadrupeds to great feline battlecats. Imperial scholars note that Khajiit differ fundamentally from men and mer in skeletal, dermal, and metabolic physiology, and their interfertility with other races remains undocumented. Specific furstocks, such as the Cathay-raht, are recorded serving as formidable soldiers in Elsweyr's armies.
topic_desc_basic: Khajiit furstocks are the varied physical forms of the Khajiit, shaped by the phases of the moons at birth. According to their legends, Azurah bound the Khajiit to the Lunar Lattice and made them of many shapes for different purposes. These forms range from elf-like to great feline beasts, differing vastly in skeletal and dermal physiology from men and mer.

title: Akavir
topic_desc: Akavir, meaning Dragon Land, is a continental landmass east of Tamriel inhabited exclusively by beast races. No Men or Mer survive there; the vampiric Serpent-Folk of Tsaesci consumed the human population ages ago. Four major nations perpetually war with one another and occasionally launch invasions westward. Kamal, the Snow Hell, spawns demon armies that seasonally assault Tang Mo, the Thousand Monkey Isles, whose brave folk now ally with Ka Po' Tun. This Tiger-Dragon's Empire, ruled by the divine Tosh Raka, surpassed Tsaesci in power after their devastating war over Dragons left both weakened. Tsaesci remains influential in Tamrielic memory because the Serpent-Folk supplied the Potentate who governed the Cyrodilic Empire for four centuries. Tamrielic understanding of Akavir is widely acknowledged as incomplete.
topic_desc_basic: Akavir, the Dragon Land, is a continent east of Tamriel inhabited by beast races. The human population was long ago consumed by the vampiric Serpent-Folk of Tsaesci. Four major nations—Kamal, Tsaesci, Tang Mo, and Ka Po' Tun—constantly war among themselves and have invaded Tamriel multiple times. Tamrielic knowledge of Akavir remains incomplete.

title: Tsaesci
topic_desc: The Tsaesci are the serpent-folk of Akavir, once the continent's strongest power before the rise of the Tiger-Dragon. Accounts of their appearance are notoriously contradictory; some describe them as tall, golden-scaled, and immortal, while others report they are indistinguishable from humans. They famously devoured the Men of Akavir, yet still resemble them. The Tsaesci enslave goblins for labor and blood, and once waged devastating war against the Dragons and the tiger-folk of Ka Po' Tun. Their profound influence on Tamriel stems from the First Era invasion, after which they served Reman I and shaped Imperial institutions. The Akaviri Potentate, ruled by Tsaesci such as Versidue-Shaie, governed the Second Empire for centuries before its assassination ended their reign.
topic_desc_basic: The Tsaesci are the vampiric serpent-folk of Akavir, described as tall, golden-scaled, and immortal. They famously devoured the Men of Akavir yet still resemble them. They profoundly shaped Tamrielic history, providing the Akaviri Dragonguard and ruling the Second Empire as Potentates for four hundred years.

title: Kamal
topic_desc: The Kamal, or snow demons, are one of the four major races of Akavir, inhabiting the frigid nation translated as 'Snow Hell'. They spend the winter frozen solid, thawing each summer to mount invasions against the monkey-folk of Tang Mo, who consistently repel them. The most historically significant Kamal was Ada'Soom Dir-Kamal, a king who led an invasion of Tamriel; his forces were destroyed at Red Mountain by Almalexia and the Underking. Beyond these seasonal campaigns and their enmity with Tang Mo, the broader culture and society of the Kamal remain largely obscure to Tamrielic scholars.
topic_desc_basic: The Kamal, or snow demons, inhabit the frozen Akaviri nation of 'Snow Hell'. They thaw from winter dormancy each summer to invade Tang Mo, though the monkey-folk always repel them. A Kamal king, Ada'Soom Dir-Kamal, once invaded Tamriel but was destroyed at Red Mountain.

title: Tang Mo
topic_desc: The Tang Mo are the monkey-folk of Akavir, inhabiting the region translated as the Thousand Monkey Isles. Numerous breeds are described as kind, brave, and simple, though often eccentric. Despite their peaceful reputation, they are formidable in conflict and repeatedly raise armies against invasion and enslavement by other Akaviri nations. Accounts claim that each summer the snow demons of Kamal thaw and attack Tang Mo, only to be driven back. The same uncertain reports describe an alliance with the tiger-folk of Ka Po' Tun and particular hatred for the Tsaesci. No reliable Tamrielic observer has documented them directly.
topic_desc_basic: The Tang Mo are the monkey-folk of Akavir, dwelling in the Thousand Monkey Isles. Tamrielic accounts describe them as kind, brave, and frequently eccentric, yet formidable in war. They repeatedly repel Kamal invasions and are said to ally with Ka Po' Tun against the Tsaesci, though reliable knowledge of them is scarce.

title: Ka Po' Tun
topic_desc: The Ka Po' Tun are a feline race of tiger-folk inhabiting the empire of Ka Po' Tun in Akavir. Formerly known as Po Tun, their realm translates to the 'Tiger-Dragon's Empire,' reflecting their cultural ambition to transform into dragons following a devastating war with the Tsaesci that exterminated Akavir's dragons. Under the divine Tosh Raka—the first of their kind to achieve this dragonhood—their empire has surpassed the Tsaesci in strength, though not at sea. Allied with the Tang Mo, the Ka Po' Tun harbor deep enmity for the vampiric Tsaesci and, under Tosh Raka, reportedly harbor ambitions to invade Tamriel. No modern Tamrielic scholar has directly observed them, leaving their true nature obscured by translation and limited sources.
topic_desc_basic: The Ka Po' Tun are a race of tiger-folk from the Akaviri nation of Ka Po' Tun, the 'Tiger-Dragon's Empire.' Ruled by the divine Tosh Raka, they seek to transform into dragons and are bitter enemies of the Tsaesci serpent-folk. Their empire is reportedly the strongest in Akavir, though no Tamrielic scholar has directly observed them.

title: Ayleids
topic_desc: The Ayleids, or Heartland High Elves, ruled Cyrodiil in the long ages of myth before recorded history. Their empire, notorious for enslaving humans, fractured through internal strife before Alessia's uprising toppled White-Gold Tower in 1E 243. Some Ayleid lords initially persisted as vassals, but the rise of the Alessian Order drove most from Cyrodiil by 1E 361, with refugees absorbed into Valenwood and High Rock. Surviving communities now dwell scattered across Tamriel's wilds, commonly called Wild Elves. They shun Tamrielic civilization, speak a variation of Old Cyrodilic, and remain deeply enigmatic. Outsiders find them taciturn, though the rare Ayleid scholar Tjurhane Fyrre insisted their isolated tribes possess vibrant, diverse cultures.
topic_desc_basic: The Ayleids, also called Heartland High Elves or Wild Elves, once ruled Cyrodiil before their empire fell to Alessia's uprising in 1E 243. Driven out by the Alessian Order, surviving Ayleids now live scattered across Tamriel's wilds, shunning outside civilization and speaking a variation of Old Cyrodilic.

title: Direnni
topic_desc: The Direnni are an aristocratic Altmer clan whose intermingling with Nedic peoples produced the Breton race. During the First Era, they ruled the Direnni Hegemony, a sovereign power that at its peak controlled High Rock and parts of Skyrim and Hammerfell, challenging both the Nordic and Alessian Empires. Under leaders like Prince Aiden Direnni, they halted the Alessian expansion at the Battle of Glenumbra Moors. Though famed for legendary warriors and monarchs, the clan laid the foundations for modern alchemy, conjuration, and enchanting. They revere Phynaster and maintain custody of the Isle of Balfiera and the Adamantine Tower, where each high-blooded Direnni touches the Zero Stone upon maturity. Their history includes catastrophic Daedric trafficking and esoteric financial magics.
topic_desc_basic: The Direnni are an influential Altmer clan who ruled much of High Rock during the First Era through the Direnni Hegemony. Their intermingling with local Nedes produced the Breton race. They remain custodians of the Adamantine Tower on the Isle of Balfiera.

title: Nedes
topic_desc: The Nedes were an ancient human people of Tamriel, now largely vanished as a distinct culture. Once widespread across Hammerfell and other regions, they constructed advanced stone architecture, including the mage towers of Elinhir, challenging assumptions that they were merely primitive. Successively conquered by the Dwemer, Ayleids, and Yokudans, the Nedes were often disparaged by their overlords to justify enslavement. Following the Ra Gada invasion, surviving Nedes migrated and intermingled with other populations, fading from the historical record. Scholars debate their precise origins; some accounts suggest they descended from the Wandering Ehlnofey alongside other human groups, while their exact relationship to the Nords and other modern peoples remains uncertain.
topic_desc_basic: The Nedes were an ancient human people of Tamriel who once inhabited regions including Hammerfell. Though often portrayed as primitive by their conquerors, they built advanced stone structures. Overwhelmed by the Dwemer, Ayleids, and Yokudans, the Nedic culture faded after the Ra Gada, with survivors intermingling into other populations.

title: Skaal standing stones
topic_desc: The Skaal standing stones are six sacred sites on Solstheim central to the isolated Nord tribe's veneration of the All-Maker. Each stone corresponds to a vital natural Gift—Water, Earth, Beasts, Trees, Sun, and Winds—and serves as a conduit through which the All-Maker communicates with mortals. Skaal tradition holds that when the Adversary, acting through the Greedy Man, stole these Gifts, the hero Aevar Stone-Singer visited each stone in turn and received the All-Maker's guidance to restore the world's balance. The stones remain active sites of pilgrimage and devotion, anchoring the Skaal's cyclical belief that nature's bounty must be actively maintained and that the Adversary perpetually threatens to disrupt it.
topic_desc_basic: The Skaal standing stones are six sacred monuments on Solstheim dedicated to the All-Maker. Each stone represents a natural Gift—Water, Earth, Beasts, Trees, Sun, or Winds—and serves as a place where the All-Maker communicates with the Skaal. They are central to the tribe's faith and the legend of Aevar Stone-Singer, who restored the stolen Gifts at these sites.

title: Aevar Stone-Singer
topic_desc: Aevar Stone-Singer is a legendary hero of Skaal tradition, central to the foundational myth of Solstheim's people. When the Adversary, manifesting as the Greedy Man, stole the gifts of the All-Maker, the young Aevar volunteered to reclaim them, arguing that his lack of standing meant he would not be missed. Guided by the All-Maker at each sacred stone, he restored Water, Earth, Beasts, Trees, Sun, and Winds through arduous trials. He used his mace to amplify the Song of the Earth in the Cave of the Hidden Music. His tale warns against complacency and teaches that the All-Maker's gifts must be defended and restored when threatened.
topic_desc_basic: Aevar Stone-Singer is a legendary Skaal hero who, according to tradition, reclaimed the stolen gifts of the All-Maker from the Greedy Man. A young man of no special standing, Aevar's arduous journey restored the bounty of Solstheim and serves as a foundational teaching for the Skaal people.

title: Maormer
topic_desc: The Maormer, or Sea Elves, are a race of Mer inhabiting the island kingdom of Pyandonea, south of Summerset Isle. Whether exiled from Summerset or separated from the Aldmeri homeland of Aldmeris, their culture is defined by an enduring hatred of the Altmer and a relentless drive to conquer Summerset. They are ruled by the deathless wizard King Orgnum, who has led every invasion of Summerset throughout the First and Second Eras, each ending in failure. The Maormer practice powerful snake magic to tame sea serpents as warbeasts and are formidable storm mages. Their last documented appearance was in 3E 110 during the War of the Isle, when the combined Imperial-Altmeri fleet and the Psijic Order destroyed Orgnum's armada, reportedly crippling his capacity to ever threaten Summerset again.
topic_desc_basic: The Maormer, or Sea Elves, are a race of Mer from the island kingdom of Pyandonea south of Summerset Isle. Driven by hatred of the Altmer, they have repeatedly invaded Summerset throughout the First and Second Eras under their immortal leader, King Orgnum. Their last major attack was in 3E 110, when the Imperial fleet and the Psijic Order destroyed their armada.

title: Sload
topic_desc: The Sload are a race of slug-like, semi-aquatic beastfolk native to the Coral Kingdoms of Thras, an archipelago west of Tamriel in the Abecean Sea. Noted for their corpulent forms and potentially limitless size and lifespan, the Sload are an isolationist people whose culture revolves heavily around necromancy. Their guttural language possesses no word for adventure, with the closest equivalent translating to tragic disaster. They are universally reviled for unleashing the Thrassian Plague in 1E 2260, a catastrophe that killed more than half of Tamriel's population and prompted the All Flags Navy's devastating retaliation against Thras. Despite this enmity, the Sload maintain some diplomatic relations with the Maormer of Pyandonea.
topic_desc_basic: The Sload, sometimes called slug-folk or worms, are a race of slug-like beastfolk inhabiting the Coral Kingdoms of Thras west of Tamriel. Semi-aquatic and exceptionally long-lived, their culture is steeped in necromancy. They are infamous for unleashing the devastating Thrassian Plague upon Tamriel in 1E 2260, killing over half the continent's population.

title: Aldmeri pantheon
topic_desc: The Aldmeri pantheon venerated by the Altmer is headed by Auri-El, soul of Anui-El and chief of the elven gods. Trinimac, the warrior spirit later associated with Malacath's origin, follows him in importance. Other honored spirits include Magnus, Syrabane, Y'ffre, Xarxes, Mara, Stendarr, and Phynaster. Lorkhan also occupies a hostile place in Altmeri theology as the Missing God blamed for sundering the elves from the spirit world. Related Aldmeri peoples preserve distinct variants: Bosmeri worship, for example, gives an explicit place to the lunar spirits Jone and Jode.
topic_desc_basic: The Altmeri pantheon is headed by Auri-El and includes Trinimac, Magnus, Syrabane, Y'ffre, Xarxes, Mara, Stendarr, and Phynaster. Lorkhan holds a hostile place as the Missing God blamed for separating elves from the spirit world. Related elven peoples preserve their own variants of this tradition.

title: Khajiiti pantheon
topic_desc: The Khajiiti pantheon venerates spirits born of the primal littermates Ahnurr and Fadomai. Central is Azurah, who received Fadomai's secrets and shaped the Khajiit from forest people, binding them to the Lunar Lattice, ja-Kha'jay. Alkosh, the Dragon King of Cats, predates the ri'Datta Dynasty and serves as a cultural time-god. Khenarthi rules the winds, Mara is the Mother Cat, and S'rendarr embodies mercy. Lorkhaj, the Moon Beast bearing a darkness-tainted heart, tricked his siblings into the mortal plane and was cursed to walk it. The Riddle'Thar co-opted earlier worship upon its establishment, though ancient deities remain popular in Elsweyr's wasteland regions. The trickster Baan Dar and the Skooma Cat, Sheggorath, also hold recognized places in this distinct mythos.
topic_desc_basic: The Khajiiti pantheon traces its gods to the primal littermates Ahnurr and Fadomai. Azurah is central, having shaped the Khajiit and bound them to the Lunar Lattice. Other revered spirits include Alkosh the Dragon King of Cats, Khenarthi the Winds, and Lorkhaj, the trickster whose dark heart forced the gods into the mortal world.

title: Redguard pantheon
topic_desc: The Redguard pantheon centers on Satakal the Worldskin, a cyclic fusion of Anu and Padomay who destroys one world to begin the next. Survival of this cosmic hunger defines the mythology; Ruptga, Tall Papa, was the first spirit to discover the Walkabout, a process of persisting beyond one lifetime, and set the stars to guide lesser spirits. Tu'whacca, god of souls, tends the Far Shores where the worthy reach the afterlife. Sep, the Snake, is Tall Papa's helper created from dead skin of past worlds; driven mad by Satakal's hunger, he convinced spirits to build an easier alternative—the mortal world—trapping them as mortals. Other deities include Morwha, the four-armed fertility goddess; Tava, the bird spirit who guided Yokudans to Herne; and Onsi, the warrior god who taught men to forge swords. Worship of these gods persists in Hammerfell, particularly among Alik'r nomads and sailors.
topic_desc_basic: The Redguard pantheon venerates deities born from Satakal the Worldskin, a cyclic god who destroys one world to begin the next. Ruptga, called Tall Papa, is chief deity who teaches spirits the Walkabout to survive Satakal's hunger. Tu'whacca guards the Far Shores afterlife, while Sep the Snake created the mortal world, trapping spirits as mortals. Morwha, Tava, and Onsi are also widely revered in Hammerfell.

title: Nordic pantheon
topic_desc: The Nordic pantheon comprises the deities revered by the Nords of Skyrim, rooted in Atmoran myth. Unlike the Imperial Nine Divines, it has no chief; Shor, the Missing God, rules the dead in Sovngarde, while Alduin, the World Eater, serves as its grim wellspring. Key figures include Kyne, the storm goddess and Mother of Men; Tsun, god of trials; Stuhn, god of ransom; and Mara, goddess of love. Orkey governs the cycle of life and death. Herma-Mora and Maloch represent feared foreign influences. Jhunal, the Rune God, has faded from modern worship. The pantheon reflects a worldview emphasizing valor, hardship, and the heroic struggle against monstrous forces.
topic_desc_basic: The Nords of Skyrim revere a distinct pantheon rooted in Atmoran tradition. It has no chief deity; Shor rules the dead, while Alduin, the World Eater, is its grim wellspring. Notable gods include Kyne, Mara, Tsun, Stuhn, and Orkey. Herma-Mora and Maloch are feared foreign spirits. Jhunal, the Rune God, is absent from modern worship.

title: The Monomyth
topic_desc: The Monomyth is a theological treatise examining the shared structural patterns underlying Tamrielic creation beliefs. It posits that all traditions begin with the dualism of Anu and Padomay—order and chaos—whose interplay birthed the et'Ada. The text identifies two universal archetypes spanning cultures: the Dragon God of Time and the Missing God of the Mortal Plane. It explores the fundamental schism between human and Aldmeri perspectives, where humans view creation as divine mercy, while mer regard it as a cruel sundering from the divine. The work includes cultural variations such as the Yokudan and Cyrodilic myths, alongside a Psijiic summary of Aurbis prepared for Uriel V.
topic_desc_basic: The Monomyth is a theological work comparing creation myths across Tamriel. It argues that all traditions share a common structure beginning with the dual forces of Anu and Padomay, and feature two universal archetypes: the Dragon God of Time and the Missing God of the Mortal Plane. The text highlights the fundamental divide between human and elven views on creation.

title: The Annotated Anuad
topic_desc: The Annotated Anuad is a widely circulated religious text that recounts a simplified version of the Anuad creation myth from the Mythic Era. It details the primordial conflict between the brothers Anu and Padomay, whose mixed blood spawned the Aedra and separate blood spawned the Daedra, and describes the Ehlnofey war that reshaped Nirn and divided the ancestors of Mer and Men. Some scholars suggest Ayleid origins for the tradition. The text exists in both standard and simplified illustrated editions, the latter commonly used for the literacy campaigns of the Imperial Commission.
topic_desc_basic: The Annotated Anuad is a popular religious book retelling the ancient Anuad creation myth. It describes the primordial conflict between Anu and Padomay, the origin of the Aedra and Daedra, and the Ehlnofey war that shaped Nirn and divided the ancestors of Mer and Men. A simplified illustrated edition is widely used to teach literacy.

title: Mysterious Akavir
topic_desc: A widely-circulated treatise surveying the continent of Akavir, the so-called Dragon Land. The text characterizes Akavir as a realm of beast-folk devoid of Men or Mer, detailing four major nations: the snow-demons of Kamal, the vampiric serpent-folk of Tsaesci, the monkey-folk of Tang Mo, and the cat-folk of Ka Po' Tun. It recounts the Tsaesci consumption of Akaviri Men, their ancient war with the Dragons, and the rise of Tosh Raka, the Tiger-Dragon who now rules Ka Po' Tun. The author speculates on Akaviri motives for invading Tamriel, citing the potentate Versidue-Shaie and the demon king Ada'Soom Dir-Kamal as proof of persistent eastern ambitions. While popular, the work blends verifiable history with uncertain claims.
topic_desc_basic: A treatise describing the continent of Akavir and its four major nations: the Kamal snow-demons, the Tsaesci serpent-folk, the Tang Mo monkey-folk, and the Ka Po' Tun cat-folk ruled by the Tiger-Dragon Tosh Raka. It speculates on why these beast-folk repeatedly attempt to invade Tamriel.

title: Varieties of Faith in the Empire
topic_desc: Brother Mikhael Karkuxor of the Imperial College authored this comparative theological treatise cataloging the pantheons and divine spirits of Tamriel's dominant cultures. It systematically lists the principal deities of eight traditions—Cyrodilic, Nordic, Altmeri, Bosmeri, Dunmeri, Yokudan, Breton, and Khajiiti—alongside scholarly annotations detailing their varied cultural interpretations and mythic roles. The work notably illustrates how singular et'Ada manifest under different names and aspects across faiths, such as the Nordic Alduin and the Altmeri Auri-El sharing origins with Akatosh. Karkuxor acknowledges the omission of Argonian worship due to contradictory accounts. Widely circulated, it remains a foundational Imperial text on comparative religion.
topic_desc_basic: A comparative religious text by Brother Mikhael Karkuxor of the Imperial College. It catalogs the principal pantheons of Tamriel's eight dominant cultures and provides scholarly notes on how different societies interpret the same divine spirits, such as Akatosh, under varied names and aspects.

title: The 36 Lessons of Vivec
topic_desc: The Thirty-Six Lessons of Vivec constitute the foundational scriptural text of the Tribunal Temple, authored by the god Vivec. Across thirty-six sermons, the warrior-poet recounts a mythopoetic prehistory, detailing his own divine birth from a netchiman's wife, his union with Almalexia and Sotha Sil, and his guidance of the Hortator Nerevar against northern invaders and the Dwemer. The Lessons embed mystical philosophy, including the six walking ways to divinity and the doctrine that love resides under will alone. Hidden numerical and acrostic ciphers within the text convey forbidden contradictions, including an apparent confession that the author stole his godhood and murdered the Hortator, a heresy suppressing orthodox veneration. Temple scholars study the Lessons for esoteric enlightenment, while dissenters note how the scripture obscures historical truth behind layers of allegory and cryptic enumeration.
topic_desc_basic: The Thirty-Six Lessons of Vivec are the holy scriptures of the Tribunal Temple, written by the god Vivec. Across thirty-six sermons, they recount his divine birth, his union with Almalexia and Sotha Sil, and his role guiding the Hortator Nerevar. The text is deeply mystical, outlining paths to divinity and praising ALMSIVI. It remains the central devotional work of the Velothi faith.

title: Nerevar at Red Mountain
topic_desc: A text from the Apographa, the Tribunal Temple's hidden writings, preserving the Ashlander tradition of the Battle of Red Mountain as transmitted by Alandro Sul. It claims that Almalexia, Sotha Sil, and Vivec murdered Indoril Nerevar using poisoned candles, robes, and invocations to seize the Heart of Lorkhan, and that Azura consequently transformed the Chimer into the Dunmer and promised Nerevar's return. Temple doctrine denounces these accounts as ignorant superstition, and the manuscript is suppressed among civilized Dunmer. It survives in restricted collections such as the Vivec Hall of Justice Secret Library.
topic_desc_basic: A suppressed Apographa text preserving the Ashlander account of the Battle of Red Mountain. It claims the Tribunal murdered Indoril Nerevar to steal divine power from the Heart of Lorkhan, prompting Azura to curse the Chimer into Dunmer. Temple doctrine rejects this as heresy.

title: Five Songs of King Wulfharth
topic_desc: A collection of legendary accounts concerning the First Era Nord hero-king Wulfharth, chronicling his deeds, death, resurrection, and role at Red Mountain. The first five songs present a mythic narrative of his Thu'um prowess, his battle against Alduin's age-shortening, and his return as the Ash King under Shor's banner. A secret sixth song offers a divergent, detailed account of the Red Mountain war, describing alliances with Orcs and Dagoth-Ur, and naming Nerevar, Dumac, and Alandro Sul as combatants. The text preserves contested and esoteric traditions about the conflict's participants and the fate of Shor's Heart.
topic_desc_basic: A legendary compilation of songs recounting the life, death, and resurrection of the First Era Nord King Wulfharth. The tales celebrate his Thu'um, his battle against the age-shortening of Alduin, and his return as the Ash King to fight at Red Mountain, preserving mythic traditions of the Nordic war for Shor's Heart.

title: Children of the Sky
topic_desc: Children of the Sky is a treatise on the Nordic worldview and the martial power of the voice. The text describes the Nords as eternal outsiders born where the sky exhaled upon the land, regarding breath and voice as their vital essence. It details the Thu'um, a shout akin to the Akaviri kiai, wielded by elite warriors called Tongues who shatter gates and command minds. The most powerful must remain gagged, communicating only through sign and runes to avoid unintended destruction. Trophy tongues woven into rope are said to hold spoken enchantment, while the far northern wastes breed elemental folk who carry the wind with them.
topic_desc_basic: Children of the Sky is a treatise describing the Nords as children of the sky and the Thu'um, the martial voice-power wielded by their greatest warriors. It claims the strongest Tongues can shatter gates with a shout, command minds, or move vast distances, while the most powerful must remain gagged to avoid causing destruction.

title: Fall of the Snow Prince
topic_desc: Fall of the Snow Prince is a Nordic chronicle of the Battle of the Moesring on Solstheim. It tells how a radiant Snow Elf champion rallied his near-defeated people, slew renowned Nord warriors, and was unexpectedly killed when the young squire Finna hurled her dead mother's sword into his breast. The account praises the Snow Prince's courage despite calling his people enemies. It records that the victorious Nords broke with their custom of burning enemy dead and buried him in a royal barrow with his gleaming armor, spear, and worthy treasures, while reserving stalhrim burial for their own people.
topic_desc_basic: Fall of the Snow Prince is a Nordic account of the Battle of the Moesring. It recounts the Snow Prince's rally of the Snow Elves, his death at the hand of the young Finna, and the honors granted to him by the victorious Nords, who buried their formidable enemy in a royal barrow.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 1
topic_desc: The opening text of Vivec's thirty-six sermons, this heavily symbolic account presents a mythic origin for the god-king. It describes a netchiman's wife chosen by Ayem (Almalexia) and Seht (Sotha Sil), who is cast into the sea, transformed by dreughs, and returned to shore to nurture a divine egg. The egg receives teachings from Mephala's codes, Veloth's prophecies, and Trinimac's forbidden lore. Seven Daedra and the Demiprince Fa-Nuit-Hen then bestow martial knowledge upon the unborn Vehk through the Barons of Move Like This. The sermon concludes with a cryptic numerological riddle and the declaration that love is under Vivec's will. As doctrine, the text blends divine revelation with deliberate obscurity, serving as both Temple scripture and esoteric philosophy.
topic_desc_basic: The first of Vivec's thirty-six sermons recounts a symbolic origin of the god-king. A netchiman's wife is transformed by dreughs and visited by Almalexia and Sotha Sil, who charge her with nurturing a divine egg. Daedric beings bestow martial knowledge upon the unborn Vehk. The text serves as Temple doctrine filled with cryptic numerology and esoteric philosophy.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 10
topic_desc: The tenth installment of the Tribunal god Vivec's esoteric doctrinal text addresses the Hortator on the nature of subterfuge, adaptation, and the primacy of Sithis. The sermon advocates assuming the skin of enemies and eschewing rigid stasis, framing true Houses as constructs of Sithisit built against stagnation. It invokes Boethiah's pledge to the Frame-maker and commands the Trinimac-eaters to divide and structure themselves akin to the Corners of the House of Troubles, only to ultimately reject division. The text concludes with a repetitive, cryptic chant affirming Sithisit's enduring motion. As with all Lessons, the account is highly symbolic, blending religious doctrine with militant philosophy.
topic_desc_basic: The tenth sermon of Vivec's doctrinal series instructs the Hortator on stealth and adaptation, urging the warrior to assume the skin of enemies. It frames true Houses as creations of Sithis opposed to stasis, invokes Boethiah, and commands the Orcs to divide like the Daedra before rejecting division. The text is highly symbolic religious doctrine.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 11
topic_desc: The eleventh installment of Vivec's doctrinal series, presented as the first lesson of ruling kings delivered to the Hortator during Resdaynia. It warns that misused power breeds a broken state and frames reality as the amnesia of dream. Vivec assigns cosmic domains—Ayem the stars, Seht the sea, himself the middle air—while granting the Hortator temporal command of the earth. The sermon introduces the Sharmat as the Hortator's double whose confusion over the symbolism of the center leads to strife. It invokes the Codes of Mephala to erase the line between theorist and terrorist and insists the ruling king must recognize no equivalent. Highly esoteric and propagandistic, it positions Vivec as the indispensable guide who alone can distinguish the Hortator from the Sharmat.
topic_desc_basic: A sermon attributed to Vivec offering the first lesson on ruling kings. It warns that abused power brings ruin, assigns cosmic spheres among the Tribunal, and introduces the Sharmat as the Hortator's double whose false belief in a sacred center causes only strife. The text invokes Mephala's codes and insists the ruling king must recognize no equal.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 12
topic_desc: Sermon Twelve of Vivec's hagiographic series recounts the warrior-poet's encounter with Molag Bal in the badlands. After observing Ayem and Seht in Mourning Hold, Vivec adopts a giant-form, prompting the Daedric Prince to sever his feet. The two negotiate a bizarre ceremonial marriage, during which Vivec utters the phrase 'AE ALTADOON GHARTOK PADHOME,' compelling Molag Bal to reveal the secret syllable of royalty, 'CHIM.' In exchange, Vivec surrenders his head for an hour, offering two poems as proof of love, though only one survives. The doctrine claims thousands of offspring resulted from this union, the mightiest bearing a string of power. As with the entire Lessons series, the account blends mystic revelation with evident propaganda, presenting esoteric theology through mythic allegory.
topic_desc_basic: The twelfth sermon of Vivec's sacred series describes the warrior-poet's confrontation and ritual marriage with the Daedric Prince Molag Bal. During this encounter, Molag Bal reveals the secret syllable 'CHIM' to Vivec. The heavily symbolic text claims the union produced thousands of offspring and serves as both mystical doctrine and Tribunal propaganda.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 13
topic_desc: The thirteenth installment of the Thirty-Six Lessons, authored as Vivec's esoteric doctrine. Set during Resdaynia, it presents the second lesson of ruling kings to the Hortator.
