The sermon employs dense symbolic geometry, mapping the cross of mortal worth within the triangle of the ALMSIVI, bordered by the Four Corners. Vivec declares himself the sword that must ultimately be removed so the dormant center may be refilled, contrasting this necessary sacrifice with the Sharmat's venomous attachment to the world of reference. As psychopomp, Vivec asserts primacy within the Triune, positioning Ayem as the plot and Seht as the ending. The text frames the ruling king's path as requiring struggle against and assimilation of Vivec's form, declaring that a ruler who perceives an equal rules nothing. The narrative is highly propagandistic and deliberately obscure.
topic_desc_basic: The thirteenth sermon of Vivec's Lessons, offering the second lesson of ruling kings to the Hortator. It uses symbolic geometry to describe the ALMSIVI's relationship to mortal worth and the Four Corners. Vivec declares himself the sword that must be removed to refill the dormant center, contrasting this with the Sharmat's folly, and asserts that a true ruler must see no equal.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 14
topic_desc: Sermon Fourteen of the Thirty-Six Lessons recounts Vivec's union with the Daedric Prince Molag Bal, described in mythic and symbolic terms as a marriage of divine forces. The narrative describes the Pomegranate Banquet, the diminishment of the Duke of Scamps, and the birth of a destructive race from the cracked earth. Vivec then forges his spear MUATRA—Milk Taker—from a secret bitten from Molag Bal, wielding it to destroy the spawned biters and render all he strikes barren. The sermon blends cosmogonic myth with esoteric doctrine, presenting divine sexuality, violence, and transformation as intertwined sacred principles. As with all Lessons, the text serves as both Temple scripture and personal revelation of Vivec, combining legend, propaganda, and layered symbolism whose full meaning remains contested among scholars.
topic_desc_basic: The fourteenth sermon of Vivec's Thirty-Six Lessons describes the warrior-poet's mythic union with the Daedric Prince Molag Bal and the creation of his spear MUATRA, the Milk Taker. The text recounts the birth and destruction of a terrible race of biters and frames divine violence as sacred doctrine. It serves as Temple scripture combining legend and esoteric symbolism.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 15
topic_desc: Sermon Fifteen of Vivec's hortatory doctrine recounts the Resdaynian era, presenting Vivec as advisor to a confused Hortator. It delivers the third lesson of ruling kings: that the true ruler will inevitably remove his maker, and that his greatest enemy is the Sharmat, the false dreamer. The text then shifts abruptly into the Sharmat's own voice, proclaiming primordial existence and demanding the world's pylons be torn down. Vivec responds that the Hortator alone can unmake this adversary, instructing him to go unarmed into the enemy's den with the words of power 'AE GHARTOK PADHOME [CHIM] AE ALTADOON.' The sermon frames existence as uncertain, declaring the world an intermittent hope and commanding the Hortator to reach heaven by violence. As with all Lessons, the narrative blends theology, prophecy, and esoteric philosophy, serving simultaneously as devotional text and political doctrine for the Tribunal Temple.
topic_desc_basic: The fifteenth sermon of Vivec's religious text presents the third lesson of ruling kings, warning that a true ruler's greatest enemy is the Sharmat, the false dreamer. It contains the Sharmat's chaotic proclamation and Vivec's instruction to confront him unarmed using words of power. The text blends Temple doctrine with esoteric philosophy.
aliases: The Thirty-Six Lessons of Vivec, Sermon Fifteen

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 16
topic_desc: The sixteenth installment of the Tribunal god's extensive doctrinal text. In this legendary account, Nerevar finds Vivec at the Temple of False Thinking, where the warrior-poet shears his hair to make room for fire and employs the truthful Water Face learned from the dreughs. When Nerevar fears his thinking is becoming slipshod, Vivec commands him to reach heaven by violence. Taking an axe from the Fight Racks, the Hortator travels to the first moon and attacks the Parliament of Craters, who reject his earthly sovereignty. A surviving Crater dismisses his violence as uncreative, arguing that he merely digs graves without supplying ghosts. As with all Lessons, the narrative serves as esoteric doctrine and propaganda, advancing the axiom ALMSIVI while deliberately obscuring the boundaries between myth and history.
topic_desc_basic: The sixteenth sermon of Vivec's doctrinal text. It depicts Nerevar visiting Vivec at the Temple of False Thinking, where the god employs his truthful Water Face. Advised to reach heaven by violence, Nerevar takes an axe and attacks the lunar Parliament of Craters, who reject his earthly rule. A survivor dismisses his assault as uncreative. The account blends esoteric doctrine with legendary propaganda.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 17
topic_desc: The seventeenth sermon of Vivec's devotional series recounts a legendary journey in which Vivec and the Hortator Nerevar travel to distant lands—Akavir, the edge of the world, the Elder Wood, and the west—gathering spokes of a cosmic wheel while learning foreign sword disciplines, including the Tsaesci idiom stroke. The narrative blends martial allegory with esoteric cosmology: the world's edge is described as teeth, and Vivec declares himself the wheel. At Red Mountain, the pair defer from confronting the Sharmat, instead engaging in ritual combat through which Nerevar acquires seven spokes. Vivec forbids assembling them into a staff, declaring the time unready. As Temple doctrine, the text interweals sword-skill instruction with symbolic cosmology, presenting Vivec as the axis of divine and mortal understanding while framing ALMSIVI rule as preordained.
topic_desc_basic: The seventeenth of Vivec's Lessons describes his legendary journey with Nerevar to foreign lands, where they learn sword styles and gather cosmic spokes. At Red Mountain, they defer from confronting the Sharmat and instead duel ritually. The sermon blends martial instruction with symbolic cosmology, presenting Vivec as the wheel of creation and ALMSIVI rule as preordained.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 18
topic_desc: Sermon Eighteen of the Thirty-Six Lessons presents Vivec in dialogue with Ayem in Mourning Hold before the Dwemer war. He declares intent to fight nine monsters escaped from the Muatra; Ayem prophesies he will find only eight, the ninth being himself, already destroyed by his decision to begin the Book of Hours. Vivec then questions whether a member of the Invisible Gate can become archaic and be superseded not by an improved model but by one more suited to the world's changing condition. Ayem responds by recounting his origin: born of a netchiman's wife, merged with the simulacrum of his mother, becoming the magic hermaphrodite and martial axiom. The sermon concludes by declaring itself forbidden and untrue, a characteristic gesture of deliberate paradox. As Temple doctrine attributed to Vivec, the text blends theology, prophecy, and self-negating mysticism, and is also valued as an alchemy instructional work.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Eighteen of the Thirty-Six Lessons of Vivec records the warrior-poet's dialogue with Ayem before the Dwemer war. Vivec discusses his nature as a Tribunal member and his origin as the magic hermaphrodite. The sermon declares itself forbidden and untrue. It is valued among Temple scholars as an alchemy instructional text.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 19
topic_desc: The nineteenth installment of Vivec's doctrinal text depicts the warrior-poet entering a transcendent mental space to assail eight monsters. Within this vision, Vivec perceives prophetic symbols: moths bearing terrible dust from a starry heart, a two-headed ruling king wearing twin crowns of flawed gems resembling shackles, and a river flowing into the king's mouth. Vivec then constructs the Provisional House at the Center of the Secret Door to observe the coming age. The sermon concludes with an enigmatic poem describing the House's four cornerstones through surreal imagery—a buried finger, a talkative tongue, a colored string, and nine bones of a black cat—before breaking off with an anxious repetition about the house's safety. As with the entire Lessons, the account blends esoteric doctrine with mythic prophecy, its reliability inseparable from its propagandistic and mystical purpose.
topic_desc_basic: The nineteenth sermon of Vivec's religious text describes the warrior-poet entering a transcendent space to battle eight monsters. He sees visions of a two-headed king with twin crowns and builds the Provisional House to observe the future. The sermon ends with an enigmatic poem about the House's four cornerstones.
aliases: The Thirty-Six Lessons of Vivec, Sermon Nineteen

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 2
topic_desc: The second sermon of Vivec's thirty-six doctrinal texts continues the allegorical gestation of the warrior-poet. A netchiman's wife bearing the egg of Vivec journeys toward Indoril lands, encountering six spirits. The first imparts the Incalculable Effort; the second is repelled; the third, At-Hatoor, wears garments of implication that the egg gradually infers meaning from. The fourth and fifth spirits—cousins bearing cosmic calamity and primordial marriage—provoke the egg's realization of its own anterior existence. The sixth, Mephala, extracts the egg, merging it with Daedric essence and retrieving ancient secrets before returning it. Mephala withholds the mother's eyes, declaring that gods hold three keys—of birth, machines, and words—and that half lie within this text. As with all Lessons, the account is deeply mythic Tribunal doctrine, blending esoteric theology with propagandist purpose.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Two of Vivec's Lessons recounts the allegorical journey of a netchiman's wife carrying the egg of Vivec. Six spirits offer instruction, including At-Hatoor and Mephala, who merges the egg with Daedric secrets. Mephala declares the sermon holds half of three divine keys. This text serves as Tribunal doctrine blending myth with esoteric theology.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 20
topic_desc: Sermon Twenty of the Thirty-Six Lessons recounts Vivec's confrontation with Moon Axle, the first of eight monsters to escape Muatra. Moon Axle, dual-natured and polyhedral, is immune to spears because he is made of straight lines that ignore true segments. Vivec defeats him using the curved sword not held, then slays him with Muatra after binding him with stolen nix-hound souls blown through a canyon. The shattered lines of Moon Axle are collected by Velothi philosophers, and Vivec teaches them to fashion these into mystery wheels, founding the first Whirling School. The sermon concludes with Vivec's meditation on the sword as estrangement from statesmanship and on his existence as cause for great density. As with all Lessons, the text is doctrinal and propagandistic, blending theology with esoteric philosophy, and its reliability as literal history is questionable.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Twenty of the Thirty-Six Lessons of Vivec describes the warrior-poet's battle with Moon Axle, a dual-natured monster immune to spears. Vivec slays him with Muatra, and the creature's shattered lines are given to Velothi philosophers, founding the first Whirling School. The sermon is Tribunal doctrine blending theology with esoteric philosophy.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 21
topic_desc: Sermon Twenty-One of Vivec's Lessons presents the Scripture of the Wheel, an esoteric cosmological doctrine framing the universe's structure through eight principles. The text identifies the eight spokes as components of chaos solidified by time and as the lent bones of the Aedra, given to Sithisit. It denounces the Aedra as liars whose proselytizing teeth devour the unenlightened, declaring that the truly enlightened remain uneaten by the world. The sermon maps sixteen spaces between these gift-limbs to the Daedric Princedoms. It culminates in mystical observations on the Tower, the second serpent, and the secret triangular gate, asserting that the secret Tower within the Tower embodies the sole name of God: I. As with all Lessons, the doctrine serves Vivec's theological authority and blends obscure metaphor with propaganda.
topic_desc_basic: The twenty-first of Vivec's Lessons presents the Scripture of the Wheel. It describes the eight spokes of chaos as the Aedra's lent bones, denounces the Aedra as deceptive devourers of the unenlightened, and maps the sixteen spaces between them to the Daedric Princedoms. The sermon concludes with mystical revelations regarding the secret Tower and the divine name I.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 22
topic_desc: Sermon Twenty-Two of the Thirty-Six Lessons depicts Vivec seeking the Treasure Wood Sword, a relic revered by the lower Velothi for granting self-knowledge. The warrior-poet confronts a bone-walker in House Mora's ancestor alcove, demanding the blade. When the undead guardian refuses, citing pacts with Mephala, Vivec subdues it by kissing three jaw-stones. He then weds the darkest mothers of the Morag Tong, transforming them into prolific agents of sacred murder across Ra'athim holdings. The King of Assassins surrenders the sword and reports placing the Mora prince in the Corner of Dagon. As Tribunal doctrine, the sermon intertwines divine authority, ancestral necromancy, and the sanctioned violence of Mephala's cult, presenting esoteric metaphor as sacred history.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Twenty-Two of the Thirty-Six Lessons describes Vivec seeking the Treasure Wood Sword from House Mora. After subduing a bone-walker guardian, he weds the dark mothers of the Morag Tong, unleashing sacred murder across Ra'athim lands. The King of Assassins yields the blade. As Tribunal doctrine, the text intertwines divine authority with Mephala's cult.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 23
topic_desc: Sermon Twenty-Three of the Thirty-Six Lessons, attributed to Vivec, presents 'The Scripture of the Sword' in eight numbered teachings. The sermon treats the sword as both weapon and metaphysical symbol—a 'Symbolic Collage' whose mastery reflects divine understanding. Vivec frames martial discipline as devotional service to ALMSIVI, declaring 'AE ALTADOON' the third law of weaponry. The text interweaves practical warrior philosophy—the 'immobile warrior' who cuts 'sleep holes' in battle—with esoteric theology, referencing the 'second walking way' and the 'birth of God from the netchiman's wife.' The true sword is said to cut 'chains of generations,' meaning the creation myths of enemies. As with all Lessons, the work is Temple doctrine blending revelation, propaganda, and deliberately obscure mysticism; its claims should be read as Vivec's self-serving theological instruction rather than objective history.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Twenty-Three of the Thirty-Six Lessons of Vivec is titled 'The Scripture of the Sword.' Attributed to the warrior-poet god Vivec, it offers eight teachings on the sword as both martial tool and sacred symbol. The sermon frames combat skill as devotion to ALMSIVI and blends practical warrior philosophy with esoteric Tribunal theology. Copies are preserved in Temple and Redoran holdings.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 24
topic_desc: Sermon Twenty-Four of Vivec's Lessons recounts the god's confrontation with Horde Mountain, a monstrous entity of hierarchically arranged warriors. After Velothi houses ensnare the creature in a net of doctrine, Vivec transforms them into the Buoyant Armigers. Piercing the monster with Muatra, he scatters its bones northeasterly; they become the foundation of the City of Swords, named after Vivec's sigil, while the net becomes its perfect streets. Almalexia and Sotha Sil then bless the new city: she grants House Indoril's protection, and he provides the spell SO-T-HA SIL to safeguard wanderers and make the city a living conduit to ALMSIVI. The sermon is deeply mythic doctrine, presenting the Tribunal's divinely ordained founding of Vivec City through allegorical violence and transformation.
topic_desc_basic: The twenty-fourth sermon of Vivec's Lessons describes his defeat of the monster Horde Mountain. After creating the Buoyant Armigers, he transforms the creature's remains into the foundation of his namesake city. Almalexia and Sotha Sil then bless the new settlement with protection and sacred spells. The work serves as mythic doctrine explaining the divine founding of Vivec City.
aliases: The Thirty-Six Lessons of Vivec, Sermon Twenty-Four

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 25
topic_desc: The Twenty-Fifth Sermon of Vivec's Lessons presents the 'Scripture of the City,' a mystical doctrine equating the god's divine form with his city. Vivec describes his body as an urban landscape, where veins become catwalks, the spine a main road, and the skull bears temples as a crown. The text claims all cities originate from 'solid light' and depicts Vivec's pre-chimerical, demonic form as the angel of Veloth. Through surreal allegory, the sermon asserts that urban civilization supersedes the primal hunt, with the city acting as a living organism that absorbs its inhabitants and their transactions. The narrative culminates in the Psijic promise of the Aurbis—'egg, image, man, god, city, state'—framing the divine-city as the ultimate metaphysical realization. As with all Lessons, the account blends hagiography with esoteric philosophy, serving both as Tribunal propaganda and deep symbolic doctrine.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Twenty-Five of the Thirty-Six Lessons presents the 'Scripture of the City,' where Vivec equates his divine body with his city. Through surreal allegory, veins become streets and the skull wears temples as a crown. The text claims cities are born of light and replace the primal hunt, framing the divine-city as a living organism and the ultimate metaphysical realization of the Aurbis.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 26
topic_desc: The twenty-sixth installment of Vivec's doctrinal scripture recounts the warrior-poet's hunt for the fourth monster, the Pocket Cabal, which had concealed itself within the spell-lists of eastern Chimeri wizards. Using Muatra as a walking dwarf to steal the monster's essential words, Vivec inadvertently caused magical chaos when the construct exploded near slave pens; the freed Cabal possessed the slaves, whose babbling disrupted reality and summoned litany fiends and Grabbers from the Adjacent Place. After slaying a powerful eastern wizard who criticized the resulting disorder, Vivec imprisoned the Pocket Cabal beneath a dome-head demon, cursing the land against sorcery. Sotha Sil later asked to treasure this confusing containment. The sermon serves as esoteric Tribunal propaganda, weaving allegorical and deeply uncertain mythic narrative to convey metaphysical doctrine regarding hidden knowledge, the dangers of uncontrolled arcane speech, and the subversion of temporal myth.
topic_desc_basic: The twenty-sixth sermon of Vivec's scripture describes the warrior-poet hunting the fourth monster, the Pocket Cabal, which hid in eastern wizards' spell-lists. After stealing its words with Muatra, the resulting chaos freed the monster into slaves, disrupting reality. Vivec ultimately imprisoned the Cabal beneath a dome-head demon, cursing the land, and allowed Sotha Sil to study the containment.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 27
topic_desc: Sermon Twenty-Seven of Vivec's Lessons presents the Scripture of the Word, an esoteric doctrine on the nature of language, meaning, and the 'third walking path.' Vivec declares language rooted in material existence and asserts that deliberate incoherence can still serve a method. He warns against seeking absolution in the 'realm of apology' and claims to have stolen certainty from the Chancellor of Exactitude in the Adjacent Place, a constructed realm of vocal illusion. The sermon insists that true meaning remains hidden, silence holds ultimate truth, and that suppressing wisdom is theft. It condemns reliance on 'broken maps'—accepted narratives mistaken for completeness—stating no word is true until consumed. As with all Lessons, the text serves as Temple doctrine and personal mythology, blending mystical philosophy with propagandistic self-aggrandizement.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Twenty-Seven of the Thirty-Six Lessons presents the Scripture of the Word, Vivec's esoteric doctrine on language and meaning. It advocates the 'third walking path,' warns against the illusion of the Adjacent Place, and insists that true meaning is hidden and no word is true until consumed. The work blends mystical philosophy with Temple doctrine.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 28
topic_desc: Sermon Twenty-Eight of Vivec's Lessons recounts the warrior-poet's battle against the fifth monster, the Ruddy Man. This creature originated as a discarded carapace of Molag Bal's ancient dreugh-form, which a Velothi child donned near Gnisis. Vivec's clash allegedly carved the West Gash. After entrusting the shell to the dreughs, who betrayed him and empowered it instead, Vivec slew the resurgent monster near Tear. He finally delivered the carapace to the Number Room mystics, commanding them to forge a philosopher's armor through obscure numerological rites. As with all Lessons, the narrative blends doctrine with mythic allegory.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Twenty-Eight of Vivec's Lessons recounts his battle with the Ruddy Man, a living carapace linked to Molag Bal's ancient dreugh-form. After defeating the monster near Gnisis, Vivec entrusted the shell to the dreughs, who betrayed him and re-empowered it. Slaying it again near Tear, he gave the carapace to mystics to forge a philosopher's armor.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 29
topic_desc: Sermon Twenty-Nine of Vivec's Lessons presents the Scripture of the Numbers, a numerological catalog assigning esoteric concepts—such as the Dragon Break, the Enantiomorph, and the Invisible Gate—to the integers one through thirty-six. The text declares that numbers are the presence of deaf witnesses clinging to the Aurbis as the last nostalgia of their godhood, and that affixing them to current applications is folly. As with all Lessons, the work serves as doctrine and propaganda for the Tribunal. Hidden within the text, a concealed message formed by extracting specific words from the thirty-six sermons reveals a startling confession: Vivec was not born a god, chose his path of his own free will, stole the godhood, and murdered the Hortator. Whether this cipher represents genuine guilt, a test of insight, or esoteric metaphor remains deeply uncertain.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Twenty-Nine of Vivec's Lessons catalogs the Scripture of the Numbers, assigning esoteric concepts to the integers one through thirty-six. The text declares that numbers are deaf witnesses clinging to the Aurbis as the last nostalgia of their godhood. A concealed message hidden across the Lessons suggests Vivec stole his divinity and murdered the Hortator, though the cipher's true intent remains uncertain.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 3
topic_desc: Sermon Three of the Thirty-Six Lessons recounts the netchiman's wife's capture by Dwemer who discover the egg of Vivec within her. Unable to extract it by knives, solid sounds, or heat, the Dwemer kill her and place the egg in magical glass. Vivec confounds his captors by channeling love, an emotion alien to Dwemer, and delivers a discourse on love's nature. A Dwemer acknowledges the Velothi possess something the Dwemer only aspire to, prophesying their doom across eight named worlds. The sermon blends hagiographic myth with esoteric philosophy, presenting Vivec's prebirth divinity and the Dwemer's fundamental incomprehension of love as their weakness. As Temple scripture attributed to Vivec, it serves doctrinal and devotional purposes, and its reliability as literal history is questionable. The closing formula ALMSIVI reinforces Tribunal theology.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Three of the Thirty-Six Lessons of Vivec tells how the netchiman's wife was captured by Dwemer who sought to extract the egg of Vivec from her womb. Failing, they killed her and studied the egg in magical glass. Vivec confounded them with love, an emotion the Dwemer could not understand. The sermon is Temple scripture attributed to Vivec.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 30
topic_desc: The thirtieth sermon of Vivec's doctrinal text recounts the hunt for the sixth monster, City-Face. Born as Ha-Note, an urge of power attuned to settled masses, it grew in the Adjacent Place by absorbing immortal emotions beyond the mortal thirty. Seized by the Grabbers, who coveted Vivec's city, it was shaped into a rival tower-hope. The narrative frames this alongside Dwemer efforts in Resdaynia, linking both to cultural mimicry. When City-Face threatens to seize Vivec's city by force, Vivec corrects the Grabbers' error and slays the monster with the Ethos Knife, the short blade of proper commerce. The sermon opens with Vivec killing a mystic who questioned higher order, declaring his nature unknowable. As with all Lessons, the account is highly esoteric and propagandistic, presenting symbolic cosmology as divine history.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Thirty of Vivec's holy text describes his battle against City-Face, a monster born from the cultural urges of settled peoples. After the entity is reshaped by beings called Grabbers into a rival city, Vivec destroys it with the Ethos Knife. The sermon's esoteric doctrine blends symbolic cosmology with Tribunal propaganda.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 31
topic_desc: Sermon Thirty-One of Vivec's devotional work recounts the warrior-poet retreating to the Litany Hall to write in his Book of Hours after battling creatures stirred up by Dwemer brass siege machines. Adopting his Water Face, he records a heretical confession that the Et'ada were liars and that his divine role fails the people, before obscuring it with ink. He replaces the passage with dense, violent metaphor proclaiming himself the mangling messiah and partaker of the Doom Drum, veiling subversive theology in esoteric doctrine.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Thirty-One describes Vivec retreating to write after fighting monsters stirred up by Dwemer siege machines. He records a private confession questioning the original spirits and his own divine adequacy, then obscures it with ink, replacing it with metaphorical proclamations of his divine authority as the mangling messiah.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 32
topic_desc: The Thirty-Six Lessons of Vivec, Sermon Thirty-Two presents the Scripture of the Mace, a cryptic doctrinal text attributed to Vivec. Through eight numbered aphorisms, the sermon frames mortal existence as imprisonment and frames annihilation as a liberating escape into the unreal. It addresses the Velothi directly, linking their suffering and bruised appearance to Boethiah's exodus. The text references the 'fourth walking way' and characterizes the Daedra as a necessary radical critique of the Aurbis, claiming their varying degrees of malice constitute a 'necessary illusion.' As with the broader Lessons, the work blends theology and philosophy into deliberately obscure propaganda, demanding interpretation rather than offering transparent truth.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Thirty-Two of Vivec's Lessons presents the Scripture of the Mace. It offers cryptic teachings on mortal existence, the Daedra's role as a radical critique of the Aurbis, and the Velothi exodus under Boethiah. The sermon blends theology and philosophy into obscure doctrine.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 33
topic_desc: The thirty-third of Vivec's Thirty-Six Lessons, attributed to the warrior-poet god Vivec himself. The sermon recounts Vivec's pursuit of the seventh monster, Lie Rock, born of his Second Aperture and cast into the heavens. Lie Rock bargains with the Void Ghost within the Scaled Blanket of thirteen not-stars. Vivec dispatches Nerevar as Hortator to the Hidden Heaven, where the pole-stars grant him red sight to track the monster. Lie Rock attacks the city of Vivec as a falling star, but Vivec freezes it above the city and pierces it with Muatra. He chooses to keep the suspended rock as a permanent warning: should the people's love for him fade, the power holding back destruction fails. Nerevar is named a Minister of Truth. The sermon blends cosmological myth with Temple doctrine, presenting Vivec's authority as contingent on popular devotion. As with all Lessons, the narrative is propagandistic and symbolically dense.
topic_desc_basic: The thirty-third sermon of Vivec's Thirty-Six Lessons. It describes the defeat of the monster Lie Rock, which fell toward Vivec's city as a shooting star. Vivec froze it overhead and pierced it with Muatra, keeping it suspended as a warning that the city's protection depends on the people's love for him. Nerevar is named a Minister of Truth. The text serves as Temple doctrine.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 34
topic_desc: Sermon Thirty-Four of Vivec's doctrinal text recounts the god and Hortator Nerevar visiting the Provisional House to confront the eighth and mightiest of Vivec's monstrous offspring, GULGA MOR JIL. The passive creature questions its obligation to die and return to oblivion. Offering consolation rather than violence, Vivec persuades it to accept Muatra; its bones then form the foundation of the City of the Dead, Narsis. When Nerevar questions why he was summoned for such a yielding foe, an exchange of silent understanding follows, culminating in Nerevar declaring himself the mightiest of Vivec's children. The sermon functions as both mythic narrative and consolatory doctrine for those facing mortality, characteristic of the Lessons' layered and unreliable theological style.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Thirty-Four of Vivec's doctrine describes him and Nerevar confronting the eighth and mightiest of Vivec's offspring. The passive creature accepts Muatra after receiving consolation, and its bones become the foundation of Narsis. Nerevar then declares himself the mightiest of Vivec's children. The text offers consolation to those destined to die.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 35
topic_desc: Sermon Thirty-Five of the Thirty-Six Lessons, attributed to Vivec, presents the 'Scripture of Love.' It frames love as sacrifice and cosmic return, linking Velothi magical tradition to the codes of Mephala—origin of sex and murder. The text prophesies future catastrophes from 'all five corners' and casts Vivec's reign as an act of highest love. It invokes the hermaphroditic ideal, the sword as instrument of divine harvest, and the number five as the world's limit. References to Anu and his double are dismissed as symbols nearing obsolescence. The sermon is explicitly doctrinal propaganda, blending mystical philosophy with Temple theology. Its esoteric language and self-referential prophecies make reliable interpretation difficult; claims about cosmic repetition and future events are presented as revelation rather than verifiable history. The sermon closes with the ALMSIVI benediction.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon Thirty-Five of the Thirty-Six Lessons of Vivec, titled the Scripture of Love, is a doctrinal text attributed to the warrior-poet Vivec. It treats love as sacrifice, invokes the codes of Mephala, and prophesies future catastrophes. The esoteric language blends Temple theology with mystical philosophy, serving as religious instruction for the faithful.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 36
topic_desc: Sermon 36 of Vivec's Lessons presents the Tribunal's doctrinal account of the War of the First Council and the Battle of Red Mountain. It describes the Dwemer's golden siege engines and tonal architects, Nerevar's slaying of Dumac, and Kagrenac's activation of a devastating 'walking star' that creates the Inner Sea. The ALMSIVI combine, extract power from the device, and remove the Dwemer from the world. They then consume Red Mountain's ash to contain the Blight. The narrative serves as Tribunal propaganda, glorifying the Triune while obscuring historical reality; a hidden acrostic reading 'FOUL MURDER' undermines the text's reliability.
topic_desc_basic: Sermon 36 recounts the Tribunal's version of the War of the First Council and the Battle of Red Mountain. It describes Nerevar slaying Dumac, Kagrenac unleashing a devastating walking star, and the ALMSIVI combining to defeat the Dwemer and contain the Blight. The account is Tribunal doctrine, though a hidden acrostic challenges its truthfulness.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 4
topic_desc: The fourth sermon of Vivec's mystico-doctrinal text continues the allegorical journey of the netchiman's wife simulacrum bearing the pre-born Vivec toward Indoril lands. Three spiritual challenges present themselves. The Coincidence Guild advocates for chance, but the embryonic Vivec argues that synchronicity's very repetition invalidates the concept of coincidence, destroying happenstance in Velothi lands. An Old Bone demands new words to confuse the world; Vivec replies with cryptic paradoxes of hidden observation, whereupon the Bone becomes milk that Vivec drinks to become a ruling king. Finally, the Chancellor of Exactitude embodies certainty, which Vivec rejects, declaring himself a letter written in uncertainty. The Chancellor breaks the universe's astrolabe, and Vivec accepts that a ruling king must weigh immeasurable matters and suffer the unendurable. The sermon serves as Tribunal doctrine promoting divine determinism and sacred paradox over chance and certitude, composed as esoteric propaganda blending metaphysical riddle with devotional narrative.
topic_desc_basic: The fourth sermon of Vivec's holy text recounts the pre-born god's allegorical encounters with spirits representing coincidence, earthly tradition, and certainty. Vivec refutes coincidence as an illusion, consumes an ancient spirit to gain sovereign power, and embraces uncertainty over exactitude. This Tribunal scripture teaches that divine will supersedes chance and that true rulership requires enduring the immeasurable.
aliases: Thirty-Six Lessons of Vivec Sermon Four

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 5
topic_desc: The fifth sermon of Vivec's devotional series continues the mythic account of the netchiman's wife simulacrum. The Dwemer-built construct breaks down along an Indoril road, where a Chimeri merchant caravan discovers it. A debate ensues: a warrior and a seer urge delivering the simulacrum to Ayem in Almalexia, sensing sacred significance, while the merchant captain intends to sell it to the Red Wives of Dagon at Noormoc, driven by lust and profit. The warrior is revealed as Nerevar. When the captain refuses Nerevar's payment, Vivec speaks cryptically into Nerevar's mind, prompting Nerevar to slay the captain and claim the caravan. The narrative blends hagiographic doctrine with legendary allegory, portraying Nerevar as an instrument of divine will while obscuring historical truth behind symbolic prose.
topic_desc_basic: The fifth of Vivec's Lessons describes the discovery of the broken netchiman's wife simulacrum by a Chimer caravan. A dispute over its fate ends when Nerevar, counselled by Vivec, kills the merchant captain and claims the construct to bring it to Ayem. The work serves as Temple doctrine, blending mythic allegory with hagiographic purpose.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 6
topic_desc: The sixth Sermon of Vivec presents esoteric doctrine through numerological and symbolic revelation, centered on the number six. It assigns roles to the Anticipations—Mephala and Azura as twin gates of tradition, Boethiah as the secret flame—and describes six formulas to reach heaven through violence. The text outlines a tripartite figure: the Father as machine, the Mother as active and clawed yet holy, and the Son as Vivec himself, bound to numerical progressions. Throughout, the sermon employs deliberate redefinition, stating that by the sword and the word it means varied concepts across repetitions. It positions the Dunmer above the savage Altmer and below a divine challenge, declaring Vivec protector of Red Mountain until an enumerated end of days. As with the broader Lessons, the work blends mystic philosophy with Temple propaganda, its obscure language resisting single interpretation.
topic_desc_basic: The sixth Sermon of Vivec delivers cryptic numerological doctrine centered on the number six. It assigns symbolic roles to the Anticipations, describes six paths to heaven by violence, and presents a triad of Father, Mother, and Son—identifying himself as the Son. The text uses deliberately shifting meanings for sword and word, blending mystic teaching with Temple doctrine.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 7
topic_desc: The seventh sermon of Vivec's devotional text depicts Nerevar's caravan traveling toward Almalexia while Daedric forces muster in opposition. A Duke of Scamps presents seven bizarre legions to the major domo of Mehrunes Dagon, but is told they cannot overcome Nerevar or the Triune way. Looking into the mortal plane, the Daedra witness the Hortator bearing a curse upon his hands, where an egg has inscribed the words of power invoking Padhome. The sermon propagandistically asserts Tribunal supremacy over the House of Troubles, casting Nerevar as a figure of metaphysical might who wields Padomaic power itself against Daedric opposition. Its symbolic language and surreal imagery resist literal interpretation.
topic_desc_basic: The seventh sermon of Vivec's religious text describes Daedric forces under Mehrunes Dagon mustering seven legions against Nerevar. A servant of Dagon declares these forces cannot overcome the Hortator or the Tribunal way, and the sermon asserts Nerevar bears words of power from Padhome written on his palms. The text serves as Tribunal doctrine affirming the Triune's supremacy over the House of Troubles.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 8
topic_desc: The eighth sermon of Vivec's doctrinal text recounts the arrival of Nerevar and the embryonic Vivec at Mourning Hold, where Ayem and the forgotten guild of the Shouts receive them. Nerevar presents the simulacrum of the netchiman's wife containing Vivec's egg, arguing that the Velothi must adopt Dwemer machines without shame. Vivec invokes Boethiah's deception of Trinimac as precedent for this transformative path. Sotha Sil manifests, and the Triune proclaims its divine unity. Vivec then merges with the maternal simulacrum, becoming a dual-natured hermaphrodite embodying manifold esoteric arts. The sermon serves as Temple doctrine and mythic propaganda, employing heavily symbolic and unreliable narration to legitimize the Tribunal's divine authority and syncretic cultural adaptations.
topic_desc_basic: The eighth sermon describes Nerevar arriving at Mourning Hold with the egg of Vivec, arguing the Velothi should adopt Dwemer machines. The Tribunal assembles as Vivec merges with his maternal simulacrum, becoming a dual-natured hermaphrodite. The text serves as symbolic Temple doctrine.

title: 36 Lessons of Vivec, Sermon 9
topic_desc: The ninth sermon of Vivec's devotional epic recounts the war against northern invaders, during which Vivec guides the Hortator into a cunning alliance with the Dwemer. It catalogues five formidable demon chieftains—Hoaga, Chemua, Bhag, Barfok, and Ysmir—detailing their unnatural powers and the devastation they inflicted upon Chimeri and Dwemeri settlements before being defeated through martial might or divine cunning. The text's allegiances and symbolism are deeply esoteric, and its portrayal of historical events blends hagiography with mythic parable, casting the warrior-poet as the indispensable savior of Velothi civilization. The sermon concludes with an enigmatic invocation of Herma-Mora.
topic_desc_basic: The ninth sermon of Vivec's scripture describes the war against northern invaders, naming five demon chieftains who threatened Velothi lands. It credits Vivec and the Hortator with defeating these foes through combat and cunning, portraying the warrior-poet as the people's indispensable savior.

title: Biography of the Wolf Queen
topic_desc: Katar Eriphanes's biography chronicles Potema, the so-called Wolf Queen of Solitude, from her birth in 3E 67 to her death in 3E 137. Born into the Imperial family and married to King Mantiarco of Solitude, Potema amassed power and orchestrated rebellion against Empress Kintyra II, sparking the War of the Red Diamond. The narrative portrays her as unambiguously evil, tracing her descent into madness after her son Uriel III's death, when she summoned daedra and undead to wage war against Emperor Cephorus I. Eriphanes recounts Potema's Elder Council speech as a model of rhetorical manipulation and notes uncertain claims that she poisoned her brother Antiochus. The author also relays unverified legends that her spirit became a daedra and that her madness infected Castle Solitude, driving her nephew Pelagius III to insanity. The work blends historical narrative with sensational anecdote and acknowledged legend, presenting a vivid but not always reliable account.
topic_desc_basic: Katar Eriphanes chronicles the life of Potema, the Wolf Queen of Solitude, portraying her as unambiguously evil. The book traces her rise, her role in the War of the Red Diamond, and her descent into madness with daedra and undead. It includes acknowledged legends about her spirit and influence over Pelagius the Mad.

title: Hallgerd's Tale
topic_desc: Tavi Dromio's dialogue-frame narrative debates the identity of history's greatest warrior. Rejecting weapon mastery and territorial conquest as measures, the storyteller Hallgerd recounts the legend of Hlaalu Pasoroth, a noble whose extraordinary skill lay in moving with supreme agility while wearing heavy armor. When his wife Mena and the armorer Taren conspire to consummate their affair by sabotaging Pasoroth's armor joints with luca dust and warning bells, Pasoroth unexpectedly walks on his hands to catch them. The tale, presented as dubious history with a ribald twist, ultimately argues that true martial mastery includes the ability to fight, move, and act while fully armored.
topic_desc_basic: Tavi Dromio's narrative debates history's greatest warrior. The storyteller Hallgerd recounts the legend of Hlaalu Pasoroth, whose extraordinary skill was moving with supreme agility in heavy armor. When his wife and an armorer sabotaged his armor to facilitate their affair, Pasoroth walked on his hands to catch them, illustrating that true mastery includes full armored capability.

title: Master Zoaraym's Tale
topic_desc: A philosophical memoir by the Khajiit monk Gi'Nanth recounting the teachings of Master Zoaraym at the Temple of the Two-Moons Dance in Torval. The narrative describes how a Dunmer servant, Taren Omathan, secretly absorbed both foundational and advanced unarmed combat techniques while cleaning the training chambers. During a graduation festival, Taren requested to compete and ultimately defeated the prideful Zoaraym in the championship bout, demonstrating that true mastery requires retaining early lessons alongside advanced skill. Taren explained that his menial position forced him to observe all levels of instruction without the forgetfulness that accompanies advancing through the Temple's prescribed curriculum. The tale illustrates the Riddle'Thar philosophy of rejecting vanity and achieving mind-body synchronicity, presenting a didactic lesson about humility rather than strict historical record.
topic_desc_basic: A memoir by the Khajiit monk Gi'Nanth about Master Zoaraym of the Temple of the Two-Moons Dance in Torval. It recounts how a Dunmer servant named Taren Omathan secretly learned unarmed combat by observing the training chambers he cleaned, ultimately defeating the prideful Zoaraym in a festival championship. The tale teaches the Riddle'Thar principle of rejecting vanity and remembering foundational lessons.

title: Mystery of Talara, Part 1
topic_desc: A historical drama by Mera Llykith set during Camlorn's millennial celebration in 3E 405. The narrative follows Gyna, a Daggerfall prostitute, who experiences uncanny familiarity with the city and bears an astonishing physical resemblance to Lady Jyllia Raze, the current King's daughter. When Jyllia's ancient nursemaid Ramke sees Gyna, she hysterically identifies her as the Princess Talara, a royal family member supposedly assassinated over twenty years prior. Jyllia refutes this, claiming her father inherited the throne after the massacre. During the Flower Festival, an unseen assailant pushes Gyna from Cavilstyr Rock. Suspended mid-fall, a childhood vision returns, restoring her memory and true identity as Talara. She then uses recalled advice to survive the plunge.
topic_desc_basic: A historical drama set in 3E 405 Camlorn. A prostitute named Gyna discovers she bears an uncanny resemblance to Lady Jyllia, the King's daughter. An old nursemaid insists Gyna is the Princess Talara, believed assassinated decades prior. After being pushed from a cliff, Gyna's memories return, revealing her true identity.

title: Mystery of Talara, Part 2
topic_desc: The second installment of Mera Llykith's serial follows the woman called Gyna after she survives being pushed from Cavilstyr Rock during Camlorn's Flower Festival. Wounded and nearly drowned, she reaches the shore and is rescued by Ramke, an elderly healer and former nursemaid. Ramke mends Gyna's grievous leg wound with Restoration magic and shares the tragic history of Lady Jyllia Raze, who witnessed the royal family's assassination and never fully recovered. Ramke notes Gyna's striking resemblance to the lost Princess Talara, whose body was never found. Accepting her true identity, Gyna chooses to return to Camlorn rather than flee to Daggerfall. On the road, she encounters Lord Strale, the Imperial ambassador, and reveals her secrets to him.
topic_desc_basic: The second part of Mera Llykith's serial about Princess Talara. After surviving an attempt on her life in Camlorn, a woman known as Gyna is healed by an old nursemaid who remarks on her resemblance to the lost princess. Accepting her true identity, she meets the Imperial ambassador and reveals her secrets.
aliases: The Mystery of Princess Talara Part II

title: Mystery of Talara, Part 3
topic_desc: The third installment of Mera Llykith's serial fiction, set in High Rock. Imperial Ambassador Lord Strale and the woman Gyna meet Emperor's agent Lady Brisienna in Umbington, seeking Imperial aid to expose a twenty-year-old assassination conspiracy connected to the late Princess Talara. Brisienna demands proof and a confession. Royal Battlemage Lord Eryl ambushes them, but Strale reveals formidable magical skill, using a conservative fire spell to counter Eryl's reckless destruction. Gnorbooth sacrifices himself, and Strale captures Eryl to interrogate him about the Duke of Oloine.
topic_desc_basic: The third part of Mera Llykith's serial fiction. Imperial Ambassador Lord Strale and Gyna seek Lady Brisienna's aid against a Camlorn conspiracy linked to Princess Talara. Royal Battlemage Lord Eryl ambushes them, but Strale counters with fire magic, captures Eryl, and demands answers about the Duke of Oloine.

title: Mystery of Talara, Part 4
topic_desc: The fourth installment of Mera Llykith's serialized mystery, set in the Breton kingdom of Camlorn. Gyna, trained in illusion by the Imperial nightblade Proseccus, uses charm and paralysis spells to ensnare the cruel Prince Sylon and locate a hidden royal archive. Imperial ambassador Lord Strale then confronts the King and Queen with an unfinished letter from their murdered predecessor, dated 3E 385, warning the Emperor of Jagar Tharn's treachery four years before the Imperial Simulacrum began. With Royal Battlemage Lord Eryl's confession and concealed nightblades, Strale arrests the royal couple. A mysterious woman resembling the long-vanished Princess Talara accompanies him. The narrative blends political intrigue with practical illustration of illusion magic and should be read as dramatic fiction drawing on real historical events rather than verified chronicle.
topic_desc_basic: The fourth part of Mera Llykith's serialized tale of Princess Talara, set in the Breton kingdom of Camlorn. It follows Gyna's use of illusion magic to entrap Prince Sylon and Imperial ambassador Lord Strale's arrest of the King and Queen using evidence linking them to the late King's assassination and the Jagar Tharn affair. A widely circulated work of historical fiction.
aliases: The Mystery of Princess Talara Part IV

title: Mystery of Talara, Part 5
topic_desc: The final installment of Mera Llykith's serial recounts the resolution of the Camlorn royal murder mystery. Imperial officer Lord Strale reveals that the Duke of Oloine hired the assassin who killed Camlorn's king and queen twenty years prior, then murdered the assassin himself to silence him. The crucial revelation is an identity swap: the woman known as Gyna is actually Lady Jyllia Raze, the Duke's daughter, while the woman raised as Jyllia is in truth Princess Talara, who survived by fleeing through a window and lost her memory in the fall. The confusion arose because the two cousins resembled each other closely, the assassin saw only one child, and a devoted nursemaid refused to accept that her charge had vanished. The narrative is dramatic fiction framed as political intrigue in the Breton kingdoms, presented as a concluded mystery rather than historical record.
topic_desc_basic: The final chapter of Mera Llykith's serial resolves the Camlorn royal murder mystery. An Imperial officer reveals that the Duke of Oloine orchestrated the assassination of Camlorn's royal family, and that two cousins swapped identities after the tragedy. The woman raised as Jyllia is actually Princess Talara, who survived the attack but lost her memory. It is dramatic fiction set in High Rock.

title: Song of the Alchemists
topic_desc: Part V of the fictional series Ancient Tales of the Dwemer, attributed to Marobar Sul but widely recognized as the work of the Interregnum-era writer Gor Felim. The poem recounts a contest between two alchemists, Ianthippus Minthurk and Umphatic Faer, hired by King Maraneon to brew an invisibility tonic. Minthurk succeeds, but Faer fails after misjudging how light filtering through crystalline domes alters ingredient hues, accidentally creating a potion that fortifies intelligence instead. The publisher's note identifies Felim's deliberately clumsy meter and absurd naming as anti-intellectual comedy aimed at Interregnum audiences, wholly misrepresenting actual Dwemer culture. The text notably omits specific Dwemer deities, reflecting the enduring puzzle surrounding their religion. The piece later became a popular tavern song in High Rock before fading into purely scholarly preservation.
topic_desc_basic: A comedic poem from the fictional Ancient Tales of the Dwemer series, actually written by Gor Felim under the pen name Marobar Sul. It tells of an alchemy contest where a competitor accidentally brews an intelligence tonic due to misreading ingredient colors. The work reflects Interregnum-era anti-intellectual humor rather than genuine Dwemer culture, and was once a popular tavern song in High Rock.
aliases: Ancient Tales of the Dwemer Part V
Marobar Sul Song of the Alchemists

title: The Art of War Magic
topic_desc: The Art of War Magic is a treatise attributed to Zurin Arctus, the legendary Imperial Battlemage of Tiber Septim, accompanied by commentary from several learned masters including Leros Chael, Sedd Mar, Marandro Ur, Thulidden dir'Tharkun, and Marandro Sul. The surviving chapter, on dispositions, advances the doctrine that the highest achievement of war magic is victory without battle, that common destructive spells represent only the lowest tier of skill, and that a battlemage must balance arcane and mundane factors when planning campaigns. Anecdotes describe Arctus advising Tiber Septim at the Battle of Five Bridges and a Chimer sorcerer turning Nord storm-shamanism against its wielders. The layered commentaries suggest a scholarly transmission tradition. Given Arctus's mythic stature in Imperial history, some episodes may be legendary rather than strictly historical.
topic_desc_basic: The Art of War Magic is a military treatise attributed to Zurin Arctus, Tiber Septim's Imperial Battlemage, with commentary by various learned masters. The surviving chapter teaches that true mastery of war magic lies in securing victory before battle begins, and that common battle spells represent only the least form of the art. It is valued by practitioners of Destruction magic.

title: The Final Lesson
topic_desc: A instructional text by Aegrothius Goth, framed as a sage's tale to his apprentices Taksim and Vonguldak. Set during the Alessian Reform, it recounts the enchanter Dalak sending his students Uthrac and Loreth to aid the isolated mage Peothil. Loreth discovers Peothil destroyed by his own flawed warding enchantment, then successfully completes the spell using Dalak's foundational teachings. After Dalak's death, the reunited apprentices diverge: Uthrac becomes a competent but minor enchanter serving Clan Direnni, while Loreth's independent experimentation leads him to forge the Balac-thurm, the Staff of Chaos. The narrative resolves the tension between formal instruction and solitary innovation, concluding that while a master's guidance prevents fatal errors, true greatness requires independent exploration.
topic_desc_basic: An instructional text by Aegrothius Goth presenting a sage's tale about two apprentices sent to aid a hermetic enchanter during the Alessian Reform. It illustrates that while a master's guidance prevents fatal magical errors, true greatness requires independent experimentation, citing the creation of the Staff of Chaos as evidence.

title: The Marksmanship Lesson
topic_desc: A instructional narrative by Alla Llaleth detailing a Bosmer archery philosophy through the account of Dob, an enslaved former highwayman. Purchased by the Dunmer plantation owner Kelmeril Brin, Dob is ordered to teach Brin's son marksmanship. Dob's Valenwood method emphasizes understanding arrow arcs and wind before targeting accuracy, a principle Brin rejects as useless. When Brin violently whips Dob for this unorthodox approach, Dob continues shouting adjustments to the weeping boy. The resulting high, arcing shot strikes Brin fatally in the neck. Whether the kill reflects genuine Valenwood technique, a calculated assassination by the rogue, or tragic accident remains ambiguous in Llaleth's account.
topic_desc_basic: A treatise on archery by Alla Llaleth, framed as a story about a Bosmer slave teaching his Dunmer master's son. The slave advocates a Valenwood method of learning arrow arcs and wind before accuracy. The master's violent rejection of this approach leads to his death when a high arcing shot strikes him, leaving the slave's intent ambiguous.

title: The Wolf Queen, Book I
topic_desc: This historical chronicle by Waughin Jarth, attributed to the sage Montocai, recounts the early life of Potema Septim. It opens with the legendary tale of Prince Pelagius and the sorceress Quintilla slaying a demon werewolf in Camlorn, binding its soul to a gem, and the whispered claim that the wolf's spirit lingered until their first child's birth. The narrative then shifts to 3E 80, depicting a young, brilliant, and criminally adept Potema. When her father Pelagius and Emperor Uriel II scheme to renege on a marriage treaty with King Mantiarco of Solitude, Potema infiltrates the Hall of Records, picking its formidable lock to steal the incriminating document. Rather than expose the deception, she retains the parchment, recognizing its immense value for blackmail or future leverage after her family barters her to the elderly Nord king.
topic_desc_basic: Waughin Jarth's historical novel chronicles the early life of Potema Septim. Drawing on the sage Montocai, it recounts Prince Pelagius's werewolf-slaying courtship and the young Potema's cunning theft of a vital treaty from the Hall of Records. Discovering her family's plan to marry her to the aged King of Solitude, she keeps the document, relishing its future value.
aliases: Life of Queen Potema, Book One

title: The Wolf Queen, Book II
topic_desc: The second volume of Waughin Jarth's historical series, drawn from the chronicles of the sage Montocai, covering the early years of Queen Potema's rule in Solitude. The narrative depicts her ruthless political machinations during the reign of her husband, King Mantiarco. It details how she conspired with Lord Vhokken to fabricate evidence of adultery between the late Queen Amodetha and Lord Thone, thereby discrediting the popular Prince Bathorgh. The forged letters' dates falsely suggest Bathorgh is Thone's bastard, ensuring Potema's newborn son, named Uriel, becomes Mantiarco's heir. The account portrays Potema as cunning and vindictive, though as a dramatized chronicle, its reliability as objective history remains uncertain.
topic_desc_basic: The second volume of Waughin Jarth's series on the notorious Queen of Solitude. It recounts how Potema orchestrated a conspiracy to discredit her stepson, Prince Bathorgh, by planting forged evidence of his mother's adultery. This ensured her own newborn son Uriel would become heir to the kingdom of Solitude.

title: The Wolf Queen, Book III
topic_desc: The third volume of Waughin Jarth's historical fiction series, drawn from the writings of the sage Montocai. It covers the death of Emperor Pelagius Septim II in 3E 98 and the subsequent succession crisis. Potema, the Wolf Queen of Solitude, conspires to block her half-brother Antiochus from the throne. Her mother, the Dowager Empress Quintilla, foretells her own death and gifts Potema a soul gem necklace enchanted with Illusion magic, which Potema uses to charm Antiochus's spy. She then forges a letter questioning Antiochus's parentage, but Antiochus detects the deception and counters with evidence of her handwriting imitation, forcing her retreat. The account blends recorded dynastic events with dramatic invention and unreliable prophecy.
topic_desc_basic: The third volume of Waughin Jarth's series on the Wolf Queen, drawn from the sage Montocai. It dramatizes the Imperial succession crisis following the death of Pelagius Septim II, as Potema schemes to keep her half-brother Antiochus from the throne, using an enchanted necklace and a forged letter before being outmaneuvered.

title: The Wolf Queen, Book IV
topic_desc: The Wolf Queen, Book IV is the fourth volume of Waughin Jarth's historical fiction series, drawn from the writings of the sage Montocai. Set in 3E 109–110, it chronicles Potema of Solitude's diplomatic machinations during the reign of her brother, Emperor Antiochus. While the debauched emperor neglects statecraft, Potema entertains King Orgnum of Pyandonea, promising to foment insurrection in exchange for support. Simultaneously, she antagonizes the Psijic Order into defending Tamriel's coast for a fraction of their original price. When the Psijics' storm annihilates Orgnum's fleet near Artaeum, Potema profits from both sides. The account presents a cynical, politically astute view of Potema, though it contains an apparent error regarding the Psijic leader's identity.
topic_desc_basic: The Wolf Queen, Book IV by Waughin Jarth recounts Potema of Solitude's cunning diplomacy in 3E 109–110. While Emperor Antiochus neglects his duties, Potema negotiates with the Pyandonean King Orgnum and manipulates the Psijic Order into defending Tamriel cheaply. When a storm destroys the invasion fleet, Potema profits from both sides of the conflict.

title: The Wolf Queen, Book V
topic_desc: The fifth volume of Waughin Jarth's serialized biography of Potema of Solitude, attributed to the Second Century sage Inzolicus, covers the years 3E 119 to 120. It recounts Emperor Antiochus Septim's final illness and death and the ensuing succession crisis. The narrative centers on Potema's address to the Elder Council, in which she publicly impugns Empress Gysilla's fidelity and declares Kintyra a bastard, urging recognition of her son Uriel as rightful heir. The account presents the speech as a model of rhetorical craft while simultaneously revealing Potema's duplicity, as she privately assures her brothers of support for the coronation even while subverting it. Kintyra's expulsion of Potema from the Imperial City closes the volume with Potema's ominous declaration of war. As a historical source, Inzolicus's account carries dramatic framing and possible sympathies that warrant cautious reading.
topic_desc_basic: The fifth volume of Waughin Jarth's biography of Potema of Solitude, narrated by the sage Inzolicus. It covers Emperor Antiochus's death in 3E 119 and the succession crisis that followed, detailing Potema's speech to the Elder Council challenging Kintyra's legitimacy and advocating her son Uriel's claim to the Imperial throne.
aliases: Life of Queen Potema Book Five

title: The Wolf Queen, Book VI
topic_desc: The Wolf Queen, Book VI is the sixth volume of Waughin Jarth's biographical series on Potema of Solitude, attributed to the Second Century sage Inzolicus. It chronicles the opening of the War of the Red Diamond in 3E 120, following Empress Kintyra II's coronation and Potema's banishment. The narrative depicts Potema's forces overwhelming the Imperial Army through nocturnal assaults and psychological terror, including rumors of undead hordes. In 3E 121, the treacherous Duke of Glenpoint lures Kintyra into a trap; through forged correspondence and stealth, Potema's agents assassinate the Empress's soldiers and capture her. As a historical drama, the account likely embellishes Potema's cunning and dialogue, presenting a dramatic but uncertain portrait of Kintyra's capture.
topic_desc_basic: The Wolf Queen, Book VI by Waughin Jarth recounts the early War of the Red Diamond. It describes how Potema's forces used stealth and terror to outmaneuver the young Empress Kintyra II, culminating in Kintyra's capture through the betrayal of the Duke of Glenpoint in 3E 121.

title: The Wolf Queen, Book VII
topic_desc: The seventh volume of Waughin Jarth's historical series, drawn from the chronicles of the sage Inzolicus, covering the later years of the War of the Red Diamond. It records the disputed date of Empress Kintyra II's execution at Glenpoint, the birth of Pelagius to King Magnus, and the critical campaign of 3E 127. The narrative centers on Potema's fierce resolve at the Battle of Falconstar, where she rallies her outnumbered army through the swamps against King Magnus's Argonian forces at Kogmenthist Castle. Even as she secures this tactical victory, a messenger reveals that her captured son, Emperor Uriel III, was burned alive by a mob en route to Gilane, and her brother Cephorus has been proclaimed Emperor.
topic_desc_basic: This historical volume covers the War of the Red Diamond's later years. It details the uncertain date of Empress Kintyra II's execution, the birth of Pelagius, and Potema's tactical victory at Falconstar in 3E 127, which is immediately overshadowed by the news that her son, Emperor Uriel III, has been killed by a mob and Cephorus proclaimed Emperor.

title: The Wolf Queen, Book VIII
topic_desc: The Wolf Queen, Book VIII is the final volume of Waughin Jarth's biography of Potema Septim, attributed to the Second Century sage Inzolicus. It covers the end of the War of the Red Diamond following Uriel III's death at Ichidag in 3E 127, Cephorus's accession, and Potema's dwindling resistance from Solitude, where she summoned daedra and undead amid growing madness. A dramatized narrative set in 3E 137 depicts young Pelagius, son of Magnus, encountering a disguised Potema near the Mages Guild during the siege of Castle Solitude. She gives him a cursed soul gem that gradually drains wisdom, claiming she read of his imperial destiny in the Elder Scrolls. The chapter closes with Potema's death and Pelagius's eventual descent into madness as emperor. The work blends historical chronicle with dramatic legend; the encounter scene is likely embellished.
topic_desc_basic: The final volume of Waughin Jarth's biography of Potema Septim, covering the end of the War of the Red Diamond and Potema's last stand in Solitude. It dramatizes a meeting between the young Pelagius and a disguised Potema, who gives him a cursed soul gem. The book is valued by students of enchantment.
aliases: Life of Queen Potema, Book Eight

title: A Less Rude Song
topic_desc: A bawdy ballad of uncertain authorship that contrasts the perceived depravity of the Iliac Bay with the vices of Morrowind. The poem dismisses Western rumors of Breton and Redguard licentiousness as mere bardic invention, arguing instead that true transgression lies eastward. It characterizes Dunmer sensuality as distinct from tepid Imperial provincial society, noting their cultural aversion to nudity while claiming their preferred forms of indulgence are far more pernicious, blending pleasure and pain. The verses serve as unreliable, satirical commentary on regional moral stereotypes rather than credible ethnography.
topic_desc_basic: A satirical bawdy ballad contrasting the rumored depravity of the Iliac Bay with the vices of Morrowind. It dismisses Western tales of Breton and Redguard licentiousness as bardic invention, claiming instead that Dunmer indulgence, while distinct from tepid Imperial norms, is far more pernicious and strange.

title: A Short History of Morrowind
topic_desc: Jeanette Sitte's historical survey traces the Dunmer from Velothi exodus through Nord domination and Great House consolidation to the Tribunal theocracy of Resdayn. It notes the province's peaceful Imperial incorporation by treaty rather than conquest. The work's substantial Vvardenfell section details the 3E 414 district reorganization, documenting administrative divisions, settlement patterns, and the competing expansionist agendas of Hlaalu and Telvanni against Temple and Redoran conservatism. Sitte frankly assesses mounting crises: Great House rivalries, Ashlander hostilities, Temple internal dissent, and the escalating Red Mountain blight. Her candid assessment that the Ghostfence may fail and force Imperial evacuation presents a stark, potentially critical perspective at odds with official Temple reassurances.
topic_desc_basic: Jeanette Sitte's survey covers the Dunmer from Velothi exodus through Great House formation and Tribunal theocracy to peaceful Imperial incorporation. It details Vvardenfell's 3E 414 reorganization, documenting settlement expansion, House rivalries, and administrative divisions. The work warns that escalating blight and political tensions threaten the district's stability.

title: Ancestors and the Dunmer
topic_desc: Ancestors and the Dunmer is a scholarly guide written for foreign visitors to Morrowind shortly after the Armistice. The unknown author explains Dunmeri ancestor veneration: the bond between living House members and departed spirits, the family shrine called the Waiting Door, and the solemn duty of interring remains at cities such as Necrom. The text describes ghost fences built from ancestral bones, the Great Ghost Fence raised by the Tribunal, the phenomenon of mad spirits, and the Dunmeri philosophical view of Oblivion as continuous with the mortal world. It contrasts Dunmer practice with Altmeri and Bosmeri customs and addresses the common human misconception equating ancestor worship with necromancy. A publisher's note marks the text as outdated, observing that the Great Ghost Fence has diverted most remains from clan fences and private tombs, and that the Temple now discourages such practices as selfish.
topic_desc_basic: Ancestors and the Dunmer is an outdated scholarly guide written for foreigners after the Armistice. It explains Dunmeri ancestor worship, family shrines called Waiting Doors, ghost fences built from ancestral bones, and the Tribunal's Great Ghost Fence. A publisher's note notes that many practices described have since fallen into disfavor.

title: Antecedants of Dwemer Law
topic_desc: A scholarly treatise tracing the evolution of Dwemer legal customs back to Altmeri roots. The author argues that Bosmeri legal development mirrors Altmeri growth, where early liability practices of surrender shifted toward compensation. The work asserts that Altmeri legal reasoning persists in modern judgments and extends this lineage into Dwemer courts. Citing the laws of Karndar Watch, it details Dwemer liability: an owner pays fines and surrenders the offending slave if it kills a freeman, and if an Animunculus kills a worker at a common workbench, the victim's associates may disassemble the machine and claim its parts within thirty days. The author contrasts this legal formalism with the primitive retaliatory customs of the Tenmar, where a marsh cat's family would avenge themselves against the killer, or even topple the responsible tree, demonstrating the varied progression of legal liability across cultures.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly study tracing Dwemer legal customs back to Altmeri origins. It argues that Dwemer liability law evolved from Altmeri principles, citing Dwemer statutes regarding slaves and Animunculi that mandate compensation or disassembly, and contrasts this formalized system with the primitive retaliatory customs of the Tenmar forests.

title: Brief History of the Empire v 1
topic_desc: Stronach k'Thojj III, an Imperial Historian, chronicles the early Septim Dynasty from Tiber Septim's unification of Tamriel through the onset of the War of the Red Diamond. The account presents a markedly pro-Imperial viewpoint, idealizing Tiber's forcible pacification as a glorious deliverance from chaos and praising the prosperity of his early successors. It candidly addresses later strife, including the Dark Brotherhood assassination of Pelagius I, the plagues under Uriel II, and Pelagius II's controversial sale of Elder Council seats. The narrative details the flamboyant Antiochus I and the War of the Isle, crediting Psijic sorcery for the Imperial victory. It concludes with the tragic overthrow of Kintyra II by her cousin Uriel III, who exploited accusations of bastardy and launched a coordinated assault on the Empire, though the historian dismisses Uriel's claims as mere political pretext.
topic_desc_basic: This Imperial historical text by Stronach k'Thojj III covers the early Septim Dynasty, from Tiber Septim's unification of Tamriel through the overthrow of Kintyra II. It presents a pro-Imperial perspective, celebrating Tiber's rule while acknowledging later conflicts like the assassination of Pelagius I and the civil strife that enabled Uriel III to usurp the throne and spark the War of the Red Diamond.
aliases: A Brief History of the Empire Part One
Brief History of the Empire Part 1

record_links.display_name: Brief History of the Empire v 1

title: Brief History of the Empire v 2
topic_desc: The second volume of Stronach k'Thojj III's imperial chronicle covers the Septim Dynasty from Kintyra II's murder through the reign of Uriel IV. The narrative traces the War of the Red Diamond, in which Pelagius II's surviving children—Potema, Cephorus, and Magnus—vied for the throne. Cephorus I ultimately defeated the Wolf Queen of Solitude after a decade of warfare. The text then addresses the troubled reign of Pelagius III, called the Mad, and the celebrated forty-six-year rule of the Dunmer Empress Katariah, whose legitimacy some disputed on racial and bloodline grounds. The author dismisses the patricide legend surrounding Pelagius as improbable and notes conspiracy theories regarding Katariah's death in Black Marsh. The volume closes with the brief reign of Cassynder and the contentious succession of Uriel IV, whose legitimacy the Elder Council questioned despite legal adoption. The work reflects official imperial historiography with occasional acknowledgment of disputed claims.
topic_desc_basic: An imperial historical text by Stronach k'Thojj III chronicling the Septim Dynasty from Kintyra II's death through Uriel IV. It covers the War of the Red Diamond, the reigns of Cephorus, Magnus, Pelagius the Mad, and the Dunmer Empress Katariah, and addresses questions of Septim bloodline purity and imperial legitimacy.
aliases: A Brief History of the Empire Part Two

record_links.display_name: Brief History of the Empire v 2

title: Brief History of the Empire v 3
topic_desc: Stronach k'Thojj III, Imperial Historian, chronicles the late Third Era emperors from Uriel IV through Uriel V. Uriel IV, legally adopted into the Septim dynasty but born of Empress Katariah's Breton consort, faced relentless opposition from the powerful Elder Council, which ultimately disinherited his son Andorak in favor of the Septim-blooded Cephorus II. The subsequent Andorak rebellion ended when the Council granted him Shornhelm. Cephorus II's reign was defined by the Camoran Usurper's devastating invasion; the Emperor's failed interventions eroded Imperial confidence. Uriel V restored martial prestige through overseas conquests—Roscrea, Cathnoquey, Yneslea, and Esroniet—before dying during his failed Akavir invasion. The narrative reflects Imperial historiography, noting the Council's dominance and regional resentment toward Imperial ineffectiveness.
topic_desc_basic: Stronach k'Thojj III's volume covers Emperors Uriel IV through Uriel V. Uriel IV's contested lineage led the Elder Council to disinherit his son. Cephorus II struggled against the Camoran Usurper's invasion, damaging Imperial prestige. Uriel V later restored martial glory through overseas conquests before dying in his failed Akavir invasion.
aliases: A Brief History of the Empire Part Three
Brief History of the Empire Part 3

record_links.display_name: Brief History of the Empire v 3

title: Brief History of the Empire v 4
topic_desc: The fourth volume of Stronach k'Thojj III's imperial chronicle covers the Septim Dynasty from Uriel VI through the reign of Uriel VII. Uriel VI, crowned as a child in 3E 290, gradually wrested authority from an Elder Council that had dominated since Katariah I's era, using veto power and revived spy networks to assert genuine rule by 3E 313. His half-sister Morihatha succeeded him, continuing centralization while reconquering rebellious provinces, until her assassination in 3E 339, commonly attributed to an aggrieved Argonian councilor. Pelagius IV inherited her patient reconquest program but achieved only partial success over a long reign. The volume concludes with Uriel VII's restoration after Jagar Tharn's decade-long impersonation, framing the current Emperor as embodying his predecessors' combined virtues. The text bears an openly imperial viewpoint, and contains a known chronological error regarding Pelagius IV's reign length.
topic_desc_basic: The fourth volume of Stronach k'Thojj III's chronicle traces the Septim Dynasty from Uriel VI through Uriel VII. It details Uriel VI's struggle to reclaim power from the Elder Council, Empress Morihatha's reconquest of rebellious provinces, Pelagius IV's continued efforts, and Uriel VII's restoration after Jagar Tharn's decade-long usurpation. The narrative is written from a loyal Imperial perspective.
aliases: A Brief History of the Empire Part Four
Brief History of the Empire Part 4

title: Famed Artifacts of Tamriel
topic_desc: This catalogue of legendary items, attributed to Yagrum Bagarn, surveys over two dozen storied relics from across Tamriel. The text blends confirmed historical artifacts with acknowledged legend, presenting each item's reputed origin, powers, and the often-capricious divine will governing its possession. Daedric gifts like the Ebony Mail and Mehrunes Razor feature alongside ancient arms such as the Dwemer Spell Breaker and the Paladin's Blade, Chrysamere. A recurring theme throughout the work is the transient nature of these artifacts; many are said to abandon their bearers or vanish when their owners become unworthy, too powerful, or simply at a deity's whim. The compilation serves as both a scholarly reference and a collection of cautionary folktales regarding the perils of possessing such potent, willful objects.
topic_desc_basic: Attributed to Yagrum Bagarn, this book catalogues over two dozen legendary Tamrielic relics. It blends confirmed history with acknowledged legend, detailing each artifact's reputed origin, powers, and the often-capricious divine will governing its possession. A recurring theme is the transient nature of these items, many of which abandon bearers deemed unworthy or too powerful.

title: For my Gods and Emperor
topic_desc: This official handbook of the Imperial Cult outlines the organization's doctrines, structure, and mission in Vvardenfell. It presents the combined worship of the Nine Divines, including the Talos cult venerating Tiber Septim, and preaches the Nine Virtues. The text serves as both doctrinal instruction and practical recruitment material, detailing membership requirements, shrine services, and paths of service such as lay healer, almoner, and shrine sergeant. It expresses clear institutional biases, praising House Hlaalu and the Imperial guilds while condemning Ashlander beliefs, Telvanni practices, and slavery. The handbook reveals ongoing theological friction with the Tribunal Temple, acknowledging Temple figures as inspirations but firmly rejecting the Temple's claim to exclusive religious truth as false.
topic_desc_basic: An official handbook for the Imperial Cult in Vvardenfell. It outlines the worship of the Nine Divines and Tiber Septim, preaches the Nine Virtues, and details membership, services, and paths of service. The text reveals institutional biases, praising Imperial allies while condemning local practices like slavery, and firmly rejects the Tribunal Temple's claim to exclusive religious truth.

title: Great Houses of Morrowind
topic_desc: This treatise surveys the five Great Houses governing Morrowind, describing their evolution from ancient clans into political parties. It details the process by which outlanders may gain entry through oath-bonded service and councilor sponsorship. The text characterizes House Redoran by its martial piety and traditional village architecture centered on Temple compounds; House Hlaalu by its Imperial accommodation, commercial dominance, and rectangular urban designs; and House Telvanni by its reclusive wizard-lords, might-makes-right philosophy, and organic mushroom towers. Houses Indoril and Dres, lacking Vvardenfell holdings, are summarized as orthodox Temple loyalists hostile to Imperial culture, with Dres dependent on slave labor for its saltrice plantations. The account presents a broadly descriptive overview, though its characterization of Hlaalu's harmonious aspirations and Imperial-era dominance reflects a perspective sympathetic to provincial integration.
topic_desc_basic: This book surveys the five Great Houses that govern Morrowind as political parties derived from ancient clans. It outlines how outlanders may join a House through loyal service and councilor sponsorship.
