The text describes Redoran's martial piety, Hlaalu's Imperial-friendly commercial dominance, Telvanni's reclusive wizard-lords and mushroom towers, and the orthodox, slave-dependent Houses Indoril and Dres, which hold no territory on Vvardenfell.

title: Guide to Vivec
topic_desc: This travel and civic guide presents Vivec City as the largest settlement on Vvardenfell, detailing its eight massive cantons arranged in a cross pattern. The text emphasizes the metropolis as Lord Vivec's holy city, reflecting Temple doctrine by attributing the suspension of the Ministry of Truth to the god-hero's mighty power and describing the Puzzle Canal as a place of worship. It provides a practical overview of each district: the Foreign Quarter for Imperial guilds and outlanders, the Temple Compound housing the High Fane and administrative halls, three Great House compounds, the Arena for public entertainment, and two residential cantons for commoners. The narrative frames the city's social order and heretic re-education through a devout Tribunal perspective, while also cataloging transportation infrastructure, bridges, and regional travel routes.
topic_desc_basic: This guidebook describes Vivec City, the largest settlement on Vvardenfell and a holy site dedicated to Lord Vivec. It outlines the city's eight cantons, which house Imperial guilds, Tribunal temples, Great House compounds, residential quarters, and the Arena. The text also details the bridges, roads, silt strider routes, and gondolas connecting the city to the region.

title: Odral's History of the Empire 1
topic_desc: Stronach k'Thojj III, an Imperial Historian, authored this official chronicle covering the early Third Era, from Tiber Septim's unification of Tamriel through the onset of the War of the Red Diamond in 3E 121. The narrative presents a markedly Imperial viewpoint, glorifying Tiber's rule as a divinely-ordained restoration of order and portraying the Septim dynasty with evident bias. It attributes Uriel III's usurpation to the machinations of Queen Potema and disgruntled kings, and treats the Psijic Order's intervention at the War of the Isle as legend. The account glosses over Pelagius II's sale of Elder Council seats as fiscal pragmatism while acknowledging his critics, and frames Antiochus I's disastrous reign with indulgent characterization, reflecting its pro-Imperial propagandistic slant.
topic_desc_basic: This Imperial chronicle by Stronach k'Thojj III covers the early Third Era, from Tiber Septim's unification through the onset of the War of the Red Diamond in 3E 121. The narrative presents a markedly pro-Imperial perspective, glorifying the Septim dynasty while treating disputed events like the Psijic intervention at the War of the Isle as legend.

title: Odral's History of the Empire 3
topic_desc: This third volume of Stronach k'Thojj III's imperial history chronicles the Septim succession from Uriel IV through Uriel V. It details Uriel IV's protracted struggles with the powerful Elder Council, which ultimately disinherited his son Andorak in favor of Cephorus II. Andorak's loyalists warred against the Empire until the Council granted him Shornhelm. The narrative then covers Cephorus II's reign, highlighting the devastating rampage of the Camoran Usurper through Valenwood and Hammerfell, a crisis the Imperial forces failed to meaningfully halt. Finally, it recounts Uriel V's ambitious overseas conquests and his fatal invasion of Akavir. The author presents a centralized imperial perspective, treating the Elder Council's ascendancy and provincial resentment as consequences of weak or distracted leadership.
topic_desc_basic: This volume chronicles the later Septim Emperors from Uriel IV through Uriel V. It covers Uriel IV's conflicts with the Elder Council, the War of the Camoran Usurper during Cephorus II's reign, and Uriel V's ambitious but ultimately fatal invasion of Akavir.
aliases: Stronach k'Thojj III History of the Empire

title: Odral's History of the Empire 4
topic_desc: Stronach k'Thojj III's imperial history covers the Septim dynasty from Uriel VI through Uriel VII. Uriel VI slowly reclaimed authority from a reluctant Elder Council using the imperial veto and spy networks. His sister Morihatha continued this centralization, reconquering rebellious provinces with deliberate tactics until her assassination, blamed on an Argonian councilman. Pelagius IV extended her cautious reunification but achieved only partial success. The narrative then extols Uriel VII's combined virtues before recounting Jagar Tharn's decade-long impersonation, ending with the Emperor's restoration and renewed effort toward a Tiberian golden age. The account is broadly orthodox imperial historiography, praising Septim rulers while minimizing the era's instability; its claim of a likely imminent golden age reflects propaganda rather than current reality.
topic_desc_basic: This imperial chronicle surveys the late Third Era Septims, from Uriel VI's struggle to reclaim power from the Elder Council through Morihatha's campaigns and assassination, Pelagius IV's partial reunification, and Uriel VII's reign and imprisonment by Jagar Tharn. It concludes with optimistic imperial propaganda forecasting a return to Tiber Septim's golden age.
aliases: Brief History of the Empire Part Four

title: On Morrowind
topic_desc: Erramanwe of Sunhold, an Altmer scholar, composed this historical synopsis of Morrowind's absorption into the Empire. The narrative traces the massing of Imperial legions after the conquest of Hammerfell, the divided responses of the five Great Houses, and Vivec's sudden announcement of a treaty with Tiber Septim guaranteeing Dunmer self-rule and religious freedom. Erramanwe notes that the Temple hierarchy was not consulted and that inter-house violence following the treaty claimed more lives than the conquest itself. The author treats as unconfirmed rumor the eastern suggestion that Vivec offered Numidium to Septim in exchange for concessions, and the western speculation that Zurin Arctus brokered the agreement. The account is broadly pro-Imperial but credits the Tribunal with pragmatism, while observing that Indoril nobles committed suicide rather than submit and that Hlaalu profited from accommodation. The work circulates among scholars of Imperial provincial history.
topic_desc_basic: A historical account by the Altmer scholar Erramanwe of Sunhold describing Morrowind's incorporation into the Empire. It covers the Great Houses' divided responses to the Imperial threat, Vivec's negotiated treaty with Tiber Septim preserving Dunmer self-rule, and the bloody inter-house struggles that followed. The author treats rumors of Numidium's involvement as unconfirmed speculation.

title: On Oblivion
topic_desc: On Oblivion by Morian Zenas is a scholarly treatise on the dimension of Oblivion and its Daedric inhabitants. Zenas traces the common term 'demon' to the Alessian Doctrines of the First Era prophet Marukh, arguing it likely derives from the Elven word 'Daedra.' He enumerates the Daedra princes known from ancient records and attempts a preliminary categorization, identifying Mehrunes Dagon, Molag Bal, Peryite, Boethiah, and Vaernima as the most consistently destructive in nature, distinguishing their individual spheres. Zenas claims to have personally summoned and conversed with Daedra lords, supplementing this with First Era diaries, journals, and Daedra-slayer guides. He expresses intent to investigate the prince Hircine and to seek a practical means for mortals to enter Oblivion. His subsequent research is documented by his apprentice in The Doors of Oblivion.
topic_desc_basic: On Oblivion by the scholar Morian Zenas examines the dimension of Oblivion and its Daedric princes. The work traces the term 'demon' to the Alessian Doctrines, lists the known Daedra lords, and categorizes several as consistently destructive. Zenas draws on both ancient texts and his own summonings of Daedra.

title: Origin of the Mages Guild
topic_desc: This historical study by Archmage Salarth traces the Mages Guild's founding in the early Second Era. It contrasts Vanus Galerion's revolutionary vision of pooled magical resources and public services with the secretive, aristocratic Psijic Order he departed. Galerion's controversial proposal to democratize magical access initially provoked widespread animosity and required royal and Psijic approval to charter. The text details the subsequent formation of the Order of the Lamp for Guild security and outlines the institution's hierarchical governance. However, it candidly acknowledges this structure often masks internal political strife, concluding with Galerion's own bitter lament that the Guild devolved into an intricate morass of infighting.
topic_desc_basic: Archmage Salarth chronicles the Mages Guild's early Second Era founding by Vanus Galerion. Departing the secretive Psijic Order, Galerion controversially proposed democratizing magic for the public. The text outlines the Guild's growth, its protective Order of the Lamp, and its formal hierarchy, while acknowledging that internal political strife ultimately corrupted Galerion's original vision.

title: Overview of Gods and Worship
topic_desc: Written by Brother Hetchfeld, an Associate Scribe at the Imperial University, this treatise examines the unpredictable nature of divine involvement in Tamriel. Hetchfeld observes that deities sometimes intervene in mortal crises and bless temple priests, yet frequently display apparent apathy during plagues or famines, suggesting mortal minds cannot comprehend divine logic. He argues that worship, sacrifice, and deeds draw a deity's attention, and conjectures that gods gain strength from their followers, with larger temples securing blessings more easily. The text further reports that certain spirits share this capacity to feed upon mortal deeds, raising the possibility that such spirits might elevate themselves to godhood. Hetchfeld cites Motusuo of the Imperial Seminary, who theorizes these spirits are faded deities who lost their followers, and acknowledges Old Ways practitioners who deny gods entirely, recognizing only greater and lesser spirits. The author cautiously proposes all three theories may hold truth.
topic_desc_basic: This treatise by Imperial University Scribe Brother Hetchfeld examines the unpredictable nature of divine intervention in Tamriel. It theorizes that deities gain strength from worship, sacrifice, and deeds, and speculates that spirits sharing this power might rise to godhood or be faded gods who lost their followers. Old Ways practitioners who recognize only greater and lesser spirits are also noted.
aliases: An Overview of Gods and Worship in Tamriel

title: Poison Song I
topic_desc: A First Era historical novel by Bristin Xel set on the island of Gorne near Mournhold. It follows Tay, an Indoril orphan who constantly hears a mysterious, ominous Song. While his family dismisses his affliction, his scarred nursemaid Edebah silently encourages him. When Tay and his cousins Baynarah and Vaster discover a scorched ruin filled with debris and a strange crystal orb, the Song overwhelms him; he murders Vaster by casting him into a gorge and conceals the artifact. The narrative frames the Song as a hereditary curse tied to the surviving remnants of House Dagoth, portraying Tay's awakening to a dark, suppressed lineage through unreliable, subjective experiences.
topic_desc_basic: A historical novel by Bristin Xel following Tay, an Indoril orphan on the island of Gorne plagued by a mysterious Song. When he and his cousins discover a scorched ruin and a strange crystal orb, the Song compels him to murder his cousin Vaster. The story explores the dark, lingering legacy of House Dagoth through Tay's cursed bloodline.

title: Poison Song II
topic_desc: The second installment of Bristin Xel's epic, set on the island of Gorne after the War of the Red Mountain. It follows the boy Tay, who feels no guilt over murdering his cousin Vaster for a crystal globe, instead experiencing a supernatural, intoxicating 'Song.' When their tutor identifies the insect crest as the destroyed House Dagoth, the children realize their scavenged relics originate from the Sixth House. Baynarah feels a corrupting aura from the artifacts and discovers Tay's nursemaid Edebah performing a Dagoth candle ritual, leading to Edebah's banishment. The narrative presents an unreliable, subjective account of Dagoth's lingering corruption and the insidious nature of its call.
topic_desc_basic: The second part of Bristin Xel's epic set after the War of the Red Mountain. It follows the boy Tay, who murders his cousin under the influence of a supernatural 'Song.' After discovering their scavenged relics bear the crest of the destroyed House Dagoth, his companion Baynarah finds Tay's nursemaid performing a forbidden Sixth House ritual, resulting in her banishment from Gorne.

title: Poison Song III
topic_desc: The third installment of Bristin Xel's epic novel, set in the aftermath of the War of the Red Mountain. It follows Tay, an orphan raised by House Indoril in Mournhold, who struggles against a hallucinatory "Song" compelling him to violence. When his former nursemaid Edebah reveals he is truly of House Dagoth—adopted by Indoril to erase the defeated House's legacy—and presents a seal ring proving his heritage, the Song overwhelms him. In a trance, Tay accepts the ring, murders Edebah, and flees after setting the tenement ablaze. The narrative presents an unreliable, madness-tinged perspective on the lingering traumatic hold of the Sixth House on its scattered survivors.
topic_desc_basic: A fictional work by Bristin Xel set after the War of the Red Mountain. It follows Tay, an Indoril-raised orphan who learns he is actually of House Dagoth. Upon accepting his heritage seal, he falls under a violent trance, murders the woman who revealed his lineage, and flees a burning tenement.

title: Poison Song IV
topic_desc: The fourth installment of Bristin Xel's epic, set in the aftermath of the War with the Dwemer and House Dagoth. Tay confesses to his lover Acra that he murdered his nursemaid Edebah, who revealed his true heritage as Dagoth-Tython and gave him House Dagoth's sealing ring. Acra claims she too hears the ancestral Song and is Dagoth-Acra. Horrified, Tay flees, killing a senior initiate who addresses him as cousin. Pursued to a cliff overlooking the Inner Sea, Tay defies the Song's demand that he embrace his destiny and leaps. On the island of Gorne, his cousin Baynarah is informed that his body has washed ashore. The narrative presents a dramatic, likely unreliable legend exploring the trauma of hidden Dagoth orphans and the destructive compulsion of ancestral blood.
topic_desc_basic: The fourth installment of Bristin Xel's fictional epic, set after the War of the First Council. It follows Tay, an Indoril youth who murders his Dagoth nursemaid after she reveals his true Sixth House heritage. Driven mad by the ancestral Song, he kills again and flees Mournhold, ultimately throwing himself from a cliff into the Inner Sea.

title: Poison Song V
topic_desc: The fifth installment of Bristin Xel's epic, attributed to the writer Ted Peterson, continuing the tragic tale of Tay, a Dagoth orphan raised as Indoril on the island of Gorne. Recovering from fever, Tay confesses to his cousin Baynarah that the ancestral 'Song' compelled him to murder his nursemaid Edebah and their kinsmen. He declares himself Dagoth-Tython and announces the Sixth House's return. Baynarah learns from Aunt Ulliah that Sixth House orphans were indeed adopted into the victorious Great Houses after the War. A supposed Temple priestess arrives, retrieves Tay's discarded Dagoth ring, and reveals herself as his sister Dagoth-Acra before escaping the blood-soaked Sandil House via Recall. The narrative dramatizes the fear that the defeated House's corruption survived through its scattered children, presenting the Song as a malevolent, irresistible ancestral call.
topic_desc_basic: The fifth part of Bristin Xel's epic about House Dagoth's aftermath. Recovering on Gorne, Tay confesses that the ancestral 'Song' compelled him to murder, declaring himself Dagoth-Tython. A false priestess then arrives, massacres the household, and vanishes, heralding the Sixth House's return.

title: Poison Song VI
topic_desc: The sixth installment of Bristin Xel's epic historical fiction, set during the turbulent aftermath of the War of the First Council and the year of Sun's Death. The narrative follows Dagoth-Tython and his sister Acra, surviving members of the dissolved House Dagoth, as they ambush a House supply caravan in Vvardenfell's scarred ashlands. Acra returns to camp via Recall, only to be captured by Indoril-Baynarah, a former acquaintance now leading House forces. Under duress, Acra reveals that the mysterious Song guiding the Dagoth rebels has warned Tython of her capture and directed him to assassinate General Indoril-Triffith. Acra escapes before Baynarah can learn more, leaving the House forces racing to warn the general. The novel portrays the Dagoth remnants as driven by a mystical, possibly unreliable inner voice, blending legend with dramatic fiction.
topic_desc_basic: A historical fiction novel by Bristin Xel set after the War of the First Council. It depicts Dagoth-Tython and his sister Acra ambushing a House caravan in Vvardenfell's ashlands. Acra is later captured by Indoril-Baynarah but escapes after revealing the Dagoth rebels' mystical Song has directed her brother to assassinate General Indoril-Triffith.

title: Poison Song VII
topic_desc: The final installment of Bristin Xel's epic, set during the Tribunal's reorganization of Morrowind after the fall of House Dagoth. Dagoth-Tython, raised as an Indoril ward, confronts his adoptive uncle General Indoril-Triffith, seeking vengeance for the destruction of his House. Baynarah pleads with Tython, arguing that the ancestral 'Poison Song' enslaves and corrupts him rather than guiding him. Tython escapes to Red Mountain and casts himself into the crater. Dagoth-Acra observes his end, retrieves his fallen signet ring, and claims the Dagoth legacy for her unborn child as a new refrain of the Song begins. The narrative frames the Song as a destructive, manipulative force driving the scattered House's survivors toward ruin and fanaticism.
topic_desc_basic: The concluding volume of Bristin Xel's epic about House Dagoth's survivors. Dagoth-Tython attempts to avenge his fallen House against his Indoril guardian but is ultimately consumed by the corrupting ancestral 'Poison Song,' perishing in Red Mountain while Dagoth-Acra claims his ring to continue the lineage.

title: Provinces of Tamriel
topic_desc: This Imperial geographical treatise surveys the nine provinces of the Tamrielic Empire, summarizing the terrain, settlements, and cultural character of each region. The text presents an Imperial perspective, celebrating Nord martial virtues and Redguard seafaring while characterizing northern Khajiit as barbarians and describing Bosmer and Altmer lands as wildernesses untouched by mercantilism. It notably emphasizes Morrowind's unique legal autonomy, retained through treaty rather than conquest, and acknowledges the persistence of illegal Dunmer slave-raiding in Black Marsh despite Imperial prohibition. The account reflects provincial stereotypes and administrative priorities rather than comprehensive ethnographic study.
topic_desc_basic: This Imperial survey summarizes the geography and peoples of Tamriel's nine provinces. It describes each region's terrain and cultural character from an Imperial perspective, noting Morrowind's unique legal autonomy from treaty rather than conquest and acknowledging the persistence of illegal Dunmer slave raids into Black Marsh.

title: Reflections on Cult Worship
topic_desc: This correspondence by the Imperial trader Cuseius Plecia, written from Vos, contrasts Imperial and Dunmer religious temperaments. Plecia argues that Heartlanders treat cults as practical social institutions, viewing the Eight Divines as distant, indifferent spirits, while the Septim emperors deliberately limit religious influence in secular affairs. Nordic hero-cults, particularly the charismatic sub-cult of Tiber Septim among the military and colonists, offer a personal counter-current to this dominant secularism. By contrast, the Tribunal Temple and its ancestral predecessor cults are profoundly intimate: Dunmer venerate living deities who walk among them and blood ancestors who judge them directly. Plecia attributes persistent political and cultural misunderstandings between Imperials and Dunmer to this fundamental divide, noting Imperial casual tolerance versus Dunmer passionate intensity and constant divine scrutiny.
topic_desc_basic: This correspondence by Imperial trader Cuseius Plecia contrasts Imperial and Dunmer religious practices. Heartlanders treat the Eight Divines as distant spirits and cults as practical social organizations, while Dunmer worship living Tribunal deities and watchful ancestors intimately. Plecia argues this fundamental divide causes persistent cultural misunderstanding.

title: Special Flora of Tamriel
topic_desc: Hardin the Herbalist's botanical survey cataloguing ten noteworthy plants across Tamriel, describing their native habitats, physical characteristics, and reputed properties. The work blends practical field observation with unverified legend and hearsay. Entries range from the fire-resistant Morrowind fire fern and the lethally toxic Black Marsh dragon's tongue—reputedly harmless to Argonians—to Valenwood's arrowroot and Elsweyr's nightshade, each tied to race-specific traditions. Many alleged magical effects, such as Hammerfell poppies granting flight or Domica redwort enhancing beauty, are attributed only to rumor or legend, reflecting folk belief as much as documented alchemy. The text remains a useful if unreliable guide for herbalists.
topic_desc_basic: A botanical survey by Hardin the Herbalist describing ten notable plants across Tamriel. It details regional flora like Morrowind's fire fern and Black Marsh's dragon's tongue alongside their physical traits and reputed alchemical properties, though many claimed magical effects are attributed only to rumor and folk legend.

title: Spirit of the Daedra
topic_desc: A Dremora-authored treatise presenting the Daedric perspective on existence, social structure, and mortals. The narrator explains that Daedra do not truly die—destroyed animus returns from the Darkness—yet they still feel pain, shame, and fear, with lesser beings like Scamps and Vermai lacking the capacity for deep dread. Dremora organize by clan and oath-bonds, serving powerful Princes like Dagon by choice for protection, though such allegiances can shift. The text frames mortals as prey in a hunt, occasionally admired for cunning but ultimately pitied for their decay, while expressing genuine bewilderment at why humans do not despair over their inevitable mortality. This hostile but philosophical viewpoint offers rare insight into Daedric self-perception, though its predatory framing and external assumptions about mortal nature mark it as an unreliable account of cross-nature understanding.
topic_desc_basic: A treatise written by a Dremora explaining the Daedric mindset. The author claims Daedra are immortal yet capable of feeling pain and fear, organize themselves through clan and oath-bonds, and view mortals as prey to be hunted. The text expresses bewilderment that humans do not despair over their mortal condition.

title: The Book of Daedra
topic_desc: This scholarly compendium catalogs the spheres and epithets of the Daedric Princes, summarizing each entity's domain over mortal and cosmic concerns. The text characterizes several Princes' spheres as obscured to mortal understanding, acknowledging the limits of such doctrine. It also details notable Daedric artifacts, including Azura's Star and Sheogorath's Wabbajack, and provides an extensive account of Scourge, Mackkan's Hammer. According to the work, Malacath blessed this weapon for mortal use against his own kin, then cursed it so that any Daedra invoking its power would be cast into Oblivion's voidstreams, preventing its use in private wars among the forsaken.
topic_desc_basic: This lengthy tome catalogs the spheres and titles of the Daedric Princes, describing their respective domains over mortal and cosmic affairs. It acknowledges that some Princes' true spheres remain obscured to mortals. The work also discusses legendary Daedric artifacts, notably detailing Scourge, a hammer blessed by Malacath and cursed to expel any Daedra who attempts to invoke its power.

title: The War of the First Council
topic_desc: This historical account by Imperial scholar Agrippa Fundilius synthesizes Imperial and Dunmer sources for Western audiences. It frames the War of the First Council as a religious conflict between the secular Houses Dwemer and Dagoth and the orthodox Houses Indoril, Redoran, Dres, Hlaalu, and Telvanni. The dispute arose over enchantments the orthodox declared profane. Despite the secular faction's early advantages and Nord and Orc allies, Nerevar unified the orthodox and Ashlanders, defeating the seculars at Red Mountain. Treason breached the stronghold; secular leaders died, and Nerevar suffered mortal wounds. Vivec, Almalexia, and Sotha Sil then assumed control of the new Grand Council, becoming the Tribunal. The narrative simplifies theological disputes and treats the Tribunal's ascension as straightforward succession.
topic_desc_basic: Imperial scholar Agrippa Fundilius wrote this account of the First Age War of the First Council for Western readers. It describes the conflict between orthodox Dunmer Houses and the secular Dwemer and Dagoth over profane sorceries, Nerevar's unification and victory at Red Mountain, his subsequent death, and the Tribunal's rise to power.

record_links.display_name: The War of the First Council

title: Thirsk, a History -- Revised
topic_desc: Bereditte Jastal's chronicle recounts the history of the Thirsk mead hall on Solstheim, founded a century ago by Skaal dissenters who rejected nature worship to embrace their ancestors' freer lifestyle. The text details the settlement's early destruction by the Udyrfrykte, an ancient beast awakened by construction, and its sealing by the sorcerer Eldrid Ice-Light. It then describes Hrothmund the Red's ascension as first chieftain after beheading the rival Drengr Bronze-Helm, establishing the tradition that any warrior claiming leadership must present a worthy battle trophy upon the hall's pedestal. A roster of subsequent chieftains follows, recording their often-violent rises and falls. The revised edition notably interpolates a legendary account of a stranger slaying the resurgent Udyrfrykte and claiming chieftainship, a passage of uncertain veracity. The work concludes with observations on Thirsk's expansion, its civil trade with the Skaal, and its pragmatic non-interference arrangement with the Imperial garrison at Fort Frostmoth.
topic_desc_basic: Bereditte Jastal's chronicle details the founding of the Thirsk mead hall by Skaal dissenters and the tradition of claiming chieftainship through battle trophies. It lists past rulers and describes the hall's relations with the Skaal and the Empire. The revised edition adds a legendary account of a stranger slaying the ancient Udyrfrykte to become chieftain.

title: Vivec and Mephala
topic_desc: This theological treatise examines the relationship between the Tribune Vivec and his Daedric Anticipation, Mephala. It introduces the Temple doctrine of Anticipations: Azura preceded Sotha Sil, Boethiah preceded Almalexia, and Mephala preceded Vivec. The text acknowledges that Vivec's public identity as benevolent Warrior-Poet and guardian of Vvardenfell is the face familiar to Westerners, while Dunmer instinctively accept darker currents beneath it. Mephala, described as the demon of murder, sex, and secrets, is said to have served as the shadowy implementer of Boethiah's revolutionary methods during the Chimeri transformation. The treatise candidly addresses the Ashlander oral tradition claiming Vivec conspired with Almalexia and Sotha Sil to murder Lord Nerevar, noting that Temple doctrine flatly contradicts this account yet the tale remains firmly established in the Dunmer imagination. The work thus bridges orthodox Temple presentation with an admission of unresolved theological tension.
topic_desc_basic: A scholarly theological work exploring the relationship between the god Vivec and his Daedric Anticipation, Mephala. It explains Temple doctrine that three Daedra Lords preceded the Tribunal: Azura for Sotha Sil, Boethiah for Almalexia, and Mephala for Vivec. The text acknowledges that Dunmer accept darker, hidden aspects beneath Vivec's benevolent public face, and addresses the disputed Ashlander claim that the Tribunal murdered Lord Nerevar.

title: Words of Clan Mother Ahnissi
topic_desc: This Khajiiti myth recounts the creation of the world and their people through a feline lens. The primordial littermates Ahnurr and Fadomai birth the first gods, but conflict arises when Fadomai bears additional litters in secret. Fleeing Ahnurr's wrath, she births Lorkhaj in the Great Darkness, where his heart becomes tainted by Namiira. Before dying, Fadomai entrusts her secrets to Azurah, commanding her to shape the Khajiit from shapeless forest folk. Azurah binds them to the Lunar Lattice and grants them diverse forms and secret wisdom. Y'ffer, lacking subtlety, then shapes the Bosmer as fixed elves. As doctrine, the text elevates secrecy, survival, and lunar devotion as core Khajiit virtues while framing their origin as distinct from other mer.
topic_desc_basic: A Khajiiti creation myth explaining the world's origin through a feline perspective. It describes the primordial cats Ahnurr and Fadomai birthing the gods, Fadomai's secret litters, and her death after entrusting Azurah with secrets. Azurah shapes the Khajiit from forest folk, binding them to the Lunar Lattice, while Y'ffer creates the Bosmer.

title: Nchunak's Fire and Faith
topic_desc: This translated account records the Dwemer Nchunak's travels among various Dwemer colonies, examining how Kagrenac's theories were received and taught. Nchunak inquires about the state of enlightenment regarding these doctrines and learns that Kherakah stands out as a center of learning. There, the precepts of Kagrenac are studied not for utility—such as planar division or the numeration of amnesia—but for understanding the self and its relationship to the Heart. The text offers a rare, though potentially unreliable or propagandistic, insider perspective on Dwemer philosophical priorities and the dissemination of Kagrenac's esoteric teachings before the civilization's disappearance.
topic_desc_basic: A translated account of the Dwemer Nchunak's travels among Dwemer colonies, examining the spread of Kagrenac's theories. It highlights the colony of Kherakah, where Kagrenac's precepts were studied to understand the self's relationship to the Heart rather than for mere utility.

title: Spirit of Nirn, God of Mortals
topic_desc: This theological treatise examines Lorkhan's dual role as the Spirit of Nirn and god of all mortals, framing the creation of the Mundus as the fundamental divide between elven and human cosmology. Most Elves revile Lorkhan as the demon who sundered them from the spirit realm, viewing mortal existence as a prison from which to escape. Conversely, most Humans revere him as the herald of existence, believing the world serves as a testing ground for transcendence. The text posits that all souls instinctively recall their pre-Nirn origins, experiencing mortal life as a cruel yet crucial step toward an uncertain next state. The author presents these conflicting doctrines as irreconcilable perspectives on the same divine act.
topic_desc_basic: A theological treatise on Lorkhan as the Spirit of Nirn. It contrasts the elven view of him as a demon who trapped souls in a mortal prison with the human view of him as the herald of existence who created the world as a testing ground for transcendence.

record_links.display_name: Spirit of Nirn, God of Mortals

title: The Cantatas of Vivec
topic_desc: The Cantatas of Vivec are doctrinal gospels composed as epic songs meant for performance or recitation. They narrate Vivec's transformation from a foolish mortal into an enlightened divine, attributing his apotheosis to his humility, unconquerable spirit, and relentless testing through trials in defense of the Dunmer. The text emphasizes his attainment of the Wisdom of the Seven Graces and acknowledges his profound debt to Almalexia the Lover and Sotha Sil the Teacher. Blending hagiography with lyric poetry, the Cantatas celebrate his failures and triumphs alike as proof of his devotion. The included excerpt, 'Brooding Beneath Red Mountain,' reflects solemnly on the dead beneath the mountain and the enduring cost of their restlessness. As a Temple text, the work presents doctrine and inspirational legend rather than objective history.
topic_desc_basic: The Cantatas of Vivec are sacred gospels written as epic songs. They celebrate Vivec's long mortal journey from foolishness to enlightened divinity through trials, humility, and defense of the Dunmer. The poetry acknowledges his debt to Almalexia and Sotha Sil and details his attainment of the Seven Graces. Composed for recitation, the work serves as Temple doctrine.

title: The Real Nerevar
topic_desc: This informal history of Nerevar, authored by an unsourced Telvanni retainer, presents a secular, pragmatic account of the First Council's formation. It claims Nerevar was merely an ambitious warlord who secured Dwemer-crafted ring Moon-and-Star to magically persuade the warring Dunmer clans into unity. The text attributes the Battle of Red Mountain to religious disputes, noting Dwemer and Dagoth alliances with Nord and Orc clans against Nerevar's coalition. It concludes that terrible sorceries caused the complete extermination of House Dwemer, House Dagoth, and their allies, and that Nerevar died in the battle. The narrative notably omits the Tribunal, Ashlander traditions, and Daedric involvement, reflecting an unreliable, heavily simplified propaganda perspective.
topic_desc_basic: An unsourced Telvanni retainer's history portraying Nerevar as an ambitious warlord who united the Dunmer clans using the enchanted ring Moon-and-Star. It attributes the Battle of Red Mountain to religious disputes and claims terrible sorceries exterminated House Dwemer and House Dagoth, killing Nerevar in the process.

title: The Waters of Oblivion
topic_desc: The Waters of Oblivion is a mythic-historical account framing the origins of Daedra as a cosmic conflict between Light and Darkness. It describes how the Bright Gods resolved to punish wayward spirits who had grown wicked in the void, regretting that they had once welcomed these dark kin as siblings. The Principalities of Victory moved to chasten the Daedric tribes, but the text laments that no oath can bind these powers, so deep is their envy. It concludes with a dire warning: once portals to Oblivion are opened, the rising tide of Darkness cannot be shut. The narrative presents a clear moralistic and theological bias, portraying Daedra as irredeemable scathers while acknowledging the terrible parity of the warring powers.
topic_desc_basic: The Waters of Oblivion recounts the mythic conflict between the Bright Gods and the wicked spirits of the void. It warns that the Daedra are bound by no oaths and that once portals to Oblivion are opened, the darkness they unleash cannot be contained.

title: Aedra and Daedra
topic_desc: This theological treatise clarifies the precise Elvish etymologies distinguishing Aedra from Daedra, terms often conflated by the lay public. Aedra translates roughly to 'ancestor,' while Daedra means 'not our ancestors,' a genealogical distinction central to Dunmer ideological schisms. The text assigns cosmological roles: Aedra embody stasis, having created the mortal world and become bound to the Earth Bones, while Daedra embody change, incapable of creation but possessing transformative power. Through the divine contract of creation, Aedra are mortal and can be killed, as demonstrated by Lorkhan. Daedra, exempt from such rules, can only be banished.
topic_desc_basic: A theological treatise clarifying the exact Elvish origins of the terms Aedra and Daedra. Aedra means 'ancestor' and are bound to the mortal world they created, while Daedra means 'not our ancestors' and embody change. Because of the divine contract of creation, Aedra can be killed, but protean Daedra can only be banished.

title: The Song of Grandfather Frost
topic_desc: A brief, rhythmic poem celebrating the legendary figure Grandfather Frost. The verses depict a joyous procession to a snow-bound workshop illuminated by lanterns, where the titular character employs a magical touch to craft abundant sweets. Emphasizing candy over conventional playthings, the song conveys the delight of children and the warmth of communal winter celebration. While presented as a cheerful folk tradition, the poem's whimsical imagery and focus on confectionery magic likely reflect a localized legend or cultural myth rather than a literal account, preserving a festive narrative tied to the northern cold.
topic_desc_basic: A cheerful winter poem celebrating the legendary Grandfather Frost. The verses describe a joyous journey to a snowy workshop where Frost uses magic to craft sweet candy treats, bringing happiness to children who favor his confections over ordinary toys.

title: The Song of Uncle Sweetshare
topic_desc: This children's rhyme celebrates the figure of Uncle Sweetshare, a jovial personality who distributes candy from a workshop in the snowy wilderness. The verses portray his confections as a joyous winter treat superior to toys, crafted with a magical touch beneath glowing lanterns. While the song presents a cheerful, festive narrative, its simplistic, rhythmic framing and emphasis on a remote workshop suggest local Solstheim folklore or legend rather than literal history, leaving the true nature of Uncle Sweetshare and his confections uncertain.
topic_desc_basic: A festive children's rhyme about Uncle Sweetshare, a cheerful figure who makes magical candy in a snowy, lantern-lit workshop. The verses celebrate his sweet confections as a wonderful winter treat, though the song's fanciful tone marks it as local folklore rather than reliable fact.

title: 2920, Evening Star
topic_desc: The final volume of Carlovac Townway's historical series dramatizes the close of the First Era. It depicts Almalexia's recovery and Vivec's departure to secure a truce with Emperor Reman III. Instead, the Akaviri Potentate Versidue-Shaie orchestrates the Emperor's assassination by the Morag Tong agent Corda, then claims regency. Vivec signs the treaty with the Potentate, while the Night Mother dispatches Corda into exile. The narrative concludes with Sotha Sil detecting a catastrophic mechanical anomaly, marking the dawn of the Second Era. Townway's account intertwines Tribunal diplomacy, Morag Tong operations, and Akaviri political maneuvering, presenting a dramatic but potentially embellished chronicle of the era's transition.
topic_desc_basic: The final volume of Carlovac Townway's historical series covers the dramatic end of the First Era. It chronicles Vivec's truce negotiations, the Morag Tong's assassination of Emperor Reman III, and the Akaviri Potentate Versidue-Shaie's rise to power, marking the start of the Second Era.

title: 2920, First Seed
topic_desc: The third volume of Carlovac Townway's historical series covering the final year of the First Era. This installment chronicles events of the month First Seed, focusing on the Four Score War between the Second Empire and Morrowind. It depicts Emperor Reman III's paranoia and reliance on Potentate Versidue-Shaie, Vivec's tactical ingenuity at the Battle of Bodrum, and the devastating Imperial defeat. Townway's narrative dramatizes Vivec's stratagem—flooding the field and trapping Imperial forces in a riverine net of wooden spears—while also following the Breton spy Cassyr Whitley and the deserter Miramor. As a historical novel, it blends reported fact with speculative dialogue and dramatization.
topic_desc_basic: The third volume of Carlovac Townway's series dramatizing the final year of the First Era. It covers the month First Seed, depicting Vivec's tactical victory over Imperial forces at the Battle of Bodrum during the Four Score War, alongside Emperor Reman III's growing paranoia and the machinations of Potentate Versidue-Shaie.

title: 2920, FrostFall
topic_desc: Volume ten of Carlovac Townway's historical fiction series 2920, The Last Year of the First Era, covering Frostfall. The narrative follows the Dunmer witch Turala's conjuration training at the Skeffington Coven in Phrygias, the disgraced spy Cassyr Whitley's public humiliation in Dwynnen after Vivec ridicules his failed intelligence, and the arrival of the Redguard priestess Corda at the Imperial Palace. Townway presents a dramatized, novelistic account of these events; the dialogue and private motivations depicted are literary invention rather than verified historical record. The work is widely valued as a conjuration instructional text.
topic_desc_basic: Volume ten of Carlovac Townway's dramatic series 2920, covering Frostfall of the First Era's final year. It depicts the Dunmer witch Turala's conjuration training, the disgraced spy Cassyr Whitley's humiliation after Vivec mocks his failures, and court intrigue in the Imperial City. Townway's novelistic dialogue and private scenes are literary invention rather than strict history. The book is commonly studied as a conjuration text.

title: 2920, Hearth Fire
topic_desc: The ninth volume of Carlovac Townway's historical series 2920, The Last Year of the First Era, covering late summer events. The narrative follows Empress Tavia's suicide at Castle Giovese after learning of her son's death, and Emperor Reman III's fearful seclusion and subsequent order for Lady Rijja's execution at the Potentate Versidue-Shaie's urging. In High Rock, the Dunmer Turala and the spy Cassyr escape an Orc hunting party near Phrygias, finding refuge with the Skeffington Coven. The witch Mynista demonstrates conjuration as a practice of communing with spirits rather than scholarly study, destroying the Orcs through spiritual intervention. Townway's account blends court intrigue with regional folk practices, though his dramatized dialogue and intimate details invite questions about his sources.
topic_desc_basic: The ninth volume of Carlovac Townway's series on the final year of the First Era. It recounts Empress Tavia's suicide, Emperor Reman III ordering Lady Rijja's execution, and the Dunmer Turala finding refuge with the Skeffington Coven of witches in High Rock after their conjured spirits save her from Orcs.

title: 2920, Last Seed
topic_desc: Book Eight of Carlovac Townway's historical series covering the final year of the First Era, this volume chronicles the final days of Last Seed. It depicts the peace negotiations at Ald Lambasi between the Tribunal—Vivec, Almalexia, and Sotha Sil—and Prince Juilek Cyrodiil, who carries his father's imperial seal after the Emperor suffers an injury. The treaty formally ends eighty years of war between Morrowind and the Cyrodiil Empire. A parallel narrative follows Cassyr Whitley, a Dunmer sympathizer, encountering the exiled Turala in Cyrodiil. The volume concludes with Prince Juilek's assassination at Dorsza Pass in Black Marsh by the mercenary Miramor, who mistakes him for the Emperor. As a dramatic historical account by a single author, the work blends documented events with novelistic dialogue and scene-building whose accuracy cannot be independently verified.
topic_desc_basic: The eighth volume of Carlovac Townway's series on the last year of the First Era. It recounts the peace treaty signed at Ald Lambasi ending the Four Score War between Morrowind and the Empire, and the subsequent assassination of Prince Juilek in Black Marsh. The narrative blends historical events with dramatic fiction.
aliases: 2920 The Last Year of the First Era Book 8

title: 2920, MidYear
topic_desc: Volume six of Carlovac Townway's historical series covering the final year of the First Era. This installment chronicles Mid Year 2920, depicting the Imperial capture of the fortress Ald Marak through a stratagem: Prince Juilek's heavy infantry crosses Lake Coronati underwater using Alteration magic, bypassing Vivec's defensive preparations. The narrative also portrays Potentate Versidue-Shaie falsely claiming credit for the tactic before Emperor Reman III, and concludes with Juilek and Vivec negotiating truce terms. Townway presents the events as dramatic historical fiction, characterizing Vivec as fallible and the Potentate as duplicitous, though the reliability of specific dialogues and motives remains uncertain.
topic_desc_basic: Volume six of Carlovac Townway's historical series about the First Era's final year. It recounts the Imperial capture of Ald Marak, where Prince Juilek's heavily armored army crosses Lake Coronati using water-breathing magic to bypass Vivec's defenses, and depicts subsequent truce negotiations. Townway's dramatic account portrays Vivec as fallible and the Potentate Versidue-Shaie as deceitful.

title: 2920, Morning Star
topic_desc: The opening volume of Carlovac Townway's historical fiction series chronicling the final year of the First Era. This installment covers January 2920 through intersecting plotlines in Morrowind, Black Marsh, and Cyrodiil. Almalexia experiences a prophetic vision warning of Morrowind's defeat unless Sotha Sil returns from Artaeum. In Gideon, the imprisoned Empress Tavia conspires against Emperor Reman III with her Kothringi guard Zuuk. At the Imperial City, Prince Juilek defeats the Akaviri Potentate's son Savirien-Chorak in an arena duel, validating Cyrodiilic heavy armor over Akaviri blade philosophy. The narrative also hints at the Duke of Mournhold's affair with Turala. Townway's dramatized account blends verifiable historical figures with imagined private dialogue, making its precise reliability uncertain.
topic_desc_basic: The first volume of Carlovac Townway's famous historical fiction series depicting the First Era's final year. Set in Morning Star of 2920, it follows Almalexia's prophetic warning, Empress Tavia's imprisonment, and a notable arena duel between Prince Juilek and an Akaviri nobleman. As a dramatized chronicle, it imagines private conversations between real historical figures.
aliases: 2920 Last Year of the First Era

title: 2920, Rain's Hand
topic_desc: Volume four of Carlovac Townway's historical fiction series covering the final year of the First Era. This installment depicts Sotha Sil negotiating with eight prominent Daedra Princes in Coldharbour to restrict direct Daedric intervention following the destruction of Gilverdale, though the terms exchanged remain undisclosed. On Artaeum, Sotha Sil instructs Psijic initiates in fire resistance charms before Almalexia arrives with visions of Morrowind's defeat in the Eighty Years' War, prompting his departure. Master Iachesis responds by prophesying Artaeum's imminent disappearance from the sea. Meanwhile, in the Imperial City, Prince Juilek recovers from suspected poisoning and prepares to lead the vanguard against Morrowind, reflecting the era's pervasive intrigue.
topic_desc_basic: The fourth volume of Carlovac Townway's series on the First Era's final year. It chronicles Sotha Sil's compact with the Daedra Princes to limit direct intervention in Tamriel, his instruction of Psijic initiates on Artaeum, and his departure with Almalexia following her visions of Morrowind's defeat. It also portrays Prince Juilek's recovery from poisoning in the Imperial City.

title: 2920, Second Seed
topic_desc: The fifth volume of Carlovac Townway's historical series chronicling the final year of the First Era. Set during Second Seed 2920, it depicts Potentate Versidue-Shaie manipulating Emperor Reman III's paranoia regarding a poisoner named Catchica, secretly directing the plot from within. The narrative follows the framing of the Emperor's consort Rijja, the Empress Tavia and her Kothringi agent Zuuk hiring the assassin Miramor in Gideon, and the exiled Dunmer Turala giving birth in the Cyrodiilic wilderness with an Ayleid's aid. The account presents Versidue-Shaie's speechcraft as a central theme while dramatizing the conspiracy's scope, though its precise reliability remains uncertain.
topic_desc_basic: The fifth volume of Carlovac Townway's series on the final year of the First Era. It chronicles events of Second Seed 2920, depicting Potentate Versidue-Shaie's manipulation of Emperor Reman III, the framing of his consort Rijja, and the Empress Tavia's secret assassination plot. It also follows the exiled Turala giving birth in the Cyrodiilic wilderness.
aliases: 2920 Last Year of the First Era Second Seed

title: 2920, Sun's Dawn
topic_desc: The second volume of Carlovac Townway's historical series 2920, The Last Year of the First Era, covering events during the month of Sun's Dawn. The narrative follows several threads: Sotha Sil instructing Psijic initiates on Mysticism and the layered nature of truth; Emperor Reman III's paranoia regarding spies and the Morrowind war; Turala's expulsion from House Redoran after bearing the Duke of Indoril's child; and King Dro'Zel of Senchal descending into madness and summoning the Daedra Molag Bal to destroy the Valenwood settlement of Gilverdale. Almalexia later arrives at the ruins of Gilverdale, bearing witness to the devastation. As a dramatized chronicle, the work blends historical figures with literary speculation and unreliable narration.
topic_desc_basic: The second volume of Carlovac Townway's dramatized chronicle 2920, The Last Year of the First Era. It recounts Sun's Dawn events including Sotha Sil's Psijic lessons, Emperor Reman III's paranoia, Turala's expulsion from House Redoran, and King Dro'Zel's mad summoning of Molag Bal that destroys the Valenwood settlement of Gilverdale.
aliases: 2920 The Last Year of the First Era v2

title: 2920, Sun's Dusk
topic_desc: Volume eleven of Carlovac Townway's historical fiction series covering the final year of the First Era. This installment chronicles several pivotal events of Sun's Dusk 2920: the Night Mother accepting a contract on Emperor Reman III from the Kothringi Lord Zuuk, the failed assassination of the Emperor at Bodrum by the overconfident assassin Miramor, and the devastating attack on Mournhold by Mehrunes Dagon. The narrative culminates in the fierce battle between the Daedric Prince and the Tribunal, resulting in Dagon's banishment but leaving Almalexia gravely wounded. Townway presents these events through a dramatized, novelistic lens, blending documented history with unverified dialogue and internal motivations, making the work an unreliable but detailed account of the era's end.
topic_desc_basic: Volume eleven of Carlovac Townway's historical series on the First Era's final year. It dramatizes the Night Mother's contract on Emperor Reman III, a failed assassination at Bodrum, and Mehrunes Dagon's devastating attack on Mournhold. The Tribunal battles and banishes the Daedric Prince, though Almalexia suffers severe wounds. Townway's account blends historical events with unverified dramatization.
aliases: 2920 The Last Year of the First Era v11

title: 2920, Sun's Height
topic_desc: The seventh volume of Carlovac Townway's historical fiction series 2920, The Last Year of the First Era, covering the month of Sun's Height. It depicts Emperor Reman III musing on the imprisoned Rijja's motives before she gouges out his eye, learning of a fragile peace with Morrowind. When Imperial forces seize the Black Gate in violation of the truce, the Tribunal convenes in Balmora. Duke of Mournhold contracts the Morag Tong to assassinate the Emperor, but Sotha Sil intercepts and destroys the payment vessel on the Inner Sea to avert the killing. Townway dramatizes these events with dialogue and intimate detail; the work remains a popular but unverified narrative of the era's end.
topic_desc_basic: Volume seven of Carlovac Townway's popular historical fiction 2920, covering Sun's Height of the First Era's final year. It narrates Reman III losing an eye to the imprisoned Rijja, the Imperial breach of a Morrowind truce, and Sotha Sil destroying a ship bearing the Duke of Mournhold's payment to the Morag Tong to prevent the Emperor's assassination.

title: A Dance in Fire, Chapter 1
topic_desc: A Dance in Fire, Chapter 1 is a work of popular fiction by Waughin Jarth, dated 7 Frost Fall, 3E 397. It follows Decumus Scotti, a complacent senior clerk dismissed from the Atrius Building Commission in the Imperial City due to competition from Lord Vanech's rival agency. Facing professional ruin, Scotti accepts an invitation from Liodes Jurus, a disgraced former colleague, to pursue reconstruction contracts in Valenwood following the recent Bosmer-Khajiit war. Scotti joins a caravan southeast, purchasing a wagonload of timber at Jurus's request. A fellow traveler, the poet and Bosmer-literature translator Gryf Mallon, discusses the Mnoriad Pley Bar and its relevance to the Green Pact. Upon camping at the Valenwood border, the caravan is raided by Cathay-raht, agile Khajiiti raiders who plunder supplies before retreating into the forest. The narrative is satirical adventure fiction, not historical record, though it references real Imperial institutions and provincial tensions.
topic_desc_basic: A work of fiction by Waughin Jarth, dated 3E 397, chronicling the dismissal of clerk Decumus Scotti from the Atrius Building Commission in the Imperial City and his subsequent journey to Valenwood seeking reconstruction contracts after the Bosmer-Khajiit war. The caravan is raided by Cathay-raht near the Valenwood border. It is satirical adventure fiction, not historical record.
aliases: A Dance In Fire Chapter I

title: A Dance in Fire, Chapter 2
topic_desc: The second installment of Waughin Jarth's serial follows the Cyrodiilic clerk Decumus Scotti as he journeys into Valenwood following a devastating Cathay-Raht raid on his caravan. Hiring Bosmer escorts, Scotti endures an arduous trek through dense jungle before arriving at Falinesti, the legendary walking graht-oak city. There, he navigates the vertical metropolis via vine-operated lifts, partakes in a raucous Morndas revelry where he consumes jagga, and awakens to a near-fatal attack by giant insects. The narrative blends travelogue with adventure, offering an outsider's vivid perspective on Bosmeri culture and the perilous reality of Valenwood's so-called peacetime.
topic_desc_basic: Waughin Jarth's serial follows the clerk Decumus Scotti as he travels through Valenwood after a Khajiiti raid on his caravan. He endures a grueling jungle trek, arrives at the walking graht-oak city of Falinesti, and survives a raucous revelry and a dangerous insect attack. The tale provides a vivid outsider's view of Bosmeri life.
aliases: A Dance in Fire Chapter Two

title: A Dance in Fire, Chapter 3
topic_desc: The third chapter of Waughin Jarth's serial fiction follows Decumus Scotti, a former clerk of the Atrius Building Commission, as he travels through Valenwood seeking his colleague Liodes Jurus. Departing the tree city of Falinesti aboard a smuggler's sloop crewed by a retired Bosmeri pirate, Scotti sails downriver toward the border village of Athay, intending to negotiate reconstruction contracts following the recent Bosmer-Khajiit war. Upon arrival, they discover Khajiiti soldiers torching the settlement. Flaming arrows ignite the ship's cargo, forcing both overboard into the Xylo River. Scotti swims past burning villages, evades predatory Senche-Tigers on the bank, and loses the inebriated captain to the current before reaching a rocky island where Bosmer refugees shelter. The narrative blends dark comedy with vivid depictions of Valenwood's geography and the brutal realities of border conflict, rendered through the perspective of an increasingly hardened Cyrodiilic bureaucrat.
topic_desc_basic: A chapter of Waughin Jarth's serial following clerk Decumus Scotti through Valenwood. Seeking his colleague in the river village of Athay, Scotti travels aboard a smuggler's sloop only to find Khajiiti soldiers burning the settlement. Shipwrecked, he swims downriver past burning villages and predatory cats before reaching Bosmer refugees on a rocky island. The tale blends dark comedy with border-war realism.

title: A Dance in Fire, Chapter 4
topic_desc: The fourth installment of Waughin Jarth's adventure serial follows Cyrodilic clerk Decumus Scotti as he flees through the Valenwood jungle with Bosmeri refugees, reaching the village of Vindisi. There, the Bosmer enter a forbidden temple to invoke an ancient defense while Scotti camps with foreign outsiders. When Khajiit warriors attack, Scotti and a rival clerk climb into the canopy. The Bosmeri ritual unleashes the Wild Hunt—a flood of monstrous, uncontrollable transformations that slaughter Khajiit and foreigners indiscriminately. Jarth's sensationalized account portrays the Hunt as a terrifying, indiscriminate force, reflecting Imperial anxieties about Bosmeri powers and the brutal reality of the Valenwood–Elsweyr conflict.
topic_desc_basic: A chapter of Waughin Jarth's adventure serial chronicling Cyrodilic clerk Decumus Scotti's experiences in Valenwood. After reaching the village of Vindisi, Scotti witnesses the Bosmer invoke the Wild Hunt, a terrifying ritual transformation that slaughters Khajiit attackers and foreign bystanders alike.

title: A Dance in Fire, Chapter 5
topic_desc: The fifth installment of Waughin Jarth's serial follows the Cyrodilic clerk Decumus Scotti as he struggles through the war-ravaged Valenwood jungle. Tormented by mimicking flying creatures that parrot his own words, Scotti survives a mudslide and discovers a destroyed fishing village, evidence of the Khajiiti incursion. There, he fashions a bow from salvaged bone and cord, recalling the proper stance and form of Falinesti archers to finally shoot one of the pests for food. Rescued by the translator Gryf Mallon, Scotti learns that Valenwood is besieged on all sides and travels to Silvenar, where Mallon explains that the Silvenar is both a person and a place serving as the closest thing to a Bosmeri leader. The narrative blends adventure with observations on archery technique and the region's desperate wartime politics.
topic_desc_basic: The fifth chapter of Waughin Jarth's adventure serial chronicling the Cyrodilic clerk Decumus Scotti's ordeal in Valenwood. Lost in the war-torn jungle, Scotti survives mimicking creatures and a mudslide, uses salvaged bone and cord to fashion a bow for hunting, and gains passage to Silvenar while learning of the province's dire military situation.

title: A Dance in Fire, Chapter 6
topic_desc: The sixth installment of Waughin Jarth's serial A Dance in Fire follows Imperial clerk Decumus Scotti reuniting with his former colleague Liodes Jurus in the city of Silvenar. Jurus and a Bosmer associate, Basth, explain the Silvenar's unique nature as a physical and emotional embodiment of the Bosmer people, whose current aspect reflects Valenwood's wartime desperation. Instructed to project benevolent disinterest rather than eagerness, Scotti enters the bizarre floral palace alone. Facing the unremarkable yet uncanny Silvenar, Scotti draws upon his observations of the Bosmer to navigate the audience, applying mercantile principles of angle and image.
topic_desc_basic: The sixth chapter of Waughin Jarth's serial A Dance in Fire. Imperial clerk Decumus Scotti reunites with his colleague Liodes Jurus in Silvenar, where they scheme to secure building contracts from the Silvenar, the strange physical embodiment of the Bosmer people's collective will.
aliases: Waughin Jarth A Dance in Fire

title: A Dance in Fire, Chapter 7
topic_desc: The final chapter of Waughin Jarth's serial, set in 3E 397. Disgraced clerk Decumus Scotti attends a Silvenar banquet, where the potent Bosmeri beverage Rotmeth loosens his tongue regarding his tenuous Imperial authority. Returning to the Imperial City, he exploits rival Building Commissions for profit while Valenwood suffers border wars. The narrative darkly satirizes mercantile opportunism, culminating when the Silvenar's gift of a delicacy called Unthrappa implies a gruesome adherence to the Bosmeri Meat Mandate.
topic_desc_basic: The final chapter of Waughin Jarth's serial follows clerk Decumus Scotti after securing Valenwood rebuilding contracts. Intoxicated on Rotmeth at a Silvenar banquet, he boastfully reveals his tenuous authority. Returning to the Imperial City, he profits from rival commissions while Valenwood suffers wars, until a gruesome gift implies the Bosmeri Meat Mandate's darker aspects.

title: A Game at Dinner
topic_desc: A Game at Dinner purports to be a letter from a spy in Prince Hlaalu Helseth's court to an address styled Dark Liege Dhaunayne. The publisher Nerris Gan relates that the letter circulated in the Vvardenfell Ashlands before reaching Helseth's palace near Almalexia, where the Prince and Queen Barenziah had it privately printed and distributed rather than suppressing it. House Dres has publicly denounced the work, and no one named Dhaunayne has been officially linked to that house. The letter itself recounts a dinner at which Helseth claims to have poisoned his advisors' cups and cutlery, offering an antidote only to those who confess disloyalty. The narrator, a Dres informant, describes alchemical ingredients including bittergreen and wickwheat, and the scene serves as a study of paranoia, political ambition, and poison craft. Whether the account is factual or imaginative remains officially unconfirmed.
topic_desc_basic: A widely circulated letter by an anonymous spy describing a dinner at Prince Hlaalu Helseth's court, where the Prince claims to have poisoned his own advisors to expose disloyalty. Published with the apparent blessing of Helseth and Barenziah, its authenticity remains unconfirmed. House Dres denies any connection to the addressee.

title: A Hypothetical Treachery
topic_desc: A one-act play by Anthil Morvir exploring the ruthless pragmatism of adventuring mages. Set in Valenwood's Eldengrove, four treasure-seekers recover the Ebony Mail but find themselves drained of magicka. When a ghost attacks, the Dark Elf Inzoliah levitates to safety, sacrificing her Argonian and Cyrodiil companions and forcing the High Elf Malvasian to expend his remaining power. The two survivors then engage in a deadly intellectual exercise, hypothetically discussing how they would betray each other for the sole healing potion and the artifact. Upon escaping, they immediately enact their treacherous scenarios. Inzoliah prevails using a slow-draining leech spell, leaving Malvasian to die at the hands of bandits while she claims the reward.
topic_desc_basic: A one-act play by Anthil Morvir depicting two battlemages who survive a Valenwood dungeon with a valuable artifact. The mages engage in a hypothetical discussion about betraying each other for the treasure and a single healing potion, only to immediately enact their treacherous scenarios upon escaping, demonstrating the ruthless pragmatism of their craft.

title: Azura and the Box
topic_desc: Part XI of the fictionalized series Ancient Tales of the Dwemer, attributed to Marobar Sul (a pseudonym of Gor Felim). It recounts the aged Dwemer sage Nchylbar testing divine omniscience by having a Chimer priest summon Azura and asking her to identify the contents of a box. Azura declares a red flower inside, but Nchylbar reveals the box is empty, seemingly proving divine fallibility through sleight of hand. The publisher's note highlights significant variant traditions: the Dunmer version depicts Azura recognizing the trick and cursing the skeptics, while older Aldmeris translations describe a different illusion entirely. The work serves as propaganda celebrating Dwemer skepticism, though the note suggests such impiety may explain the dwarven disappearance.
topic_desc_basic: A fictional tale from the Ancient Tales of the Dwemer series. It tells of the sage Nchylbar who tricked Azura into falsely identifying the contents of an empty box to test divine omniscience. The publisher notes that Dunmer and Aldmeris versions differ significantly, with the Dunmer account claiming Azura saw through the trick and cursed the skeptics.
aliases: Ancient Tales of the Dwemer Part XI

title: Bone, Part One
topic_desc: A tavern tale by Tavi Dromio framing a philosophical debate among three patrons—Garaz, Xiomara, and Hallgerd—on the origins of great inventions: happenstance, diligence, or extraordinary need. Hallgerd champions the latter with an acknowledged fiction about the noble Arslic Oan, whose remote stronghold is besieged by cannibalistic Nords after the water supply is poisoned. Desperate for water, Oan forces his armorer Gorkith to craft progressively better armor for slave water-bearers. Heavy metal armor proves too cumbersome, and lighter leather proves too flimsy, so Gorkith fashions the first bonemold from the available corpses, yielding armor of intermediate weight and protection. The tale explicitly frames itself as unreliable legend, and its continuation is promised in a second volume.
topic_desc_basic: A tavern tale by Tavi Dromio in which the patron Hallgerd tells a plainly fictional story to argue that necessity drives invention. In it, the noble Arslic Oan and his armorer Gorkith create the first bonemold armor to survive a siege by cannibalistic Nords after metal and leather armors both fail. A continuation follows in a second volume.

title: Bone, Part Two
topic_desc: A macabre tale by Tavi Dromio, presented as a tavern yarn narrated by Hallgerd. It continues the legend of bonemold armor's invention during a Nord siege. After exhausting livestock bones, the lord Arslic Oan implicitly orders his armorer Gorkith to use the bones of dead slaves for new suits. The slaves wearing this armor fare better against the cannibal Nords, but the stolen bones exact a supernatural vengeance. Boneless, gelatinous corpses of the enslaved rise through the stronghold walls, demanding their bones back, and ultimately leave Arslic Oan folded bonelessly alongside his murdered armorer. The narrative functions as an unreliable, gruesome ghost story explaining bonemold's origins while offering practical observations on medium armor mobility and reinforcement points.
topic_desc_basic: A gruesome tavern tale by Tavi Dromio about the invention of bonemold armor. Besieged by cannibal Nords, a lord forces his armorer to craft new suits from the bones of dead slaves. The stolen bones eventually exact a supernatural revenge, with boneless corpses rising to destroy the lord and his armorer.

title: Breathing Water
topic_desc: Breathing Water is a treatise on Alteration magic by Haliel Myrm, framed as a cautionary narrative. The sorceress Seryne Relas instructs an unnamed smuggler in water breathing, emphasizing that Alteration requires understanding possibilities and breaking the rules of the cosmos, not merely following rote practice. She warns that desire alone cannot sustain a spell against reality's pressure. Her pupil ignores this final lesson, using his skill to loot a sunken vessel; his concentration breaks, and he drowns clutching unused water-breathing potions. The work illustrates Alteration's philosophy and its perils through unreliable narration and dark irony.
topic_desc_basic: Breathing Water by Haliel Myrm uses a cautionary tale to explain Alteration magic. A sorceress teaches a smuggler to breathe water by embracing impossible possibilities, but warns that reality will always overcome mere desire. Ignoring her, he drowns while looting a wreck, holding unused potions.

title: Chance's Folly
topic_desc: Zylmoc Golge's cautionary tale recounts the Balmoran burglar Minevah Iolos, known as Chance, who recruits a mad Breton warrior, Ulstyr Moresby, to plunder the Heran Ancestral Tomb. Ulstyr's seemingly nonsensical ramblings—advising chitin armor, a fire-enchanted blade, and propping a rock—prove prophetic, suggesting Daedric Prince Sheogorath speaks through the insane. Interpreting his mention of her stolen vitality-draining ring as a threat, Chance plots to betray Ulstyr once they secure the treasure. Instead, she is trapped inside the vault by an illusionary door that becomes a solid wall, realizing too late that Ulstyr's prophecies foretold her doom. She dies imprisoned, hearing Sheogorath's laughter, while Ulstyr returns two months later to prop the door open with a rock and claim the gold. The narrative serves as a moralistic warning against treachery, implying divine retribution for the faithless.
topic_desc_basic: A cautionary tale by Zylmoc Golge about the Balmoran thief Minevah Iolos, called Chance. She partners with a mad Breton to plunder the Heran Ancestral Tomb, intending to betray him. Instead, his seemingly nonsensical prophecies come true, and she becomes trapped within the vault, dying while hearing the laughter of Sheogorath.

title: Charwich-Koniinge, Volume 1
topic_desc: The first letter in the Charwich-Koniinge correspondence, written by Charwich from Kambria, High Rock, in 3E 411. The author recounts his investigation into Hadwaf Neithwyr, a figure connected to both a local plague and the Daedric artifact Azura's Star. Charwich traces Neithwyr to a patron named Baliasir, ultimately confronting a lycanthropic cemetery caretaker in Grimtry Garden. Through unarmored combat, Charwich survives until dawn, learning that Neithwyr remains in Morrowind and that Baliasir currently frequents Queen Elysana's court in Wayrest. The narrative serves as Charwich's personal account of his search, blending folklore with an unreliable narrator's self-aggrandizing tale of survival.
topic_desc_basic: A letter from Charwich to Koniinge, dated 3E 411, documenting Charwich's search for Azura's Star in High Rock. He investigates the mysterious Hadwaf Neithwyr and his patron Baliasir, survives a night fighting a werewolf unarmored, and learns his quarry may be found in Morrowind and Wayrest.

title: Charwich-Koniinge, Volume 2
topic_desc: The second letter in the Charwich-Koniinge correspondence, dated 3 Last Seed 3E 411 and sent from Tel Aruhn by Koniinge to his partner Charwich. The two are pursuing Hadwaf Neithwyr, who reportedly summoned Azura and received Azura's Star. Koniinge recounts contacting a Dissident Priest named Minerath, who confirmed Neithwyr performed the ceremony in Morrowind and intended to return to High Rock. After receiving Charwich's report from Grimtry Garden, Koniinge confronted Minerath again, seeking information about a mysterious patron named Baliasir. The priest denied knowing the name but mentioned a woman present at the ceremony, identified as Neithwyr's sister Peryra. Koniinge then murdered Minerath. The letter is a first-person account by an unreliable narrator who candidly describes assassination as a routine method, making all his claims suspect. No independent corroboration of Neithwyr, Baliasir, or the Star's location is established.
topic_desc_basic: The second of the Charwich-Koniinge letters, written in 3E 411 by Koniinge from Tel Aruhn. It reports his search for Hadwaf Neithwyr, who allegedly received Azura's Star from the Daedra Prince. Koniinge describes contacting and then killing a Dissident Priest who knew Neithwyr. The narrator's candid admission of murder marks the letter as an unreliable account of the hunt for the artifact.

title: Charwich-Koniinge, Volume 3
topic_desc: The third letter in the Charwich-Koniinge correspondence, dated 13 Last Seed 3E 411 and written from Wayrest. Charwich addresses his colleague Koniinge while dying from a daedric assault. He recounts infiltrating Queen Elysana's court through Lady Moorling's connections to approach a courtier named Baliasir, whom he believed possessed Azura's Star. After engaging Baliasir on the school of mysticism, Charwich was invited to Klythic's Cairn, where he attempted to seize the Star by force. Baliasir revealed himself as a colossal daedra, effortlessly reclaimed the artifact, and struck Charwich with a lingering fatal spell. Charwich escaped only by casting Recall, teleporting to Moorling's doorstep. The letter deteriorates into illegible fragments as death overtakes the writer. The account is inherently unreliable: it is a desperate, uncorroborated first-person narrative from a dying man, and whether Charwich actually perished remains uncertain given the existence of a fourth volume.
topic_desc_basic: The third Charwich-Koniinge letter, written in 3E 411 from Wayrest. Charwich, dying from a daedric wound, recounts his attempt to seize Azura's Star from a courtier named Baliasir, who revealed himself as a daedra lord and struck Charwich with a fatal spell. Charwich escaped via Recall magic but expected death before healers arrived. The narrative is an uncorroborated, desperate first-person account.

title: Charwich-Koniinge, Volume 4
topic_desc: The final letter in the Charwich-Koniinge correspondence, dated 3E 412, written by the murdered estate banker Syrix Goinithi under duress from the assassin Koniinge. Addressed to prospective buyer Lord Gemyn, the document lures him into a trapped villa while recounting Koniinge's violent investigation into his former partner Charwich. The narrative reveals that Charwich fabricated tales of a Daedra lord named Baliasir and his own death to abandon Koniinge and keep Azura's Star, partnering with Lady Moorling instead. After the Star inevitably vanished, the couple separated. Koniinge tracked Moorling down, strangled her for Charwich's location, and now awaits his betrayer in the Summurset estate. The entire account presents an unreliable, darkly ironic narration from a dead man forced to chronicle his own killer's revenge.
topic_desc_basic: The concluding letter of the Charwich-Koniinge correspondence, dated 3E 412. Written by a murdered estate banker under duress from the assassin Koniinge, it recounts how Charwich betrayed Koniinge to keep Azura's Star and faked his own death. After strangling Charwich's new partner for his location, Koniinge now waits to ambush his former friend in a trapped Summurset Isle villa.

title: Cherim's Heart of Anequina
topic_desc: Volume eighteen of the 'Interviews With Tapestrists' series by Livillus Perus, a professor at the Imperial University, profiles the Khajiiti master weaver Cherim, whose tapestries have been celebrated across the Empire for some thirty years. The interview focuses on one of Cherim's earliest masterpieces, 'The Heart of Anequina,' depicting a pivotal battle of the Five Year War between Elsweyr and Valenwood (3E 394–399). Cherim served as a Khajiiti foot soldier in the conflict and attributes Elsweyr's turnaround to the rejection of Nord-advised heavy plate armor in favor of traditional medium-weight lacquered leather, which allowed greater mobility and permitted arrows to pass cleanly through rather than remain lodged. The text blends art criticism with Cherim's firsthand military commentary, and includes a self-deprecating self-portrait detail acknowledging Khajiiti stereotypes. The account is partly anecdotal and reflects the artist's personal perspective rather than a formal military history.
topic_desc_basic: A volume of the 'Interviews With Tapestrists' series by Imperial University professor Livillus Perus, profiling the renowned Khajiiti tapestry weaver Cherim. The interview discusses his early masterpiece 'The Heart of Anequina,' depicting a key battle of the Five Year War between Elsweyr and Valenwood. Cherim, who fought in the war, explains the practical advantages of traditional Khajiiti medium armor over heavy plate.

title: Death Blow of Abernanit
topic_desc: This epic poem, annotated by the sage Geocrates Varnus, recounts the Siege of Abernanit in 3E 150. Rangidil Ketil, commander of the Temple Ordinators and blessed by the Tribunal, led Ordinators and Buoyant Armigers against Dagoth Thras, a daedra-worshipper of unknown origin who claimed descent from the Sixth House and held the fortress through power granted by Mehrunes Dagon. The poem narrates how Thras, shielded by a dread blessing, exhausted Rangidil's warriors one by one in a narrow tower stairwell until Rangidil feigned defeat and asked his foe to explain his blocking technique. When Thras paused to answer, Rangidil struck the killing blow. Varnus's footnotes date the poem to roughly fifty years after the siege and identify its allegorical references. The work functions as Temple heroic legend and is valued as an instructional text on shield technique.
topic_desc_basic: A Temple epic poem with scholarly annotations by Geocrates Varnus, recounting the 3E 150 siege of Abernanit. Ordinator commander Rangidil Ketil confronted Dagoth Thras, a daedra-worshipper claiming Sixth House heritage, whose impenetrable shield exhausted all challengers until Rangidil tricked him into explaining his technique and struck the fatal blow.

title: Feyfolken I
topic_desc: The first volume of Waughin Jarth's historical fiction, presented as a lecture by the Great Sage to his students. The narrative contrasts the structured, elitist traditions of the Psijic Order with Vanus Galerion's democratization of magic through the Mages Guild. It details Galerion's early, fully automated enchanting and alchemical tools, which allowed untrained laymen to create powerful items without understanding the underlying principles, and his subsequent replacement of them with safer, skill-requiring implements. To illustrate the dangers of the original devices, the Sage recounts the tale of Thaurbad, a mute scribe in Second Era Alinor who sends his messenger to the new Guild with a fortune and a quill. The boy uses the automated Itemmaker to bind a potent daedric spirit called Feyfolken into the writing instrument, leaving the outcome unresolved at the volume's end.
topic_desc_basic: A popular instructional tale by Waughin Jarth about the early Mages Guild. It explains how founder Vanus Galerion originally created automated enchanting tools for the untrained masses, and introduces the story of a mute scribe who dangerously over-enchants a quill with a daedric spirit named Feyfolken.

title: Feyfolken II
topic_desc: Feyfolken II is the second volume of Waughin Jarth's series, framed as a conjuration lesson delivered by the Great Sage to his students Vonguldak and Taksim. The narrative follows Thaurbad Hulzik, a mute scribe of the Temple of Auri-El whose quill has been enchanted with the daedric spirit Feyfolken. The quill transforms routine Temple Bulletins into illuminated masterpieces, drawing ecstatic praise from the archpriest and parishioners, quadrupling Thaurbad's salary, and driving the hostile secretary Alfiers to resign. When inspiration fails, Feyfolken seizes full control of the writing, rendering Thaurbad a mere reader of his own work. The students deduce that Feyfolken serves Clavicus Vile. The tale is presented as entertaining fiction with pedagogical intent rather than reliable doctrine on daedric spirits.
